concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: A spanning family with redundant vectors is not a basis.

concepts.title: Linear maps · Matrix
concepts.summary: The matrix of a linear map records the coordinates of the images of basis vectors in chosen domain and codomain bases.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: The matrix of a linear map records the coordinates of the images of basis vectors in chosen domain and codomain bases.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: The columns of the standard matrix of $T(x,y)=(x+y,y)$ are $(1,0)^T$ and $(1,1)^T$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: A matrix represents a map only after the two bases and their order are fixed.

concepts.title: Linear maps · Change of basis
concepts.summary: A change-of-basis matrix converts coordinate columns between two ordered bases; an endomorphism matrix changes by similarity.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: A change-of-basis matrix converts coordinate columns between two ordered bases; an endomorphism matrix changes by similarity.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: If $P$ has the new basis vectors as old-coordinate columns, then $[T]_{new}=P^{-1}[T]_{old}P$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Conjugating by $P$ is valid for an endomorphism with the same basis change in domain and codomain.

concepts.title: Algebra · Group
concepts.summary: A group has an associative operation, an identity, and an inverse for every element.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: A group has an associative operation, an identity, and an inverse for every element.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: $(\mathbb Z,+)$ is a group with identity $0$ and inverse $-n$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: $(\mathbb N,+)$ is not a group because positive integers lack additive inverses in $\mathbb N$.

concepts.title: Algebra · Ring
concepts.summary: A ring has an abelian addition and an associative multiplication linked by distributivity.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: A ring has an abelian addition and an associative multiplication linked by distributivity.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: $\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z$ is a commutative ring.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: A ring may contain zero divisors, so cancellation under multiplication is not automatic.

concepts.title: Algebra · Field
concepts.summary: A field is a commutative ring in which every nonzero element has a multiplicative inverse.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: A field is a commutative ring in which every nonzero element has a multiplicative inverse.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: $\mathbb Q$, $\mathbb R$, and $\mathbb C$ are fields.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: $\mathbb Z$ is not a field because $2$ has no inverse in $\mathbb Z$.

concepts.title: Algebra · Morphism
concepts.summary: A morphism preserves the operations and distinguished elements of the algebraic structures involved.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: A morphism preserves the operations and distinguished elements of the algebraic structures involved.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: Evaluation $P\mapsto P(a)$ is a ring morphism from $K[x]$ to $K$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: A function between groups is not a homomorphism merely because it is bijective.

concepts.title: Permutations · Cycles
concepts.summary: Every permutation decomposes into disjoint cycles, unique up to cycle order and cyclic rotation.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: Every permutation decomposes into disjoint cycles, unique up to cycle order and cyclic rotation.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Composition order matters; permutation products are generally not commutative.

concepts.title: Permutations · Signature
concepts.summary: The signature is the homomorphism from the symmetric group to $\{\pm1\}$ that assigns $-1$ to a transposition.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: The signature is the homomorphism from the symmetric group to $\{\pm1\}$ that assigns $-1$ to a transposition.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: A $k$-cycle has signature $(-1)^{k-1}$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: The number of transpositions in a decomposition is not unique, but its parity is.

concepts.title: Determinants · Multilinear
concepts.summary: The determinant is the unique alternating multilinear function of the columns that equals $1$ on the standard basis.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: The determinant is the unique alternating multilinear function of the columns that equals $1$ on the standard basis.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: Adding a multiple of one column to another leaves the determinant unchanged.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Linearity holds in one column at a time, not under simultaneous arbitrary changes to several columns.

concepts.title: Asymptotic comparison · Big-O notation
concepts.summary: $f(x)=O(g(x))$ as $x\to a$ means that $|f(x)|\le C|g(x)|$ near $a$ for some constant $C>0$.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: $f(x)=O(g(x))$ as $x\to a$ means that $|f(x)|\le C|g(x)|$ near $a$ for some constant $C>0$.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: $\sin x=O(x)$ as $x\to0$ because $|\sin x|\le|x|$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: $f=O(g)$ does not imply $f/g\to1$; boundedness of the ratio is weaker than asymptotic equivalence.

concepts.title: Asymptotic comparison · Little-o notation
concepts.summary: $f(x)=o(g(x))$ as $x\to a$ means that $f(x)/g(x)\to0$ wherever the quotient is defined near $a$.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: $f(x)=o(g(x))$ as $x\to a$ means that $f(x)/g(x)\to0$ wherever the quotient is defined near $a$.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: $x^2=o(x)$ as $x\to0$ because $x^2/x=x\to0$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: $f=O(g)$ does not imply $f=o(g)$; for example, $x=O(x)$ but $x\ne o(x)$ as $x\to0$.

concepts.title: Asymptotic comparison · Equivalence
concepts.summary: $f\sim g$ near a point means $f/g\to1$ where the quotient is defined.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: $f\sim g$ near a point means $f/g\to1$ where the quotient is defined.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: $\sin x\sim x$ as $x\to0$ because $\sin x/x\to1$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Equivalence is not preserved by arbitrary subtraction; leading terms may cancel.

concepts.title: Asymptotic comparison · Expansion
concepts.summary: An asymptotic expansion lists successive comparison terms with a remainder smaller than the last retained scale.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: An asymptotic expansion lists successive comparison terms with a remainder smaller than the last retained scale.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Terms cannot be divided or composed without checking that the remainder remains controlled.

concepts.title: Integration · Segment
concepts.summary: The integral of a continuous function on $[a,b]$ is the signed area encoded by the limit of Riemann sums.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: The integral of a continuous function on $[a,b]$ is the signed area encoded by the limit of Riemann sums.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Changing the order of endpoints changes the sign: $\int_b^a f=-\int_a^b f$.

concepts.title: Integration · Fundamental theorem of calculus
concepts.summary: The fundamental theorem links integration and differentiation: if $F(x)=\int_a^x f(t)dt$ for continuous $f$, then $F'=f$.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: The fundamental theorem links integration and differentiation: if $F(x)=\int_a^x f(t)dt$ for continuous $f$, then $F'=f$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: The integrand's dummy variable and the upper-limit variable play different roles.

concepts.title: Integration · Substitution
concepts.summary: Substitution applies the chain rule inside an integral and transforms both the integrand and the bounds.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: Substitution applies the chain rule inside an integral and transforms both the integrand and the bounds.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: $\int_0^1 2x e^{x^2}dx=\int_0^1e^u du=e-1$ with $u=x^2$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Changing variables without changing the bounds mixes two coordinate systems.

concepts.title: Integration · Parts
concepts.summary: Integration by parts is $\int_a^b u v'=[uv]_a^b-\int_a^b u'v$.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: Integration by parts is $\int_a^b u v'=[uv]_a^b-\int_a^b u'v$.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: $\int_0^1xe^x dx=[xe^x]_0^1-\int_0^1e^x dx=1$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: The boundary term is part of the formula and cannot be omitted.

concepts.title: Summation · Summation by parts
concepts.summary: Summation by parts is the discrete product rule used to transfer a difference from one sequence to another.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: Summation by parts is the discrete product rule used to transfer a difference from one sequence to another.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Index endpoints must be derived rather than guessed; one shifted term changes the boundary.

concepts.title: Riemann sums · Sum
concepts.summary: A Riemann sum samples a function on a fine partition and converges to its integral under the theorem's hypotheses.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: A Riemann sum samples a function on a fine partition and converges to its integral under the theorem's hypotheses.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: $\frac1n\sum_{k=1}^n(k/n)^2\to\int_0^1x^2dx=1/3$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Recognizing a sum shape does not justify the limit unless the mesh and sampling match a valid Riemann-sum theorem.

concepts.title: Multiple sums · Double sums
concepts.summary: A finite double sum may be reordered by describing the same finite index set in a different order.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: A finite double sum may be reordered by describing the same finite index set in a different order.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: $\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^i a_{ij}=\sum_{j=1}^n\sum_{i=j}^n a_{ij}$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: The inner bounds must change when the order changes; copying rectangular bounds alters a triangular index set.

concepts.title: Numerical series · Basic
concepts.summary: A numerical series $\sum u_n$ converges when its partial sums converge.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: A numerical series $\sum u_n$ converges when its partial sums converge.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: The geometric series $\sum_{n\ge0}q^n$ converges to $1/(1-q)$ for $|q|<1$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: The condition $u_n\to0$ is necessary but not sufficient for series convergence.

concepts.title: Numerical series · Positive
concepts.summary: A series with nonnegative terms converges exactly when its increasing partial sums are bounded.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: A series with nonnegative terms converges exactly when its increasing partial sums are bounded.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: $\sum 1/n^2$ converges by comparison with an integral.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: A comparison must preserve inequality direction and apply from some index onward.

concepts.title: Summable families · Summable
concepts.summary: A nonnegative family is summable when the supremum of all finite subsums is finite; an absolutely summable family may then be reordered.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: A nonnegative family is summable when the supremum of all finite subsums is finite; an absolutely summable family may then be reordered.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: $(2^{-i-j})_{i,j\ge1}$ is summable because the iterated geometric sums are finite.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Conditional series cannot be treated as order-independent summable families.

concepts.title: Numerical series · Cauchy products
concepts.summary: The Cauchy product has coefficients $c_n=\sum_{k=0}^n a_kb_{n-k}$ and represents a product under suitable convergence hypotheses.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: The Cauchy product has coefficients $c_n=\sum_{k=0}^n a_kb_{n-k}$ and represents a product under suitable convergence hypotheses.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: $(\sum x^n)^2$ has coefficient $n+1$ at $x^n$ for $|x|<1$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Multiplying two conditionally convergent series requires a theorem; formal coefficient manipulation alone is insufficient.

concepts.title: Inner-product spaces · Inner products
concepts.summary: An inner product is a positive-definite symmetric or Hermitian bilinear form that defines length and angle.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: An inner product is a positive-definite symmetric or Hermitian bilinear form that defines length and angle.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: The standard real inner product is $\langle x,y\rangle=\sum_i x_iy_i$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: A bilinear form with $\langle x,x\rangle=0$ for a nonzero $x$ is not an inner product.

concepts.title: Inner-product spaces · Cauchy Schwarz
concepts.summary: Cauchy–Schwarz states $|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\|y\|$, with equality exactly for linearly dependent vectors.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: Cauchy–Schwarz states $|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\|y\|$, with equality exactly for linearly dependent vectors.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: The equality condition must be checked separately; a strict inequality is typical.

concepts.title: Inner-product spaces · Projection
concepts.summary: The orthogonal projection onto a subspace is the unique point in that subspace whose error is orthogonal to it.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: The orthogonal projection onto a subspace is the unique point in that subspace whose error is orthogonal to it.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: Projection onto $\operatorname{span}(u)$ is $\langle x,u\rangle u/\|u\|^2$ for $u\ne0$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: The displayed formula is invalid for $u=0$ and changes for a nonorthonormal basis.

concepts.title: Inner-product spaces · Gram–Schmidt orthogonalization
concepts.summary: Gram–Schmidt subtracts earlier orthogonal projections to turn an independent family into an orthonormal family with the same successive spans.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: Gram–Schmidt subtracts earlier orthogonal projections to turn an independent family into an orthonormal family with the same successive spans.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: From $(1,0)$ and $(1,1)$ it produces $(1,0)$ and $(0,1)$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: If the original family is dependent, one residual becomes zero and cannot be normalized.

concepts.title: Combinatorics · Counting
concepts.summary: Counting builds bijections or partitions so every admissible object is counted exactly once.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: Counting builds bijections or partitions so every admissible object is counted exactly once.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: There are $\binom nk$ subsets of size $k$ of an $n$-element set.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Multiplying stage counts is valid only when every first-stage choice has the stated number of continuations.

concepts.title: Combinatorics · Inclusion–exclusion
concepts.summary: Inclusion–exclusion corrects overcounting by alternating intersections.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: Inclusion–exclusion corrects overcounting by alternating intersections.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: $|A\cup B|=|A|+|B|-|A\cap B|$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Adding set sizes without subtracting overlaps counts common elements more than once.

concepts.title: Probability · Finite
concepts.summary: A finite probability assigns nonnegative masses with total $1$; event probabilities are sums of their outcome masses.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: A finite probability assigns nonnegative masses with total $1$; event probabilities are sums of their outcome masses.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Equal outcome probabilities may be assumed only when the model states symmetry or fairness.

concepts.title: Probability · Conditional probability
concepts.summary: For events $A$ and $B$ with $P(B)>0$, the conditional probability is $P(A\mid B)=P(A\cap B)/P(B)$.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: For events $A$ and $B$ with $P(B)>0$, the conditional probability is $P(A\mid B)=P(A\cap B)/P(B)$.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: For a fair die, $P(\text{even}\mid >3)=2/3$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Conditioning on an event of probability zero is not defined by this finite formula.

concepts.title: Probability · Bayes
concepts.summary: Bayes' formula reverses a condition by combining conditional probabilities with prior probabilities.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: Bayes' formula reverses a condition by combining conditional probabilities with prior probabilities.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: $P(A\mid B)=P(B\mid A)P(A)/P(B)$ when $P(B)>0$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Confusing $P(A\mid B)$ with $P(B\mid A)$ ignores the base rates.

concepts.title: Probability · Independence
concepts.summary: Events $A,B$ are independent when $P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)$.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: Events $A,B$ are independent when $P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)$.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: For two fair coin tosses, the events 'first is heads' and 'second is heads' are independent.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Disjoint nonempty events are not independent because their intersection has probability zero.

concepts.title: Random variables · Finite Law
concepts.summary: The law of a finite random variable lists each possible value and its probability, with total mass $1$.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: The law of a finite random variable lists each possible value and its probability, with total mass $1$.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: A fair die variable has $P(X=k)=1/6$ for $k=1,\ldots,6$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: A table with probabilities that are negative or do not sum to $1$ is not a probability law.

concepts.title: Random variables · Expectation
concepts.summary: $E[X]=\sum_x xP(X=x)$ is the probability-weighted average of a finite random variable.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: $E[X]=\sum_x xP(X=x)$ is the probability-weighted average of a finite random variable.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: A fair die has expectation $(1+\cdots+6)/6=7/2$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Expectation need not be a possible observed value.

concepts.title: Random variables · Variance
concepts.summary: $\operatorname{Var}(X)=E[(X-E[X])^2]=E[X^2]-E[X]^2$ measures squared dispersion.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: $\operatorname{Var}(X)=E[(X-E[X])^2]=E[X^2]-E[X]^2$ measures squared dispersion.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: A constant random variable has variance $0$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Variance is not $E[X^2]$ unless $E[X]=0$.

concepts.title: Multivariable calculus · Open
concepts.summary: A subset $U$ of $\mathbb R^2$ is open when every point $p\in U$ is the center of some open disk contained in $U$.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: A subset $U$ of $\mathbb R^2$ is open when every point $p\in U$ is the center of some open disk contained in $U$.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: The disk $U=\{(x,y):x^2+y^2<1\}$ is open because a point at distance $r<1$ from the origin has a disk of radius $(1-r)/2$ contained in $U$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: The closed disk $\{(x,y):x^2+y^2\le1\}$ is not open because no disk centered at a boundary point remains inside it.

concepts.title: Multivariable calculus · Continuity
concepts.summary: A map $f:U\subseteq\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R^m$ is continuous at $p\in U$ when $f(q)\to f(p)$ as $q\to p$ within $U$.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: A map $f:U\subseteq\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R^m$ is continuous at $p\in U$ when $f(q)\to f(p)$ as $q\to p$ within $U$.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: The polynomial map $f(x,y)=x^2+xy+y^2$ is continuous on $\mathbb R^2$ because sums and products of coordinate functions are continuous.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Existence of separate one-variable limits along horizontal and vertical lines does not by itself prove a two-variable limit.

concepts.title: Multivariable calculus · Partial derivatives
concepts.summary: The partial derivative $\partial_x f(a,b)$ is the one-variable limit $\lim_{h\to0}[f(a+h,b)-f(a,b)]/h$ when it exists; $\partial_y$ is defined analogously.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: The partial derivative $\partial_x f(a,b)$ is the one-variable limit $\lim_{h\to0}[f(a+h,b)-f(a,b)]/h$ when it exists; $\partial_y$ is defined analogously.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: For $f(x,y)=x^2+xy$, the difference quotient in the $x$ direction tends to $2x+y$, while the $y$ quotient tends to $x$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: The existence of both partial derivatives at a point does not by itself prove that the function is differentiable there.

concepts.title: Multivariable calculus · Chain rule
concepts.summary: For differentiable maps $f$ and $g$, the derivative of the composition is $D(g\circ f)(x)=Dg(f(x))\circ Df(x)$.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: For differentiable maps $f$ and $g$, the derivative of the composition is $D(g\circ f)(x)=Dg(f(x))\circ Df(x)$.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: If $h(t)=f(t,t^2)$, then $h'(t)=\partial_xf(t,t^2)+2t\,\partial_yf(t,t^2)$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: The chain rule cannot be invoked at a point where the required differentiability hypotheses have not been checked.

concepts.title: Multivariable calculus · Extrema
concepts.summary: At an interior local extremum of a differentiable function, the derivative is zero. A definite Hessian classifies a nondegenerate critical point; an indefinite Hessian gives a saddle.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: At an interior local extremum of a differentiable function, the derivative is zero. A definite Hessian classifies a nondegenerate critical point; an indefinite Hessian gives a saddle.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: For $f(x,y)=x^2+y^2$, the origin is the only critical point and the positive-definite Hessian proves a strict local minimum.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: A zero gradient is necessary at an interior differentiable extremum but is not sufficient; $f(x,y)=x^3$ has zero gradient at the origin without an extremum.

concepts.title: Algebra · Ideal
concepts.summary: An ideal is an additive subgroup closed under multiplication by arbitrary elements of the ring.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: An ideal is an additive subgroup closed under multiplication by arbitrary elements of the ring.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: $(x^2+1)$ is the principal ideal of multiples of $x^2+1$ in $\mathbb R[x]$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: A subring need not be an ideal; ideal closure uses multipliers from the whole ambient ring.

concepts.title: Algebra · Quotient
concepts.summary: In $R/I$, two elements define the same class exactly when their difference lies in $I$.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: In $R/I$, two elements define the same class exactly when their difference lies in $I$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Equality in a quotient need not be equality of the original representatives in $R$.

concepts.title: Algebra · Algebra
concepts.summary: A $K$-algebra is a ring with a compatible scalar action by the field $K$.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: A $K$-algebra is a ring with a compatible scalar action by the field $K$.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: $K[x]$ is a $K$-algebra, and evaluation at a scalar is a $K$-algebra morphism.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: A ring morphism need not preserve a specified $K$-scalar action unless it is a $K$-algebra morphism.

concepts.title: Linear maps · Stable subspaces
concepts.summary: A subspace $E$ is stable under $T$ when $T(E)\subseteq E$.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: A subspace $E$ is stable under $T$ when $T(E)\subseteq E$.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: Every eigenspace and the kernel of a polynomial in $T$ are stable under $T$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: A subspace containing one image vector is not necessarily stable under all images of its vectors.

concepts.title: Linear maps · Eigen
concepts.summary: $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue of $T$ when some nonzero $v$ satisfies $T(v)=\lambda v$.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue of $T$ when some nonzero $v$ satisfies $T(v)=\lambda v$.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: For $\operatorname{diag}(2,3)$, the coordinate axes are eigenspaces for $2$ and $3$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: The zero vector is never an eigenvector.

concepts.title: Linear maps · Characteristic polynomial
concepts.summary: The characteristic polynomial is $\chi_T(t)=\det(tI-[T])$ and is independent of basis.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: The characteristic polynomial is $\chi_T(t)=\det(tI-[T])$ and is independent of basis.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: For $\operatorname{diag}(2,3)$, $\chi_T(t)=(t-2)(t-3)$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: A root of the characteristic polynomial gives an eigenvalue only over a field containing that root.

concepts.title: Linear maps · Diagonalization
concepts.summary: An endomorphism is diagonalizable when the space has a basis of eigenvectors.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: An endomorphism is diagonalizable when the space has a basis of eigenvectors.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: A real symmetric matrix is orthogonally diagonalizable.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Having a characteristic polynomial that splits is not enough when eigenspace dimensions are too small.

concepts.title: Linear maps · Triangularization
concepts.summary: An endomorphism is triangularizable when some basis gives an upper-triangular matrix.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: An endomorphism is triangularizable when some basis gives an upper-triangular matrix.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: Over $\mathbb C$, every endomorphism of a nonzero finite-dimensional space is triangularizable.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Triangularizable does not mean diagonalizable; nonzero entries may remain above the diagonal.

concepts.title: Linear maps · Nilpotent
concepts.summary: $N$ is nilpotent when $N^k=0$ for some positive integer $k$.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: $N$ is nilpotent when $N^k=0$ for some positive integer $k$.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: A strictly upper-triangular $n\times n$ matrix satisfies $N^n=0$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: A matrix with only zero eigenvalues need not be the zero matrix.

concepts.title: Linear maps · Trace
concepts.summary: The trace is the sum of diagonal entries, is basis independent, and satisfies $\operatorname{tr}(AB)=\operatorname{tr}(BA)$.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: The trace is the sum of diagonal entries, is basis independent, and satisfies $\operatorname{tr}(AB)=\operatorname{tr}(BA)$.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: A triangular matrix has trace equal to the sum of its eigenvalues with algebraic multiplicity.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Trace is not multiplicative: generally $\operatorname{tr}(AB)\ne\operatorname{tr}(A)\operatorname{tr}(B)$.

concepts.title: Linear maps · Minimal polynomial
concepts.summary: The minimal polynomial is the monic polynomial of least positive degree that annihilates an endomorphism.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: The minimal polynomial is the monic polynomial of least positive degree that annihilates an endomorphism.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: For a diagonal matrix with distinct diagonal values $2,3$, the minimal polynomial is $(t-2)(t-3)$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: The minimal polynomial divides the characteristic polynomial but need not equal it.

concepts.title: Linear maps · Kernel decomposition
concepts.summary: If coprime polynomials $P_i$ satisfy $\prod P_i(T)=0$, the space decomposes as the direct sum of the kernels $\ker P_i(T)$.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: If coprime polynomials $P_i$ satisfy $\prod P_i(T)=0$, the space decomposes as the direct sum of the kernels $\ker P_i(T)$.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: Distinct eigenvalue factors give the direct sum of their generalized eigenspaces.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Coprimality is essential; overlapping factors do not give the same direct-sum conclusion.

concepts.title: Linear maps · Cayley–Hamilton theorem
concepts.summary: Cayley–Hamilton states that every square matrix annihilates its own characteristic polynomial.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: Cayley–Hamilton states that every square matrix annihilates its own characteristic polynomial.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: If $A^2-3A+2I=0$, powers of $A$ reduce to linear combinations of $I$ and $A$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: The theorem substitutes the matrix into its polynomial; it does not say the polynomial is the zero polynomial in its scalar variable.

concepts.title: Linear maps · Characteristic Subspace
concepts.summary: A characteristic subspace is defined intrinsically from the endomorphism, for example as a kernel or image of a polynomial in it, so it is stable under every commuting automorphism.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: A characteristic subspace is defined intrinsically from the endomorphism, for example as a kernel or image of a polynomial in it, so it is stable under every commuting automorphism.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: $\ker(T-\lambda I)^k$ is a generalized eigenspace determined by $T$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: A subspace chosen from one convenient basis need not be characteristic.

concepts.title: Euclidean spaces · Adjoint
concepts.summary: The adjoint $T^*$ is defined by $\langle Tx,y\rangle=\langle x,T^*y\rangle$ for all $x,y$.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: The adjoint $T^*$ is defined by $\langle Tx,y\rangle=\langle x,T^*y\rangle$ for all $x,y$.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: In an orthonormal real basis, the adjoint matrix is the transpose.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Taking a transpose gives the adjoint matrix only in orthonormal coordinates.

concepts.title: Euclidean spaces · Orthogonal
concepts.summary: An orthogonal matrix satisfies $Q^TQ=I$ and preserves the inner product.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: An orthogonal matrix satisfies $Q^TQ=I$ and preserves the inner product.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: A plane rotation matrix is orthogonal with determinant $1$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Columns of equal length are not enough; distinct columns must also be orthogonal.

concepts.title: Euclidean spaces · Isometry
concepts.summary: A linear isometry preserves norms, equivalently inner products in a real Euclidean space.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: A linear isometry preserves norms, equivalently inner products in a real Euclidean space.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: Reflections and rotations are linear isometries.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: A general affine isometry may include a translation and therefore need not be linear.

concepts.title: Euclidean spaces · Self-adjoint operators
concepts.summary: An endomorphism $T$ of a Euclidean space is self-adjoint when $\langle Tx,y\rangle=\langle x,Ty\rangle$ for all vectors $x,y$, equivalently $T=T^*$.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: An endomorphism $T$ of a Euclidean space is self-adjoint when $\langle Tx,y\rangle=\langle x,Ty\rangle$ for all vectors $x,y$, equivalently $T=T^*$.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: A real symmetric matrix represents a self-adjoint endomorphism in an orthonormal basis.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: A matrix that is symmetric in a nonorthonormal basis need not represent a self-adjoint map.

concepts.title: Euclidean spaces · Spectral
concepts.summary: The spectral theorem gives an orthonormal eigenbasis for a self-adjoint endomorphism of a finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: The spectral theorem gives an orthonormal eigenbasis for a self-adjoint endomorphism of a finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: Every real symmetric matrix is orthogonally diagonalizable with real eigenvalues.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: The theorem does not apply to an arbitrary real matrix.

concepts.title: Euclidean spaces · Positive
concepts.summary: A self-adjoint operator is positive when $\langle Tx,x\rangle\ge0$ for every $x$.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: A self-adjoint operator is positive when $\langle Tx,x\rangle\ge0$ for every $x$.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: A diagonal self-adjoint matrix is positive exactly when all diagonal eigenvalues are nonnegative.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Positive determinant does not imply a matrix is positive.

concepts.title: Normed vector spaces · Definition
concepts.summary: A norm is nonnegative, vanishes only at zero, is absolutely homogeneous, and satisfies the triangle inequality.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: A norm is nonnegative, vanishes only at zero, is absolutely homogeneous, and satisfies the triangle inequality.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: $\|x\|_1=\sum_i|x_i|$ is a norm on $\mathbb R^n$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: $|x_1|$ is not a norm on $\mathbb R^2$ because it vanishes on nonzero vectors with first coordinate zero.

concepts.title: Normed vector spaces · Standard
concepts.summary: Standard finite-dimensional norms include $\|x\|_1$, $\|x\|_2$, and $\|x\|_\infty$.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: Standard finite-dimensional norms include $\|x\|_1$, $\|x\|_2$, and $\|x\|_\infty$.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: For $x=(1,-2)$, the three norms are $3$, $\sqrt5$, and $2$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Numerical norm values depend on the chosen norm even though finite-dimensional convergence does not.

concepts.title: Normed vector spaces · Operator
concepts.summary: The operator norm is $\|T\|=\sup_{\|x\|=1}\|Tx\|$ and is the smallest constant with $\|Tx\|\le\|T\|\|x\|$.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: The operator norm is $\|T\|=\sup_{\|x\|=1}\|Tx\|$ and is the smallest constant with $\|Tx\|\le\|T\|\|x\|$.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: For a diagonal map in Euclidean norm, the operator norm is the largest absolute diagonal entry.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: The operator norm is not generally the sum of absolute matrix entries.

concepts.title: Topology · Sequence
concepts.summary: In a metric space, $x_n\to x$ when the distance $d(x_n,x)$ tends to zero.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: In a metric space, $x_n\to x$ when the distance $d(x_n,x)$ tends to zero.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: Coordinatewise convergence in $\mathbb R^n$ is equivalent to convergence in any norm.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: A sequence may be bounded without converging.

concepts.title: Topology · Open
concepts.summary: A set is open when every point has a ball contained in the set.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: A set is open when every point has a ball contained in the set.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: $(0,1)$ is open in $\mathbb R$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Whether a set is open depends on the ambient topology; $[0,1]$ is open in itself with the subspace topology.

concepts.title: Topology · Closed
concepts.summary: A set is closed when it contains the limits of all convergent sequences from the set, in metric spaces.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: A set is closed when it contains the limits of all convergent sequences from the set, in metric spaces.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: $[0,1]$ is closed in $\mathbb R$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Closed does not mean bounded; $[0,\infty)$ is closed and unbounded.

concepts.title: Topology · Closure
concepts.summary: The closure $\overline A$ is the smallest closed set containing $A$, equivalently the set of points approached by sequences from $A$ in metric spaces.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: The closure $\overline A$ is the smallest closed set containing $A$, equivalently the set of points approached by sequences from $A$ in metric spaces.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: The closure of $(0,1)$ in $\mathbb R$ is $[0,1]$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: A point in the closure need not belong to the original set.

concepts.title: Normed vector spaces · Equivalence
concepts.summary: Two norms are equivalent when each bounds the other up to positive constants, so they define the same convergent sequences and open sets.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: Two norms are equivalent when each bounds the other up to positive constants, so they define the same convergent sequences and open sets.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: On $\mathbb R^n$, $\|x\|_\infty\le\|x\|_2\le\sqrt n\|x\|_\infty$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Equivalence constants may depend on dimension and need not be uniform across changing spaces.

concepts.title: Topology · Compactness
concepts.summary: A subset of a metric space is compact when every sequence has a convergent subsequence whose limit remains in the set.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: A subset of a metric space is compact when every sequence has a convergent subsequence whose limit remains in the set.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: In $\mathbb R^n$, closed and bounded sets are compact.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Closed and bounded need not imply compactness in an arbitrary infinite-dimensional normed space.

concepts.title: Topology · Path-connected sets
concepts.summary: A set is path connected when any two points can be joined by a continuous path lying in the set.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: A set is path connected when any two points can be joined by a continuous path lying in the set.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: Every convex subset of a normed space is path connected by the line segment path.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Connectedness need not imply path connectedness in general topological spaces.

concepts.title: Mappings · Continuous linear maps
concepts.summary: A linear map between finite-dimensional normed spaces is continuous; in general, continuity is equivalent to boundedness.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: A linear map between finite-dimensional normed spaces is continuous; in general, continuity is equivalent to boundedness.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: $\|Tx\|\le C\|x\|$ proves continuity of a linear map.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Linearity alone does not guarantee continuity between arbitrary infinite-dimensional normed spaces.

concepts.title: Mappings · Multilinear
concepts.summary: A multilinear map is linear in each argument separately while the other arguments are fixed.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: A multilinear map is linear in each argument separately while the other arguments are fixed.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: The determinant is multilinear in its columns.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: A bilinear map is not linear on the product space under simultaneous scalar multiplication: $B(\lambda x,\lambda y)=\lambda^2B(x,y)$.

concepts.title: Numerical series · Vector
concepts.summary: A vector series converges when its partial sums converge in the vector-space norm.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: A vector series converges when its partial sums converge in the vector-space norm.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: In finite dimension, $\sum v_n$ converges exactly when every coordinate series converges.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Coordinatewise reasoning requires a fixed finite-dimensional basis or a theorem appropriate to the space.

concepts.title: Numerical series · Absolute
concepts.summary: A vector series is absolutely convergent when $\sum\|v_n\|$ converges; this implies convergence in a complete finite-dimensional space.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: A vector series is absolutely convergent when $\sum\|v_n\|$ converges; this implies convergence in a complete finite-dimensional space.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: If $\|v_n\|\le2^{-n}$, then $\sum v_n$ converges absolutely.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Convergence of $\sum v_n$ need not imply convergence of $\sum\|v_n\|$.

concepts.title: Numerical series · Tests
concepts.summary: A convergence test is selected from the term's sign, comparison scale, quotient, root, or oscillation structure.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: A convergence test is selected from the term's sign, comparison scale, quotient, root, or oscillation structure.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: $\sum n!/n^n$ converges by a quotient test with limiting ratio below $1$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: A quotient tending to $1$ makes the ratio test inconclusive.

concepts.title: Numerical series · Remainder
concepts.summary: The remainder after $n$ terms is the tail $R_n=\sum_{k>n}u_k$, estimated with a theorem suited to the terms.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: The remainder after $n$ terms is the tail $R_n=\sum_{k>n}u_k$, estimated with a theorem suited to the terms.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: For a positive decreasing function, integral comparison bounds the series tail by neighboring improper integrals.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: A remainder estimate must control the full infinite tail, not only the next term unless an alternating-series theorem applies.

concepts.title: Sequences of functions · Pointwise
concepts.summary: $f_n\to f$ pointwise when, for each fixed $x$, the scalar sequence $f_n(x)$ tends to $f(x)$.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: $f_n\to f$ pointwise when, for each fixed $x$, the scalar sequence $f_n(x)$ tends to $f(x)$.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: $x^n\to0$ for each $x\in[0,1)$ but equals $1$ at $x=1$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: The index at which accuracy begins may depend on $x$, so pointwise convergence gives no uniform control.

concepts.title: Sequences of functions · Uniform
concepts.summary: $f_n\to f$ uniformly when $\sup_x|f_n(x)-f(x)|\to0$.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: $f_n\to f$ uniformly when $\sup_x|f_n(x)-f(x)|\to0$.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: $x/n\to0$ uniformly on $[0,1]$ because the supremum error is $1/n$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Pointwise convergence to a discontinuous limit on a compact interval cannot be uniform when all $f_n$ are continuous.

concepts.title: Series of functions · Normal
concepts.summary: $\sum f_n$ converges normally when $\sum\|f_n\|_\infty$ converges.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: $\sum f_n$ converges normally when $\sum\|f_n\|_\infty$ converges.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: If $|f_n(x)|\le2^{-n}$ for every $x$, the series converges normally.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Uniform convergence of the series does not by itself imply convergence of the sup-norm series.

concepts.title: Series of functions · Integrate
concepts.summary: Uniform convergence of continuous terms on a compact interval permits termwise integration.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: Uniform convergence of continuous terms on a compact interval permits termwise integration.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: If partial sums $S_n$ converge uniformly to $S$, then $\int S_n\to\int S$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Pointwise convergence alone does not justify interchanging sum and integral.

concepts.title: Series of functions · Differentiate
concepts.summary: Termwise differentiation follows when the derivative series converges uniformly and the original series converges at one point.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: Termwise differentiation follows when the derivative series converges uniformly and the original series converges at one point.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: Under those hypotheses, the sum is differentiable and its derivative is the sum of derivatives.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Differentiability of every term plus pointwise convergence is insufficient.

concepts.title: Approximation · Weierstrass
concepts.summary: The Weierstrass approximation theorem says every continuous real function on a compact interval is uniformly approximable by polynomials.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: The Weierstrass approximation theorem says every continuous real function on a compact interval is uniformly approximable by polynomials.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: Bernstein polynomials approximate a continuous function uniformly on $[0,1]$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: The theorem gives uniform approximation, not equality with one finite polynomial.

concepts.title: Power series · Radius
concepts.summary: A power series has a radius $R$ with absolute convergence for $|z|<R$ and divergence for $|z|>R$.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: A power series has a radius $R$ with absolute convergence for $|z|<R$ and divergence for $|z|>R$.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: The geometric power series $\sum_{n\ge0}z^n$ has radius of convergence $1$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: The radius criterion gives no automatic answer on the boundary $|z|=R$.

concepts.title: Power series · Domain
concepts.summary: The convergence domain is the open disc together with whichever boundary points converge after separate analysis.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: The convergence domain is the open disc together with whichever boundary points converge after separate analysis.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: $\sum z^n/n$ converges at $z=-1$ but diverges at $z=1$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: All boundary points share the same modulus but may have different convergence behavior.

concepts.title: Power series · Operations
concepts.summary: Inside the common convergence disc, power series may be added, scaled, and composed when the inner series stays in the outer domain.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: Inside the common convergence disc, power series may be added, scaled, and composed when the inner series stays in the outer domain.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: Adding $\sum a_nz^n$ and $\sum b_nz^n$ gives coefficients $a_n+b_n$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Formal composition is not justified when the substituted values leave the convergence disc.

concepts.title: Power series · Cauchy
concepts.summary: The product of two power series has Cauchy-product coefficients $c_n=\sum_{k=0}^na_kb_{n-k}$ inside the common disc.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: The product of two power series has Cauchy-product coefficients $c_n=\sum_{k=0}^na_kb_{n-k}$ inside the common disc.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: $(1-z)^{-2}=\sum_{n\ge0}(n+1)z^n$ follows by squaring the geometric series.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Coefficient convolution does not enlarge the proven convergence domain.

concepts.title: Power series · Differentiate
concepts.summary: A power series may be differentiated term by term inside its radius without changing that radius.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: A power series may be differentiated term by term inside its radius without changing that radius.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Termwise differentiation at a boundary point requires a separate argument.

concepts.title: Power series · Integrate
concepts.summary: A power series may be integrated term by term inside its radius, with an independently determined constant.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: A power series may be integrated term by term inside its radius, with an independently determined constant.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: $-\log(1-z)=\sum_{n\ge1}z^n/n$ for $|z|<1$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Forgetting the integration constant prevents identification of the correct function.

concepts.title: Vector-valued functions · Derivative
concepts.summary: A vector-valued derivative is the vector limit of the difference quotient, equivalent to coordinate differentiation in finite dimension.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: A vector-valued derivative is the vector limit of the difference quotient, equivalent to coordinate differentiation in finite dimension.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: For $r(t)=(\cos t,\sin t)$, $r'(t)=(-\sin t,\cos t)$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Differentiating coordinates presupposes a finite-dimensional coordinate representation.

concepts.title: Vector-valued functions · Integral
concepts.summary: A continuous vector-valued function is integrated coordinatewise in finite dimension, producing a basis-independent vector.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: A continuous vector-valued function is integrated coordinatewise in finite dimension, producing a basis-independent vector.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Integrating the norm is not the same as taking the norm of the vector integral.

concepts.title: Vector-valued functions · Taylor
concepts.summary: Taylor's formula for a vector-valued function applies componentwise with a vector remainder estimate.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: Taylor's formula for a vector-valued function applies componentwise with a vector remainder estimate.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: $r(t+h)=r(t)+hr'(t)+O(h^2)$ for a twice differentiable plane curve.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: A componentwise expansion needs one remainder control valid for the chosen vector norm.

concepts.title: Improper integrals · Definition
concepts.summary: An improper integral is defined as a limit of proper integrals at an infinite endpoint or singularity.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: An improper integral is defined as a limit of proper integrals at an infinite endpoint or singularity.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: $\int_1^\infty x^{-2}dx=\lim_{R\to\infty}(1-1/R)=1$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Writing an antiderivative at infinity without a limit is not a definition.

concepts.title: Improper integrals · Comparison
concepts.summary: Comparison transfers convergence between nonnegative functions with a proven local inequality near the improper endpoint.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: Comparison transfers convergence between nonnegative functions with a proven local inequality near the improper endpoint.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: $0\le e^{-x}\le x^{-2}$ for large $x$ helps prove integrability at infinity.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: A comparison away from the singular endpoint says nothing about improper convergence there.

concepts.title: Improper integrals · Parts
concepts.summary: Integration by parts for an improper integral is performed on finite truncations before passing to the limit.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: Integration by parts for an improper integral is performed on finite truncations before passing to the limit.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: $\int_1^R(\log x)/x^2dx$ is integrated by parts first, then $R\to\infty$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: The limiting boundary term must exist; formal endpoint notation cannot replace that check.

concepts.title: Dominated convergence · Convergence
concepts.summary: Dominated convergence combines pointwise convergence with one integrable majorant independent of the sequence index.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: Dominated convergence combines pointwise convergence with one integrable majorant independent of the sequence index.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: If $|f_n|\le g\in L^1$ and $f_n\to f$ pointwise, then $\int f_n\to\int f$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: A different majorant $g_n$ for each $n$ does not satisfy the theorem.

concepts.title: Parameter-dependent integrals · Integral
concepts.summary: Continuity of a parameter integral follows by combining pointwise continuity in the parameter with an integrable local domination.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: Continuity of a parameter integral follows by combining pointwise continuity in the parameter with an integrable local domination.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: $F(x)=\int_0^1e^{-xt}dt$ is continuous for $x\ge0$ by domination with $1$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Pointwise continuity of the integrand is not enough on an improper domain without domination.

concepts.title: Parameter-dependent integrals · Differentiate
concepts.summary: Differentiation under the integral requires a parameter derivative and an integrable bound for that derivative on a neighborhood.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: Differentiation under the integral requires a parameter derivative and an integrable bound for that derivative on a neighborhood.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: $d[\int_0^1e^{-xt}dt]/dx=\int_0^1-te^{-xt}dt$ after the hypotheses are checked.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Formally differentiating the integrand before finding a uniform integrable bound is not a proof.

concepts.title: Probability · Countable
concepts.summary: A countable discrete law assigns nonnegative masses to countably many values with total $1$.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: A countable discrete law assigns nonnegative masses to countably many values with total $1$.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: $P(X=k)=2^{-k}$ for $k\ge1$ is a law because the geometric sum equals $1$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Point masses whose series diverges or sums below $1$ do not define the stated full law.

concepts.title: Probability · Bernoulli
concepts.summary: A Bernoulli variable takes values $1$ and $0$ with probabilities $p$ and $1-p$.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: A Bernoulli variable takes values $1$ and $0$ with probabilities $p$ and $1-p$.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: For $X\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)$, $E[X]=p$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X)=p(1-p)$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: A Bernoulli model describes one binary trial, not a count over several trials.

concepts.title: Probability · Binomial theorem
concepts.summary: A binomial variable counts successes in $n$ independent Bernoulli trials with the same success probability $p$.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: A binomial variable counts successes in $n$ independent Bernoulli trials with the same success probability $p$.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: $P(X=k)=\binom nkp^k(1-p)^{n-k}$ for $0\le k\le n$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Changing success probabilities or dependence between trials invalidates the binomial model.

concepts.title: Probability · Geometric
concepts.summary: A geometric variable counts trials until the first success, with $P(X=k)=(1-p)^{k-1}p$ on $k\ge1$.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: A geometric variable counts trials until the first success, with $P(X=k)=(1-p)^{k-1}p$ on $k\ge1$.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: Its memoryless property is $P(X>m+n\mid X>m)=P(X>n)$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Some conventions count failures before success and start at $0$; the support must be stated.

concepts.title: Probability · Poisson
concepts.summary: A Poisson variable with parameter $\lambda>0$ has $P(X=k)=e^{-\lambda}\lambda^k/k!$.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: A Poisson variable with parameter $\lambda>0$ has $P(X=k)=e^{-\lambda}\lambda^k/k!$.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: Its expectation and variance both equal $\lambda$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: A Poisson variable has unbounded countable support, unlike a binomial variable.

concepts.title: Probability · Independent families
concepts.summary: A family is mutually independent when every finite subfamily has product probabilities for all corresponding events.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: A family is mutually independent when every finite subfamily has product probabilities for all corresponding events.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: Independent coordinate variables on a product probability space form an independent family.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Pairwise independence does not generally imply mutual independence.

concepts.title: Probability · First absolute moment
concepts.summary: $L^1$ consists of integrable random variables with $E[|X|]<\infty$.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: $L^1$ consists of integrable random variables with $E[|X|]<\infty$.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: If $E[X^2]<\infty$, then Cauchy–Schwarz implies $E[|X|]<\infty$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: A finite expectation written through cancellation does not replace absolute integrability.

concepts.title: Probability · Second moment
concepts.summary: $L^2$ consists of square-integrable random variables with $E[X^2]<\infty$.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: $L^2$ consists of square-integrable random variables with $E[X^2]<\infty$.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: Variance is finite for every $L^2$ variable.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Being in $L^1$ does not imply being in $L^2$.

concepts.title: Probability · Covariance
concepts.summary: $\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=E[(X-E[X])(Y-E[Y])]$ measures linear joint variation.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: $\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=E[(X-E[X])(Y-E[Y])]$ measures linear joint variation.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: Independent square-integrable variables have covariance zero.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Zero covariance does not imply independence in general.

concepts.title: Probability · Probability-generating functions
concepts.summary: The probability generating function of a nonnegative integer-valued variable is $G_X(s)=E[s^X]$ on its domain.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: The probability generating function of a nonnegative integer-valued variable is $G_X(s)=E[s^X]$ on its domain.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: For a Poisson variable, $G_X(s)=e^{\lambda(s-1)}$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Differentiating at $1$ requires the corresponding moment to be finite and the operation justified.

concepts.title: Probability · Markov
concepts.summary: For a nonnegative random variable, Markov's inequality is $P(X\ge a)\le E[X]/a$ for $a>0$.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: For a nonnegative random variable, Markov's inequality is $P(X\ge a)\le E[X]/a$ for $a>0$.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: If $E[X]=10$, then $P(X\ge50)\le1/5$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: The variable must be nonnegative; applying the inequality directly to a signed variable is invalid.

concepts.title: Probability · Chebyshev
concepts.summary: Chebyshev's inequality is $P(|X-E[X]|\ge t)\le\operatorname{Var}(X)/t^2$.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: Chebyshev's inequality is $P(|X-E[X]|\ge t)\le\operatorname{Var}(X)/t^2$.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: A variable of variance $4$ lies within $6$ of its mean with probability at least $8/9$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: The bound is valid but may be loose; it is not an equality claim.

concepts.title: Probability · Weak law of large numbers
concepts.summary: The weak law states that sample averages converge in probability to the common mean under suitable independence and variance hypotheses.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: The weak law states that sample averages converge in probability to the common mean under suitable independence and variance hypotheses.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: For iid variables of variance $\sigma^2$, the sample-mean variance is $\sigma^2/n$, so Chebyshev proves convergence in probability.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: The weak law does not assert almost-sure convergence without a stronger theorem.

concepts.title: Differential equations · Linear systems
concepts.summary: A linear system has the form $Y'=A(t)Y+B(t)$; its homogeneous solution set is a vector space.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: A linear system has the form $Y'=A(t)Y+B(t)$; its homogeneous solution set is a vector space.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: For diagonal constant $A$, each coordinate solves $y_i'=\lambda_i y_i$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Diagonalization may be used only over a field and basis in which the matrix is genuinely diagonalizable.

concepts.title: Differential equations · General scalar equations
concepts.summary: A scalar linear differential equation has the unknown and its derivatives appearing linearly with coefficient functions on a stated interval.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: A scalar linear differential equation has the unknown and its derivatives appearing linearly with coefficient functions on a stated interval.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: $a_2(x)y''+a_1(x)y'+a_0(x)y=b(x)$ is second order where $a_2$ does not vanish.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Crossing a zero of the leading coefficient may change the order and invalidate an existence theorem.

concepts.title: Differential equations · Variation of constants
concepts.summary: Variation of constants replaces a homogeneous constant parameter by a function chosen to produce the forcing term.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: Variation of constants replaces a homogeneous constant parameter by a function chosen to produce the forcing term.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: For $y'+a(x)y=b(x)$, an integrating factor gives the variation-of-constants formula.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: The formula is local to intervals where the coefficients meet the continuity hypotheses.

concepts.title: Differential equations · Power Series
concepts.summary: A power-series solution substitutes $y=\sum a_nx^n$ into the equation and equates coefficients to obtain a recurrence.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: A power-series solution substitutes $y=\sum a_nx^n$ into the equation and equates coefficients to obtain a recurrence.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: For $y'=y$, coefficient comparison gives $a_{n+1}=a_n/(n+1)$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: A formal coefficient recurrence does not prove convergence unless a theorem or radius estimate is supplied.

concepts.title: Differential calculus · Frechet
concepts.summary: $f$ is Fréchet differentiable at $a$ when $f(a+h)=f(a)+Df(a)h+o(\|h\|)$ for one linear map $Df(a)$.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: $f$ is Fréchet differentiable at $a$ when $f(a+h)=f(a)+Df(a)h+o(\|h\|)$ for one linear map $Df(a)$.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: For $f(x)=\|x\|^2$, $Df(x)h=2\langle x,h\rangle$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Existence of all directional derivatives does not by itself give one uniform linear approximation.

concepts.title: Differential calculus · Directional
concepts.summary: The directional derivative in direction $v$ is the one-variable limit $\lim_{t\to0}[f(a+tv)-f(a)]/t$.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: The directional derivative in direction $v$ is the one-variable limit $\lim_{t\to0}[f(a+tv)-f(a)]/t$.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: For $f(x,y)=x^2+y^2$, the directional derivative at $a$ is $2\langle a,v\rangle$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Directional derivatives may exist in every direction without assembling into a linear derivative.

concepts.title: Differential calculus · Curve
concepts.summary: For a differentiable curve $\gamma$ and differentiable $f$, $(f\circ\gamma)'(t)=Df(\gamma(t))\gamma'(t)$.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: For a differentiable curve $\gamma$ and differentiable $f$, $(f\circ\gamma)'(t)=Df(\gamma(t))\gamma'(t)$.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: Along $\gamma(t)=(t,t^2)$, the derivative of $f(\gamma(t))$ uses the tangent vector $(1,2t)$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: A curve test sees only chosen directions and cannot alone prove full Fréchet differentiability.

concepts.title: Differential calculus · Chain rule
concepts.summary: The finite-dimensional chain rule is $D(g\circ f)(x)=Dg(f(x))\circ Df(x)$.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: The finite-dimensional chain rule is $D(g\circ f)(x)=Dg(f(x))\circ Df(x)$.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: Jacobian matrices multiply in composition order.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: The order of the two derivative maps cannot be reversed, and both differentiability hypotheses are required.

concepts.title: Differential calculus · Gradient
concepts.summary: In an inner-product space, the gradient is the vector satisfying $Df(x)h=\langle\nabla f(x),h\rangle$.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: In an inner-product space, the gradient is the vector satisfying $Df(x)h=\langle\nabla f(x),h\rangle$.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: For $f(x)=x^TAx$ with symmetric $A$, $\nabla f(x)=2Ax$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: A coordinate column of partial derivatives represents the gradient only relative to the chosen inner product and orthonormal coordinates.

concepts.title: Differential calculus · Hessian
concepts.summary: The Hessian represents the second derivative as a symmetric bilinear form when $f$ is twice continuously differentiable.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: The Hessian represents the second derivative as a symmetric bilinear form when $f$ is twice continuously differentiable.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: For $f(x,y)=x^2+3y^2$, the Hessian is $\operatorname{diag}(2,6)$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: A singular Hessian gives an inconclusive second-order test rather than proving there is no extremum.

concepts.title: Differential calculus · Optimization
concepts.summary: At an interior differentiable local extremum, the derivative vanishes; second-order information then classifies nondegenerate critical points.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: At an interior differentiable local extremum, the derivative vanishes; second-order information then classifies nondegenerate critical points.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: $x^2+y^2$ has a strict minimum at the origin because its gradient vanishes and Hessian is positive definite.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: A zero gradient is necessary but not sufficient: $x^3$ has a critical point at zero without an extremum.

lessons.title: Week 1, Day 1 · Make finite sums and products explicit
lessons.summary: Finite sums and products require explicit inclusive bounds, justified index changes, and visible boundary terms.
objectives: Justify an index change and derive a shifted telescoping formula while preserving every boundary term—the core work of Finite calculations · Finite sums and products.

content.markdown:
# Week 1 begins with indexed calculations

You will learn to read the bounds, operation, and summand before calculating. By the end, a telescoping cancellation will be a proof with visible boundary terms rather than a visual shortcut.

## Read an indexed family as a function

An indexed family $(u_k)_{k=p}^{q}$ is a function whose input is an integer index and whose output is the corresponding term. The notation $u_k$ means the value at $k$; it does not mean multiplication by an unnamed variable.

Before summing, write the first and last legal indices. This makes the domain of the index function visible and prevents an off-by-one term.

content.title: Expand an indexed family
content.introMarkdown: List the four ordered pairs $(k,u_k)$ and state the domain of the index function.

data.markdown:
### Repair guide for “Expand an indexed family”

Use this guide only after reading Forge’s assessment of your submitted answer.

Check first whether the index domain includes both endpoints and whether every value was evaluated at the stated integer.

A missing or extra index changes every later finite sum or product.

Repair only the first indexing error, then keep the corrected domain visible while you move to proof language.

content.markdown:
## A complete model for changing an index

Consider $A=\sum_{r=0}^{3}(2r+3)$. We want to rewrite the same four terms with an index that starts at $1$, without changing either the summand or the endpoints by guesswork.

Set $j=r+1$, so $r=j-1$. When $r=0$, the new lower index is $j=1$; when $r=3$, the new upper index is $j=4$. The map $r\mapsto r+1$ is a bijection from $\{0,1,2,3\}$ to $\{1,2,3,4\}$.

Substituting in the summand gives $2r+3=2(j-1)+3=2j+1$. Therefore

$$A=\sum_{j=1}^{4}(2j+1).$$

Expanding both versions gives $3+5+7+9$, which checks the calculation but does not replace the proof: the substitution, both transformed bounds, and the one-to-one index correspondence justify the equality for the indexed expressions.

The next question uses a different shift. Rebuild all four pieces rather than copying this model's bounds.

content.title: Justify a change of index
content.introMarkdown: Prove that the two finite sums are equal by naming the substitution and transforming both bounds.

data.markdown:
### Repair guide for “Justify a change of index”

Use this guide only after reading Forge’s assessment of your submitted answer.

Locate the first place where the substitution, a bound, or the new summand was left implicit.

A correct-looking list of terms is not yet a general justification for an index change.

Write the missing bound transformation or bijection sentence, then use that proof discipline in the finite-sum definition.

content.markdown:
## Why finite notation matters

Concours calculations often compress many terms into one symbol. Expanding a few terms reveals the index pattern, while a correct reindexing or telescoping argument turns that pattern into a formula valid for every permitted integer.

## Finite sums, products, and telescoping

A finite sum $\sum_{k=p}^{q}u_k$ adds one term for each integer index from $p$ through $q$; a finite product $\prod_{k=p}^{q}u_k$ multiplies those terms. A telescoping sum is rewritten so all non-boundary terms cancel in matched pairs.

The bounds $p$ and $q$ belong to the notation: changing either bound changes the object. A telescoping proof first rewrites the summand as a difference, expands enough terms to exhibit opposite pairs, and then keeps the unmatched boundary terms.

content.title: Separate a sum from a product
content.introMarkdown: Compute $\sum_{k=1}^{4}u_k$ and $\prod_{k=1}^{4}u_k$, then explain the different operations encoded by $\sum$ and $\prod$.

data.markdown:
### Repair guide for “Separate a sum from a product”

Use this guide only after reading Forge’s assessment of your submitted answer.

Check whether the first incorrect line changes an index, omits a term, or confuses addition with multiplication.

The notation identifies both the index set and the operation; either error changes the mathematical object.

Correct the expansion first, then carry the same explicit-term habit into the telescoping model.

content.markdown:
Compute $\sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac{1}{k(k+1)}$ for an integer $n\ge1$.

### Target

Rewrite the summand as a difference, display the cancellations, and retain the exact boundary terms.

### Strategy

Use partial fractions: seek constants so that $1/(k(k+1))$ becomes a difference of two consecutive reciprocal terms.

### Hypotheses

The index $k$ runs from $1$ to the positive integer $n$, so neither denominator $k$ nor $k+1$ vanishes.

### Complete solution

Since $\frac{1}{k(k+1)}=\frac1k-\frac1{k+1}$,

$$\sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac{1}{k(k+1)}=\left(1-\frac12\right)+\left(\frac12-\frac13\right)+\cdots+\left(\frac1n-\frac1{n+1}\right).$$

Every interior reciprocal occurs once with each sign. The unmatched terms are $1$ and $-1/(n+1)$, so the sum equals $1-1/(n+1)=n/(n+1)$.

### Boundary check

The formula depends on starting at $k=1$. If the lower bound were $k=2$, the first surviving term would be $1/2$, not $1$.

content.title: Track the surviving terms
content.introMarkdown: Identify each cancelling pair and state the two terms that survive.

data.markdown:
### Repair guide for “Track the surviving terms”

Use this guide only after reading Forge’s assessment of your submitted answer.

Find the earliest reciprocal that was cancelled without an equal term of the opposite sign.

Telescoping keeps boundary terms; deleting them is the main source of a false closed form.

Restore the first unmatched term, recompute the boundary difference, and then transfer the pattern to shifted denominators.

content.markdown:
## Shift the telescoping window

A shifted denominator changes both surviving boundary terms. For $1/((k+1)(k+2))$, the useful difference is $1/(k+1)-1/(k+2)$.

Do not copy the previous answer. Recompute the first and last indices after the shift.

content.title: Transfer telescoping to shifted factors
content.introMarkdown: Derive a closed formula for $S_n$ and verify it directly when $n=1$.

data.markdown:
### Repair guide for “Transfer telescoping to shifted factors”

Use this guide only after reading Forge’s assessment of your submitted answer.

Inspect the first denominator shift, then the last surviving reciprocal, before checking any later algebra.

An incorrect boundary term produces a plausible but false formula for every $n$.

Repair the first shifted index, recheck $n=1$, and keep the validated telescoping structure for tomorrow's binomial sum.

content.markdown:
## Further reading

Use the page card for “Week 1, Day 1 · Make finite sums and products explicit.”

Reference: section “Programme de mathématiques MPSI — Calculs algébriques”; anchor `CALC.SUM_PRODUCT`; French Ministry CPGE mathematics programmes.

## What is now established

A finite sum or product includes both bounds, and a telescoping proof preserves the unmatched boundary terms. Day 2 treats the binomial theorem as a finite indexed sum whose coefficients and signs must be tracked with the same care.

lessons.title: Week 1, Day 2 · Control coefficients and signs in the binomial theorem
lessons.summary: State and apply Finite calculations · Binomial theorem, preserve scalar powers and signs, and compute an unfamiliar mixed coefficient independently.
objectives: State and apply Finite calculations · Binomial theorem, preserve scalar powers and signs, and compute an unfamiliar mixed coefficient independently.

content.markdown:
# The binomial theorem is an indexed calculation

Today each term has a coefficient, two complementary exponents, and possibly a sign. You will keep those pieces separate until the final simplification.

## Why the theorem matters

A full expansion is expensive and error-prone when the degree grows. The indexed formula lets you compute one requested coefficient directly and exposes exactly where a missing mixed term or sign error enters.

## Reactivate the indexed-sum language

In $\sum_{k=0}^{n}\binom nk x^{n-k}y^k$, the index $k$ chooses one term. The lower and upper bounds say that the expansion contains $n+1$ terms.

A proof of an identity must explain why each coefficient and exponent has that value; listing a memorized row is not enough when signs or scaled variables change.

content.title: Read the five pieces of a binomial term
content.introMarkdown: State the term obtained at $k=2$ and explain how the two exponents add to the fixed total degree.

data.markdown:
### Repair guide for “Read the five pieces of a binomial term”

Use this guide only after reading Forge’s assessment of your submitted answer.

Check the substitution into $5-k$ before checking the binomial coefficient.

A wrong exponent changes the degree and therefore cannot be repaired by a later coefficient calculation.

Correct the exponent pair, confirm that it sums to five, and then introduce the full theorem.

content.markdown:
## The binomial theorem

For an integer $n\ge0$, the binomial theorem is $(x+y)^n=\sum_{k=0}^{n}\binom nk x^{n-k}y^k$, where $\binom nk=n!/(k!(n-k)!)$.

The integer hypothesis $n\ge0$ controls the finite coefficient row. When one input contains a scalar or a minus sign, that factor is raised to the term's exponent; it must be carried through every coefficient calculation.

content.title: Extract one coefficient
content.introMarkdown: Compute the coefficient of $x^2$ from the binomial theorem without expanding all five terms.

data.markdown:
### Repair guide for “Extract one coefficient”

Use this guide only after reading Forge’s assessment of your submitted answer.

Find the first mismatch between the requested power of $x$ and the index chosen in the general term.

The binomial index controls both exponents, so guessing the middle coefficient can lose the scalar factor.

Repair the index equation and power of two, then follow the complete signed derivation.

content.markdown:
For real or complex numbers $x$ and $y$, expand $(2x-y)^4$ completely and identify the coefficient of $x^2y^2$.

### Target

Apply the binomial theorem with the scaled and signed inputs, expand all terms, and isolate the requested coefficient.

### Strategy

Set $a=2x$ and $b=-y$ in the theorem. Keep $(-y)^k$ intact until the sign and coefficient of each term have both been determined.

### Hypotheses

The exponent is the nonnegative integer $4$, and $x,y$ may be real or complex, so the algebraic binomial identity applies.

### Complete solution

The exponent is the nonnegative integer $4$, so the binomial theorem applies with $a=2x$ and $b=-y$. Thus

$$(2x-y)^4=\sum_{k=0}^{4}\binom4k(2x)^{4-k}(-y)^k.$$

Writing the five terms in increasing powers of $y$ gives

$$16x^4-32x^3y+24x^2y^2-8xy^3+y^4.$$

The middle coefficient is $\binom42 2^2(-1)^2=6\cdot4=24$, so the coefficient of $x^2y^2$ is $24$.

### Boundary check

The mixed terms cannot be discarded. For example, the false shortcut $(2x-y)^4=(2x)^4+(-y)^4$ gives $17$ at $x=y=1$, whereas the original expression equals $1$. The missing terms are required by the binomial coefficients.

content.title: Diagnose a signed coefficient
content.introMarkdown: Identify the exact missing sign factor and derive the correct $xy^3$ term.

data.markdown:
### Repair guide for “Diagnose a signed coefficient”

Use this guide only after reading Forge’s assessment of your submitted answer.

Check the parity of the exponent on the negative input before recomputing the numerical coefficient.

A sign error changes both the expansion and any later cancellation or inequality built from it.

Restore the factor $(-1)^k$, simplify the term, and then test the missing-mixed-term shortcut.

content.markdown:
## Mixed terms cannot be omitted

The formula $(a+b)^n=a^n+b^n$ is generally false for integers $n\ge2$. A numerical substitution gives a fast counterexample, while the binomial theorem shows exactly which mixed terms were discarded.

A counterexample refutes the universal shortcut; it does not replace the correct expansion.

content.introMarkdown: Refute the claim with one explicit pair and name at least one mixed term supplied by the correct theorem.

data.markdown:
### Repair guide for “Refute the false shortcut”

Use this guide only after reading Forge’s assessment of your submitted answer.

Check first whether the chosen numerical pair actually makes the two sides unequal.

A counterexample must falsify the stated universal equality, and the omitted term explains why it fails structurally.

Replace an inconclusive pair or incorrect mixed term, then expand a new scaled binomial independently.

content.markdown:
## Transfer to a new degree and two positive scales

For $(3x+2y)^5$, the target degree determines the index, while both scalar factors contribute powers. Start from the general term before substituting the requested exponents.

Finish with a degree check: the exponents on $x$ and $y$ must add to five.

content.markdown:
# A formula for every integer needs a proof

Today the triangular-sum identity becomes an indexed proposition. You will see where the induction hypothesis is permitted, where it is forbidden, and how the new summand creates the next formula.

## Why induction is the right tool

The rank-$(n+1)$ sum contains the rank-$n$ sum plus one visible term. Induction turns that recursive structure into a proof for every positive integer without checking the cases one by one.

## Reactivate statements indexed by an integer

An induction proof concerns a family of propositions $P(n)$, one for each integer in a stated domain. It needs a base case, a conditional induction step, and a conclusion that names the entire domain.

For a sum identity, $P(n)$ includes both the summation bounds and the proposed closed formula.

content.introMarkdown: Write $P(n)$ with its domain and state the exact implication required in the induction step.

content.markdown:
## State the triangular-sum target

For every integer $n\ge1$, the target is

$$\sum_{k=1}^{n}k=\frac{n(n+1)}2.$$

The base case checks the first legal integer. The induction step adds the new last term $n+1$ to the sum already controlled by the hypothesis.

content.markdown:
Prove that $\sum_{k=1}^{n}(2k-1)=n^2$ for every integer $n\ge1$.

### Target

Exhibit the base case, use the induction hypothesis once, add the correct new term, and close the quantified conclusion.

### Strategy

At the step from $n$ to $n+1$, split off the new last odd number $2(n+1)-1=2n+1$.

### Hypotheses

Fix an arbitrary integer $n\ge1$ and assume $\sum_{k=1}^{n}(2k-1)=n^2$.

### Complete solution

For $n=1$, the sum is $1=1^2$. Assume the identity holds for one integer $n\ge1$. Then

$$\sum_{k=1}^{n+1}(2k-1)=\sum_{k=1}^{n}(2k-1)+(2(n+1)-1)=n^2+2n+1=(n+1)^2.$$

Thus $P(n)\Rightarrow P(n+1)$. By induction, the identity holds for every integer $n\ge1$.

### Boundary check

Writing $n^2+2n=(n+1)^2$ would omit the constant term and fail the step. The new summand is $2n+1$, not $2n$.

content.markdown:
## Avoid circular induction

The induction step may assume $P(n)$, but it may not assume $P(n+1)$ or the theorem for every integer. A line that begins by replacing the whole rank-$(n+1)$ sum with the desired formula has already assumed the conclusion.

The repair is to split off the new term before using the hypothesis on the shorter sum.
