content.markdown:
## Week 1 substantial problem

Five-part problem, 90 minutes; feedback follows each attempt.

### Shared stem

For real numbers, prove a sequence of increasingly independent inequalities. Each part must name the nonnegative quantity or theorem that controls the sign, and every equality case must be justified.

data.markdown: Likely issue: the chosen square was not expanded into the requested difference, or equality was asserted without returning to the zero-square condition. First repair: rewrite the difference as one square, then derive equality from that square alone.

Likely issue: a cross term was lost in the difference, or only one direction of the equality condition was proved. First repair: expand both sides on separate lines and compare the mixed terms before checking equality in both directions.

Likely issue: the coefficient pair does not produce $x+y$, or the square-root step ignores nonnegativity. First repair: identify the two coefficients used in Part 2, then justify taking square roots and carry the same equality condition through.

Likely issue: the square-root substitution was used before stating $u,v\ge0$, or equality was not translated back to the original variables. First repair: verify that both roots are real, apply Part 1, and translate its equality condition.

Likely issue: the induction step multiplied by $1+t$ without checking its sign, or equality cases from the three conclusions were merged. First repair: isolate the nonnegative-factor step, then audit each later substitution and equality case separately.

Treat these three independent tasks: (i) $\sum_{k=1}^{n}(1/k-1/(k+1))$; (ii) the coefficient of $x^2$ in $(1+x)^5$; (iii) prove $2uv\le u^2+v^2$ for real $u,v$.

Name the correct method for each task, obtain its exact result, and state the equality condition in the inequality.

Use telescoping for (i), the binomial theorem for (ii), and a nonnegative square for (iii); show the decisive line in each.

## Further reading

Use the page card for “Week 1, Day 4 · Prove inequalities with explicit sign conditions.”

Reference: section “Programme de mathématiques MPSI — Inégalités”; anchor `CALC.INEQUALITY`; French Ministry CPGE mathematics programmes.

## What is now established

A square-based proof supplies both an inequality and its equality condition, while multiplication or division needs an explicit sign. Day 5 closes the week by retrieving the indexed calculation and repairing a false cancellation without reopening the worked pages first.

activities.title: Part 1 · Start from one square
activities.promptMarkdown: For arbitrary real $x$ and $y$, prove $2xy\le x^2+y^2$ by expanding one nonnegative square. Determine the equality case and explain why no sign hypothesis is needed.

rubric.label: Method and dependency
rubric.description: Select and justify the result needed from the preceding part.

rubric.label: Verified result
rubric.description: Complete the calculation or proof and state the verified conclusion.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: The identity $x^2+y^2-2xy=(x-y)^2\ge0$ proves the inequality. Equality holds exactly when $(x-y)^2=0$, hence when $x=y$. A real square is nonnegative for every pair of real inputs, so no positivity assumption is required. This also proves the converse equality statement because a real square vanishes only at zero.

activities.title: Part 2 · Prove two-variable Cauchy–Schwarz
activities.promptMarkdown: Use $(ay-bx)^2\ge0$ to prove $(ax+by)^2\le(a^2+b^2)(x^2+y^2)$ for all real $a,b,x,y$. Expand the exact difference, justify its sign, and prove the equality condition in both directions.

rubric.label: Method and dependency
rubric.description: Select and justify the result needed from the preceding part.

rubric.label: Verified result
rubric.description: Complete the calculation or proof and state the verified conclusion.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Expansion gives $(a^2+b^2)(x^2+y^2)-(ax+by)^2=a^2y^2+b^2x^2-2abxy=(ay-bx)^2\ge0$. Equality holds exactly when $ay=bx$, which says that $(a,b)$ and $(x,y)$ are linearly dependent, including the zero-vector cases. The identity is exact, so the equality condition is necessary as well as sufficient.

activities.title: Part 3 · Derive a sum inequality
activities.promptMarkdown: Apply Part $2$ with a deliberate choice of $(a,b)$ to prove $(x+y)^2\le2(x^2+y^2)$. Then derive $|x+y|\le\sqrt2\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$ and state both equality cases.

rubric.label: Method and dependency
rubric.description: Select and justify the result needed from the preceding part.

rubric.label: Verified result
rubric.description: Complete the calculation or proof and state the verified conclusion.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Choose $(a,b)=(1,1)$ in Part $2$. Then $(x+y)^2\le2(x^2+y^2)$. Taking nonnegative square roots gives $|x+y|\le\sqrt2\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$. Equality in Part $2$ requires $y=x$; the square-root step is equivalent, so both inequalities have equality exactly when $x=y$. No implication is reversed when square roots are taken because both sides are nonnegative.

activities.title: Part 4 · Prove arithmetic–geometric mean
activities.promptMarkdown: For $u,v\ge0$, use Part $1$ with $x=\sqrt u$ and $y=\sqrt v$ to prove $\sqrt{uv}\le(u+v)/2$. Justify the substitution and determine equality.

rubric.label: Method and dependency
rubric.description: Select and justify the result needed from the preceding part.

rubric.label: Verified result
rubric.description: Complete the calculation or proof and state the verified conclusion.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Nonnegativity makes $\sqrt u$ and $\sqrt v$ real. Part $1$ gives $2\sqrt u\sqrt v\le u+v$, hence $\sqrt{uv}\le(u+v)/2$. Equality requires $\sqrt u=\sqrt v$, equivalently $u=v$. Without $u,v\ge0$, this real square-root formulation need not be defined. The domain hypothesis is essential: it makes both square roots real before Part $1$ is applied.

activities.title: Part 5 · Prove Bernoulli and combine
activities.promptMarkdown: For an integer $n\ge1$ and $t\ge-1$, prove Bernoulli's inequality $(1+t)^n\ge1+nt$ by induction, treating the factor $1+t$ explicitly. Then use Bernoulli with $t=(v-u)/u$ for $0<u\le v$ to prove $v^n\ge u^n+nu^{n-1}(v-u)$, and use Part $4$ to prove $(2\sqrt{uv})^n\le(u+v)^n$ for $u,v\ge0$. State all equality cases.

rubric.label: Method and dependency
rubric.description: Select and justify the result needed from the preceding part.

rubric.label: Verified result
rubric.description: Complete the calculation or proof and state the verified conclusion.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: The case $n=1$ is equality. If the claim holds, multiplication by $1+t\ge0$ gives $(1+t)^{n+1}\ge1+(n+1)t+nt^2\ge1+(n+1)t$, so induction proves Bernoulli. For $0<u\le v$, the choice $t=(v-u)/u\ge0$ gives $(v/u)^n\ge1+n(v-u)/u$; multiplication by $u^n>0$ yields $v^n\ge u^n+nu^{n-1}(v-u)$. Equality holds when $n=1$ or $u=v$. Part $4$ gives $2\sqrt{uv}\le u+v$; both sides are nonnegative, so raising to the integer power $n$ gives $(2\sqrt{uv})^n\le(u+v)^n$. Equality holds exactly when $u=v$, including $u=v=0$. The induction step uses $nt^2\ge0$; this is the term that closes the comparison.

content.markdown:
Audit the claim that $\sum_{k=1}^{n}(k-(k-2))$ telescopes to two boundary terms.

### Target

Expand the summand, determine whether consecutive opposite pairs exist, and replace the false cancellation claim with the correct sum.

### Strategy

Simplify the summand before looking for cancellation. If it becomes a constant, sum that constant over the exact number of indices.

### Hypotheses

$n$ is a positive integer, so the sum contains exactly $n$ terms.

### Complete solution

For every $k$, $k-(k-2)=2$. Therefore

$$\sum_{k=1}^{n}(k-(k-2))=\sum_{k=1}^{n}2=2n.$$ 

Expanding the unsimplified form gives $(1-(-1))+(2-0)+(3-1)+\cdots+(n-(n-2))$; these are not consecutive opposite pairs.

### Boundary check

The visual presence of a subtraction sign does not create telescoping. Cancellation requires the same expression to occur later with the opposite sign.

content.markdown:
# Trigonometry begins with a point, not a table

Today every exact value and sign will come from the coordinates of a unit-circle point. Periodicity and symmetry will be geometric transformations whose coordinate effects remain visible.

## Why geometry controls the algebra

Memorized values become fragile when angles are negative or larger than one turn. Reducing an angle and locating its quadrant supplies a route that still works when the familiar table is no longer written in front of you.

## Trigonometry · Circle

On the unit circle, the point at oriented angle $x$ has coordinates $(\cos x,\sin x)$; angles that differ by $2\pi$ determine the same point.

The coordinates determine both the identity $\cos^2x+\sin^2x=1$ and the sign of sine and cosine in each quadrant. Adding $2\pi$ returns to the same point, while adding $\pi$ reaches the antipodal point.

content.title: Locate an angle on the unit circle
content.introMarkdown: State its quadrant, the signs of its coordinates, and its reference angle.

data.markdown:
### Repair guide for “Locate an angle on the unit circle”

Use this guide only after reading Forge’s assessment of your submitted answer.

Check the first incorrect comparison with the quadrant boundaries $\pi/2$ and $\pi$.

The quadrant fixes both coordinate signs before any exact value is substituted.

Repair the quadrant and signs, then use the antipodal geometry in a complete symmetry model.

content.markdown:
Determine $\cos(7\pi/6)$ and $\sin(7\pi/6)$ from the point at angle $\pi/6$.

### Target

Use a rotation by $\pi$ to derive the coordinates and verify the signs from the quadrant.

### Strategy

Write $7\pi/6=\pi/6+\pi$. The second point is antipodal to the first, so both coordinates change sign.

### Hypotheses

The unit-circle point at $\pi/6$ is $(\sqrt3/2,1/2)$, and a half-turn maps $(u,v)$ to $(-u,-v)$.

### Complete solution

Because $7\pi/6=\pi/6+\pi$, the corresponding point is antipodal to $(\sqrt3/2,1/2)$. Therefore

$$\cos(7\pi/6)=-\frac{\sqrt3}{2},\qquad \sin(7\pi/6)=-\frac12.$$

The angle lies in quadrant III, where both coordinates are negative, so the signs agree with the geometry.

### Boundary check

A half-turn changes both signs. A reflection across the horizontal axis would change only the sine and represents the angle $-\pi/6$, not $7\pi/6$.

## Reduce an angle modulo a full turn

Angles that differ by $2k\pi$ have the same unit-circle point. Choose the integer $k$ so the reduced angle lies in a familiar interval, and preserve both coordinates.

A reduction modulo $\pi$ is not generally valid because a half-turn changes both coordinate signs.

## Test whether coordinates can come from an angle

Every unit-circle point satisfies $u^2+v^2=1$. This condition is necessary, so a pair whose squared coordinates do not sum to one cannot equal $(\cos x,\sin x)$ for any real angle.

The equation alone does not select a unique angle because adding $2\pi$ preserves the point.

content.markdown:
# An identity is universal; an equation selects angles

Today the same unit-circle facts play two roles. They prove equalities valid for every angle and generate periodic families whose intersection with a stated interval must be complete.

## Why the distinction matters

Testing a few angles cannot prove an identity, while finding one valid angle cannot solve an equation. Separating derivation from solution-set construction prevents both errors.

## Reactivate zeros and periodicity on the circle

The cosine coordinate is zero at the two vertical points. Therefore $\cos u=0$ exactly when $u=\pi/2+k\pi$ for an integer $k$.

An interval restriction is applied only after the periodic family has been derived.

content.introMarkdown: Give one integer family and explain it using the horizontal unit-circle points.

data.markdown:
### Repair guide for “Recover a periodic zero family”

Use this guide only after reading Forge’s assessment of your submitted answer.

Omitting one parity loses half of the periodic solutions.

Repair the integer family, then introduce identities as universal equalities derived from the circle.

content.markdown:
## Trigonometry · Identities

A trigonometric identity is an equality valid for every angle in its stated domain and is derived from geometric or algebraic definitions, not from a few numerical checks.

An identity keeps its full domain. Squaring may hide sign information, and taking a square root produces an absolute value. Derivations must therefore record both the algebraic equality and any sign boundary.

content.title: Derive a universal identity

## Trigonometry · Equations

Solving a trigonometric equation means describing every angle in the stated interval, or every periodic family when the domain is $\mathbb R$.

The unrestricted solution is usually an integer family. On a bounded interval, completeness requires intersecting that family with both endpoints and checking whether the right endpoint is included.

content.markdown:
Solve $\cos(2x)=0$ for every $x$ in the interval $[0,2\pi)$, giving the complete list without using a calculator.

### Target

Derive the full integer family for the doubled angle and intersect it exactly with $[0,2\pi)$.

### Strategy

Set $u=2x$, use the complete zero family for cosine, divide the family by two, and only then determine the admissible integers.

### Hypotheses

The domain is real, the interval is half-open, and multiplication by two is invertible on real numbers.

### Complete solution

For a real angle $u$, $\cos u=0$ exactly when $u=\pi/2+k\pi$ for some integer $k$. With $u=2x$, this gives

$$2x=\frac\pi2+k\pi,\qquad x=\frac\pi4+\frac{k\pi}{2}.$$

The interval condition $0\le x<2\pi$ is satisfied for $k=0,1,2,3$. Therefore the complete solution set is

$$\left\{\frac\pi4,\frac{3\pi}4,\frac{5\pi}4,\frac{7\pi}4\right\}.$$

Substitution makes $2x$ an odd multiple of $\pi/2$ in every case, so each listed value is valid.

### Boundary check

Giving only $x=\pi/4$ solves one branch but ignores periodicity. The equation is solved only after every integer family has been intersected with the stated interval.

content.markdown:
# The addition formulas have a proof

Today a dot product gives the cosine difference identity, parity gives the addition formula, and standard-angle coordinates produce exact values that are not in the basic table.

## Why derivation is safer than recall

The most common errors are the signs between sine products and unsafe square roots after squaring. A short derivation reconstructs the correct formula and exposes where domain or sign information can be lost.

## Reactivate unit vectors at two angles

The vectors $u=(\cos a,\sin a)$ and $v=(\cos b,\sin b)$ both have length one. Their dot product is $\cos a\cos b+\sin a\sin b$.

Geometrically, the angle between them is $a-b$, so the same dot product is $\cos(a-b)$.

content.title: Compute two descriptions of a dot product
content.introMarkdown: Write their coordinate dot product and the geometric expression using their angle difference.

data.markdown:
### Repair guide for “Compute two descriptions of a dot product”

Use this guide only after reading Forge’s assessment of your submitted answer.

Those are the two inputs to the addition-formula derivation.

content.markdown:
Derive the cosine difference and cosine addition formulas from the dot product of unit vectors.

### Target

Prove $\cos(a-b)=\cos a\cos b+\sin a\sin b$ and obtain the addition formula by replacing $b$ with $-b$.

### Strategy

Equate the coordinate and geometric dot products, then use the evenness of cosine and oddness of sine.

### Hypotheses

$a$ and $b$ are real angles, so their unit-circle coordinate vectors are real unit vectors.

### Complete solution

For $u=(\cos a,\sin a)$ and $v=(\cos b,\sin b)$, coordinates give $u\cdot v=\cos a\cos b+\sin a\sin b$. Geometry gives $u\cdot v=\cos(a-b)$. Hence

$$\cos(a-b)=\cos a\cos b+\sin a\sin b.$$

Replace $b$ by $-b$. Since $\cos(-b)=\cos b$ and $\sin(-b)=-\sin b$,

$$\cos(a+b)=\cos a\cos b-\sin a\sin b.$$

### Boundary check

The sign between the sine products changes between difference and sum. Copying the plus sign into $\cos(a+b)$ fails already at $a=b=\pi/2$.

## Derive double-angle formulas without unsafe square roots

Setting $a=b=x$ gives $\cos(2x)=\cos^2x-\sin^2x$. Combining this with $\cos^2x+\sin^2x=1$ gives the two equivalent forms $2\cos^2x-1$ and $1-2\sin^2x$.

Solving for cosine from a square requires an absolute value or a quadrant sign; $\sqrt{\cos^2x}=|\cos x|$.

Five-part problem, 90 minutes; feedback follows each attempt.

### Shared stem

For a real parameter $m$, study $\cos x+m\sin x=1$ on $[0,2\pi)$.

data.markdown: Likely issue: the sine and cosine coefficients do not match after expansion, or the interval fixing $\varphi$ was omitted. First repair: expand $R\cos(x-\varphi)$ and solve the two coefficient equations with the stated angle interval.

content.title: Part 2 · Existence and the exceptional tangent case

data.markdown: Likely issue: attainment of level $1$ was confused with tangency at the maximum. First repair: compare the level with the amplitude and separate the equality case from the strict-interior case before counting solutions.

Likely issue: one sign branch or its representative in $[0,2\pi)$ was lost. First repair: solve the cosine equation modulo $2\pi$ first, then reduce each branch separately for positive and negative $m$.

Likely issue: the second circle-line intersection was written without checking both defining equations. First repair: compute its two coordinates from the doubled angle and substitute them into the circle and line equations.
Likely issue: the cases were classified by $\lambda$ rather than by $|\lambda|$ relative to the amplitude. First repair: make a three-row comparison table and only then specialize it to level $1$.

## What is now established

Factoring retains all zero branches, sum-to-product formulas follow from addition identities, and exact checks can refute but not prove universal claims. Day 5 tests whether those structures survive without the worked pages.

activities.title: Part 1 · Normalize the linear form
activities.promptMarkdown: For every real $m$, construct the unique angle $\varphi\in(-\pi/2,\pi/2)$ and amplitude $R>0$ such that $\cos x+m\sin x=R\cos(x-\varphi)$. Prove the coefficient identities and relate the signs of $m$ and $\varphi$.

rubric.label: Method and dependency
rubric.description: Select and justify the result needed from the preceding part.

rubric.label: Verified result
rubric.description: Complete the calculation or proof and state the verified conclusion.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Take $R=\sqrt{1+m^2}$, $\cos\varphi=1/R>0$, and $\sin\varphi=m/R$. They determine a unique $\varphi\in(-\pi/2,\pi/2)$ with the same sign as $m$. Expanding $R\cos(x-\varphi)$ recovers $\cos x+m\sin x$, and the normalization gives $\tan\varphi=m$. The coefficient comparison also verifies $R^2=1+m^2$, so no second positive amplitude is possible.

activities.title: Part 2 · Existence and the exceptional tangent case
activities.promptMarkdown: Use the amplitude form to prove existence for every $m$. Determine exactly when level $1$ is a maximum rather than an interior value, and deduce the number of solutions in one period.

rubric.label: Method and dependency
rubric.description: Select and justify the result needed from the preceding part.

rubric.label: Verified result
rubric.description: Complete the calculation or proof and state the verified conclusion.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: The range is $[-R,R]$, where $R=\sqrt{1+m^2}\ge1$, so level $1$ is attained. It equals the maximum only when $R=1$, hence $m=0$; then there is one solution modulo $2\pi$. If $m\ne0$, then $R>1$ and there are two solutions in a full period. This separates existence from multiplicity: the range proves the first, while tangency controls the second.

activities.title: Part 3 · Enumerate without losing branches
activities.promptMarkdown: Assume $m\ne0$. Solve modulo $2\pi$ from the normalized form, reduce the answer to two branches involving $\varphi$, and give representatives in $[0,2\pi)$ separately for $m>0$ and $m<0$.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: The equation is $\cos(x-\varphi)=1/R=\cos\varphi$. Hence $x-\varphi=\pm\varphi\pmod{2\pi}$, so $x=0$ or $x=2\varphi$. If $m>0$, the representatives are $0$ and $2\varphi$. If $m<0$, they are $0$ and $2\pi+2\varphi$. Reducing modulo $2\pi$ after solving preserves both branches and prevents endpoint duplication.

rubric.label: Method and dependency
rubric.description: Select and justify the result needed from the preceding part.

rubric.label: Verified result
rubric.description: Complete the calculation or proof and state the verified conclusion.

activities.title: Part 4 · Geometric reconstruction
activities.promptMarkdown: Interpret the equation as the intersection of the unit circle with a line. Compute the second intersection point from angle $2\varphi$ and verify that it satisfies the line equation.

rubric.label: Method and dependency
rubric.description: Select and justify the result needed from the preceding part.

rubric.label: Verified result
rubric.description: Complete the calculation or proof and state the verified conclusion.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Writing $X=\cos x$ and $Y=\sin x$ gives $X+mY=1$, which contains $(1,0)$. The second point is $((1-m^2)/(1+m^2),2m/(1+m^2))$. Substitution gives $[(1-m^2)+2m^2]/(1+m^2)=1$. For $m=0$, the two points coalesce at $(1,0)$. The direct substitution checks the geometric construction independently of the trigonometric derivation.

activities.title: Part 5 · General level classification
activities.promptMarkdown: For a second real parameter $\lambda$, classify the number of solutions of $\cos x+m\sin x=\lambda$ in $[0,2\pi)$ as $0$, $1$, or $2$. State every boundary case and recover $\lambda=1$.

rubric.label: Method and dependency
rubric.description: Select and justify the result needed from the preceding part.

rubric.label: Verified result
rubric.description: Complete the calculation or proof and state the verified conclusion.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: The normalized equation is $\cos(x-\varphi)=\lambda/R$. If $|\lambda|>R$, there is no solution. If $|\lambda|=R$, there is one solution modulo $2\pi$. If $|\lambda|<R$, there are two: $x=\varphi\pm\arccos(\lambda/R)\pmod{2\pi}$. For $\lambda=1$, only $m=0$ is the one-solution boundary case. At $|\lambda|=R$, the two cosine branches coalesce, which explains the single-solution boundary.

# Friday separates recall from recognition

The first checkpoints are closed-notes retrieval. You will recover one Week 1 boundary calculation and one trigonometric derivation before auditing a missing periodic branch.

## Why completeness is part of mastery

A familiar final formula can conceal a lost sign or branch. Delayed reconstruction and exact substitution show whether the underlying route remains available.

## Reactivate the circle and proof checks

Close the worked pages. Recall that a real angle maps to one unit-circle point, while a proof must preserve its domain and every nonzero condition.

That sign-and-domain discipline also prepares a one-week retrieval of Week 1 inequality reasoning in the new trigonometric setting.

## Deliberate review: Week 1 sign conditions

Without reopening Week 1, recall what information is lost when an equality is squared and what must be restored when taking a square root.

This retrieval moves the earlier sign discipline from elementary inequalities to a trigonometric identity.

content.markdown:
Reconstruct $\cos(a+b)$ from the dot-product difference formula, with only the substitution $b\mapsto-b$ supplied.

### Target

Recover the parity steps and the correct sign between the sine products.

### Strategy

Begin with $\cos(a-b)=\cos a\cos b+\sin a\sin b$, replace $b$ by $-b$, and apply parity one factor at a time.

### Hypotheses

$a,b$ are real; cosine is even and sine is odd.

### Complete solution

Replacing $b$ by $-b$ gives

$$\cos(a+b)=\cos a\cos(-b)+\sin a\sin(-b).$$

Since $\cos(-b)=\cos b$ and $\sin(-b)=-\sin b$, this becomes

$$\cos(a+b)=\cos a\cos b-\sin a\sin b.$$

### Boundary check

The minus sign comes only from sine's oddness. Treating cosine as odd would change the cosine-product sign incorrectly.

A claimed interval solution should be checked against the period of the transformed equation. If a scaled argument has period smaller than $2\pi$, several solutions may fit in one standard interval.

Substitution verifies listed values; deriving the integer family proves that none are missing.

content.markdown:
## Week 2 · 25-minute correction synthesis and error log

If you attempted Week 2 practice and feedback identified an error, spend 10 minutes locating the first mathematical step that failed, 10 minutes solving that question again without looking at feedback, and 5 minutes stating the corrected reasoning aloud.

If you skipped the Week 2 optional practice, or every attempted answer was correct, use the same 25 minutes for a closed-notes question from Day 2 and a complete standard exercise from Day 3.

For this week, check these mathematical details: Preserve angle domains, periodic branches, and sign choices throughout each trigonometric reduction.

In the Week 2 record, include only errors that actually occurred: write the incorrect step, its correction, and one concrete check you will use next time.

## Further reading

Use the page card for “Week 2, Day 5 · Retrieve identities and audit complete solution sets.”

Reference pages: 7–10.

## Week 2 closure

You can now derive unit-circle identities, transform them without losing zero branches, and intersect scaled periodic families with exact intervals. Week 3 moves to complex-number algebra, where conjugation and modulus impose similarly strict sign and domain rules.

content.markdown:
# Cartesian form makes every component visible

Today complex equality, conjugation, modulus, and division will be handled as exact two-coordinate algebra. Every reciprocal will carry its nonzero hypothesis.

## Evaluate a polynomial at a complex input

A polynomial expression is evaluated by substituting the input into every power while preserving the coefficient field. The equality $P(z)=0$ is an exact algebraic statement, not a claim about a graph crossing an axis.

content.title: Evaluate at the imaginary unit
content.introMarkdown: Compute $P(i)$ in Cartesian form.

data.markdown:
### Repair guide for “Evaluate at the imaginary unit”

Every later root or factor claim depends on exact evaluation.

content.markdown:
## Activate the canonical complex-root definition

A complex number $z$ is a root of a polynomial $P$ exactly when $P(z)=0$. The equality is checked in $\mathbb C$: both its real and imaginary parts must vanish.

content.markdown:
## Why conjugation is the useful operation

Multiplying by a conjugate removes the imaginary part of a denominator while preserving an equivalent quotient. The same operation also exposes real and imaginary components without guessing them from notation.

## Complex algebra in Cartesian form

For $z=x+iy$, the conjugate is $\bar z=x-iy$ and the modulus satisfies $|z|^2=z\bar z=x^2+y^2$.

Conjugation preserves the real part and reverses the imaginary part. The product $z\bar z$ is the nonnegative real number $|z|^2$, which becomes the denominator in every legal reciprocal formula.

content.introMarkdown: Compute $\bar z$, $z\bar z$, and $|z|$, distinguishing the square from the modulus.

Those two distinctions control every conjugate and reciprocal calculation.

Repair the first one, then use conjugation to separate real and imaginary parts in a complete proof.

content.markdown:
For $z=x+iy$, prove that $z+\bar z$ is real and $z-\bar z$ is purely imaginary.

### Target

Compute both expressions and identify their Cartesian components.

### Strategy

Write the conjugate explicitly before adding or subtracting.

### Hypotheses

$x,y$ are real and $z=x+iy$.

### Complete solution

$\bar z=x-iy$. Therefore $z+\bar z=(x+iy)+(x-iy)=2x$, which is real. Also $z-\bar z=(x+iy)-(x-iy)=2iy$, whose real part is zero, so it is purely imaginary.

### Boundary check

Purely imaginary includes zero. When $y=0$, the difference is $0$, which still has real part zero.

content.introMarkdown: Compute $(z+\bar z)/2$ and $(z-\bar z)/(2i)$ and interpret both values.

content.markdown:
## Transfer conjugation to a reciprocal

For $z\ne0$, multiplying $1/z$ by $\bar z/\bar z$ gives $\bar z/(z\bar z)=\bar z/|z|^2$. The nonzero hypothesis is what makes the real denominator positive.

content.markdown:
# A quotient is complete only after its domain and check

Today conjugation converts a complex denominator into a positive real squared modulus. The original multiplication then verifies both Cartesian components.

## Why the check matters

A sign error in one cross product can leave a plausible-looking answer. Multiplying the result by the untouched denominator gives a decisive, local check.

## Reactivate Cartesian equality for a quotient

A quotient calculation must preserve both real and imaginary coordinates. Compare them separately after conjugating, and keep the denominator's nonzero condition visible.

content.title: Solve a two-parameter Cartesian equality
content.introMarkdown: Determine both $a$ and $b$ by comparing real and imaginary parts.

data.markdown:
### Repair guide for “Solve a two-parameter Cartesian equality”

Use this guide only after reading Forge’s assessment of your submitted answer.

Complex equality is a pair of real equalities.

Repair the omitted component equality, then apply both coordinates to the quotient model.

content.markdown:
Write the complex quotient $(2+i)/(1-2i)$ in Cartesian form $a+ib$. State why the division is defined.

### Target

Use the conjugate denominator, simplify both parts, and verify the quotient in the original multiplication.

### Strategy

Multiply numerator and denominator by $1+2i$, whose product with $1-2i$ is the positive real squared modulus.

### Hypotheses

The denominator $1-2i$ is nonzero, so its squared modulus is positive.

### Complete solution

The denominator $1-2i$ is nonzero, and its conjugate is $1+2i$. Multiplying numerator and denominator by that conjugate gives

$$\frac{2+i}{1-2i}=\frac{(2+i)(1+2i)}{(1-2i)(1+2i)}.$$

The denominator is $1^2+2^2=5$. The numerator is $2+4i+i+2i^2=5i$. Hence

$$\frac{2+i}{1-2i}=\frac{5i}{5}=i.$$

Multiplying $i(1-2i)=2+i$ checks the result in the original quotient.

### Boundary check

The identity $1/z=\bar z/|z|^2$ cannot be used at $z=0$, because then $|z|^2=0$ and the proposed denominator vanishes. Conjugation removes an imaginary part; it does not make division by zero legal.

The reciprocal identity contains $|z|^2$ in its denominator. At $z=0$, both the original and conjugated denominators vanish, so no equivalent quotient exists.

content.markdown:
# Conjugate equations describe exact Cartesian sets

Today component comparison becomes a proof of if-and-only-if characterizations and geometric line equations.

## Why both directions matter

Deriving a necessary coordinate condition is not yet a characterization. The converse confirms that every point on the proposed line or axis satisfies the original complex equation.

## Reactivate Cartesian equality for conjugate characterizations

To prove that $z=\bar z$ or $z=-\bar z$ characterizes a Cartesian axis, compare the real and imaginary components separately and preserve both directions of each equivalence.

content.markdown:
Prove $z\in\mathbb R$ if and only if $z=\bar z$, and prove that $z$ is purely imaginary if and only if $z=-\bar z$.

### Target

Establish both equivalences from Cartesian components.

### Strategy

Write $z=x+iy$ and its conjugate, then compare real and imaginary components.

### Hypotheses

$x,y$ are real.

### Complete solution

Let $z=x+iy$. The equation $z=\bar z$ is $x+iy=x-iy$, hence $2iy=0$, so $y=0$; conversely $y=0$ gives equality. Thus $z$ is real exactly when $z=\bar z$. Similarly, $z=-\bar z$ gives $x+iy=-x+iy$, hence $2x=0$; conversely $x=0$ gives the equation. Thus $z$ is purely imaginary exactly when $z=-\bar z$.

### Boundary check

Zero satisfies both characterizations: it is both real and purely imaginary.

## Week 3 substantial problem

Five-part problem, 90 minutes; feedback follows each attempt.

### Shared stem

Let $M(z)=(z-i)/(z+i)$ for $z\ne-i$. Study how $M$ transforms the real axis and the unit circle.

content.title: Part 1 · Real axis to unit circle

data.markdown: Likely issue: numerator and denominator moduli were not compared before Cartesian expansion, or the unattained point was inferred from a limit. First repair: prove the modulus identity first, then solve the finite-point equation separately from the two limits.

Likely issue: squaring the modulus equality was treated as one-way, or the pole was left in the locus. First repair: write an equivalence chain with nonnegative quantities and check the excluded denominator point at the end.

Likely issue: division by the exceptional value was hidden while solving for $z$, or only one composition was checked. First repair: isolate the coefficient of $z$, state when it is nonzero, and verify both substitutions before proving reality.

content.title: Part 4 · Unit circle to imaginary axis

data.markdown: Likely issue: the conjugate calculation does not end with the negative of the original value, or the inverse image was not checked on the circle. First repair: simplify the conjugate quotient line by line, then verify modulus and exclusion for the inverse point.

Likely issue: a missing point or the pole-at-infinity correspondence was omitted. First repair: write the two image statements as bijections with exclusions, then test the three named points and both infinite limits against them.

Use the page card for “Week 3, Day 4 · Solve conjugate systems and shifted modulus loci.”

Reference: section “Programme de mathématiques MPSI — Module et conjugaison”; anchor `C.ALGEBRA.MODULUS`; French Ministry CPGE mathematics programmes.

## What is now established

Two independent conjugate equations can determine both Cartesian components, and a shifted modulus gives a proved circle equation. Day 5 retrieves the nonzero-domain rule and synthesizes quotient and locus reasoning.

activities.title: Part 1 · Real axis to unit circle
activities.promptMarkdown: For real $x$, prove $|M(x)|=1$ and compute $M(x)$ in Cartesian form. Decide whether $1$ is attained and identify both limits as $x\to\pm\infty$.

rubric.label: Method and dependency
rubric.description: Select and justify the result needed from the preceding part.

rubric.label: Verified result
rubric.description: Complete the calculation or proof and state the verified conclusion.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: For real $x$, $|x-i|=|x+i|=\sqrt{x^2+1}$, so $|M(x)|=1$. Multiplying by $x-i$ gives $M(x)=(x^2-1)/(x^2+1)-[2x/(x^2+1)]i$. The equation $M(x)=1$ would imply $-i=i$, so no finite $x$ works. Both limits equal $1$. The Cartesian formula also records the sign of the imaginary part on each half-axis.

activities.title: Part 2 · Converse locus
activities.promptMarkdown: Let $z=x+iy\ne-i$. Starting from $|M(z)|=1$, reduce to a Cartesian equation, prove that squaring introduced no extra point, and state each reversible implication explicitly.

rubric.label: Method and dependency
rubric.description: Select and justify the result needed from the preceding part.

rubric.label: Verified result
rubric.description: Complete the calculation or proof and state the verified conclusion.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: $|M(z)|=1$ is equivalent to $|z-i|=|z+i|$. Squaring gives $x^2+(y-1)^2=x^2+(y+1)^2$, hence $y=0$. The converse holds for every real $z$, and the pole $-i$ is not real. Every implication has been reversed explicitly, so the Cartesian equation is an equivalent locus description.

activities.title: Part 3 · Construct the inverse
activities.promptMarkdown: Solve $w=M(z)$ for $z$, identify the exceptional value of $w$, and verify both compositions. Use the inverse to prove that every $|w|=1$ with $w\ne1$ has a real preimage.

rubric.label: Method and dependency
rubric.description: Select and justify the result needed from the preceding part.

rubric.label: Verified result
rubric.description: Complete the calculation or proof and state the verified conclusion.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: From $w(z+i)=z-i$, obtain $z=i(1+w)/(1-w)$, requiring $w\ne1$. Direct substitution verifies both compositions. If $|w|=1$, then $\overline w=1/w$; conjugating the inverse leaves it unchanged, so the preimage is real. The excluded value $w=1$ corresponds to the point at infinity rather than a lost finite preimage.

activities.title: Part 4 · Unit circle to imaginary axis
activities.promptMarkdown: Assume $|z|=1$ and $z\ne-i$. Prove by conjugation that $M(z)$ is purely imaginary. Then prove that every purely imaginary $w$ has a unique preimage on the unit circle other than $-i$.

rubric.label: Method and dependency
rubric.description: Select and justify the result needed from the preceding part.

rubric.label: Verified result
rubric.description: Complete the calculation or proof and state the verified conclusion.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Since $\overline z=1/z$, $\overline{M(z)}=(1+iz)/(1-iz)=-M(z)$, using $1+iz=i(z-i)$ and $1-iz=-i(z+i)$. Conversely, for $w=it$ with $t\in\mathbb R$, the inverse $z=i(1+it)/(1-it)$ has modulus $1$ and is not $-i$. The relation $\overline{M(z)}=-M(z)$ is exactly the conjugation test for a purely imaginary number.

activities.title: Part 5 · Extended geometric synthesis

# Friday tests whether the domain rule survives

The first work is closed-notes retrieval of the nonzero condition shared with Week 2's no-division rule. Later tasks combine conjugation, modulus, and component characterizations.

## Why a constant quotient is a useful final test

A parameterized expression can simplify completely only when every cross term and domain condition is controlled. Verification prevents a surprising simplification from being accepted on appearance.

## Reactivate Cartesian equality for synthesis

In a mixed quotient-and-locus problem, compare both Cartesian components and preserve each excluded denominator point before using a geometric conclusion.

## Deliberate review: do not divide away a zero branch

Recall Week 2's factor-before-division rule. In complex algebra the corresponding check is $z\ne0$ before using $1/z=\bar z/|z|^2$.

content.markdown:
For $z\ne0$, reconstruct the proof of $1/z=\bar z/|z|^2$.

### Target

Supply the missing multiplication by one and identify the positive real denominator.

### Strategy

Multiply numerator and denominator by $\bar z$.

### Hypotheses

$z\ne0$, so $|z|^2>0$.

### Complete solution

$1/z=(1/z)(\bar z/\bar z)=\bar z/(z\bar z)=\bar z/|z|^2$. The inserted factor is legal because $z\ne0$ implies $\bar z\ne0$.

### Boundary check

At zero, neither the original reciprocal nor the inserted factor $\bar z/\bar z$ is defined.

The identity $|zw|=|z||w|$ follows from squared moduli. In contrast, $|z+w|$ is generally bounded by, not equal to, $|z|+|w|$.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown:
For real $t$, $1-ti\ne0$ because its real part is one. Multiplying by $1+ti$ gives

$$\frac{(t+i)(1+ti)}{1+t^2}=\frac{t-t+i(t^2+1)}{1+t^2}=i.$$

The quotient is always $i$, whose imaginary part is one, so it is never real.

content.markdown:
# Polar form separates scale from angle

Today nonzero complex numbers acquire a positive modulus and an argument class. Quadrant signs and branch language remain explicit.

## Why representation matters

Cartesian form makes addition easy; polar form makes products, powers, and roots transparent. Choosing the representation by operation reduces algebra without weakening the domain.

## Reactivate the exact prerequisite for this lesson

Evaluate the polynomial exactly and identify the second root. Begin with the concrete case Verify that $i$ is a root of $X^2+1$. and keep every root, modulus, argument, and domain statement explicit.

content.markdown:
## Complex numbers · Polar

Every nonzero complex number has the form $z=re^{i\theta}$ with $r>0$; its arguments are the numbers $\theta+2k\pi$.

The modulus is uniquely determined and positive; the argument is a congruence class modulo $2\pi$. Multiplication multiplies moduli and adds arguments, while a chosen principal argument is only one representative.

content.markdown:
Write $-\sqrt3-i$ in polar form.

### Target

Determine modulus and an argument from exact coordinates and quadrant.

### Strategy

Compute the squared modulus, locate quadrant III, and use reference angle $\pi/6$.

### Hypotheses

The number is nonzero, so it has arguments.

### Complete solution

The modulus is $\sqrt{3+1}=2$. Both coordinates are negative, so the point is in quadrant III. The reference angle is $\pi/6$, hence one argument is $7\pi/6$. Therefore $-\sqrt3-i=2e^{7i\pi/6}$.

### Boundary check

The angle $\pi/6$ has the right tangent magnitude but the wrong coordinate signs.

# Roots divide an entire argument family

Today the positive root of the modulus is only half the work. The argument class splits into exactly as many residues as the exponent.

## Why branch enumeration matters

Reporting one principal root answers a branch convention, not the polynomial equation. The regular angular spacing provides both completeness and a geometric check.

## Reactivate the exact prerequisite for this lesson

Give one polar form and state all arguments. Begin with the concrete case Write $-8$ with a positive modulus and a full argument family. and keep every root, modulus, argument, and domain statement explicit.

content.markdown:
## Complex numbers · Roots

If $w=\rho e^{i\phi}\ne0$, its $n$th roots are $\rho^{1/n}e^{i(\phi+2k\pi)/n}$ for $k=0,\ldots,n-1$.

The modulus has one positive $n$th root, while the argument family splits into exactly $n$ residues modulo $2\pi$. Consecutive roots differ by the rotation $e^{2\pi i/n}$.

content.markdown:
Find all four complex solutions of $z^4=-16$, write them in polar form, and verify that their fourth powers equal $-16$.

### Target

Derive the root modulus and all four argument residues, then verify powers and distinctness.

### Strategy

Write the target argument as $\pi+2k\pi$ before dividing by four.

### Hypotheses

The target is nonzero and the exponent four is a positive integer.

### Complete solution

The number $-16$ has modulus $16$ and an argument $\pi$ modulo $2\pi$. A fourth root therefore has modulus $16^{1/4}=2$ and argument

$$\frac{\pi+2k\pi}{4}=\frac\pi4+\frac{k\pi}{2}$$

for $k=0,1,2,3$. The complete list is

$$2e^{i\pi/4},\quad2e^{3i\pi/4},\quad2e^{5i\pi/4},\quad2e^{7i\pi/4}.$$

Raising any listed number to the fourth power gives modulus $16$ and argument $\pi+2k\pi$, hence $-16$. Their arguments are distinct modulo $2\pi$, so the roots are distinct.

### Boundary check

Dividing only the principal argument and reporting $2e^{i\pi/4}$ misses three roots. The integer $k$ must run through four consecutive residues because fourth powers identify angles that differ by $2\pi/4$.

# Powers and quotients separate cleanly in polar form

Today moduli are powered or divided while arguments are multiplied or subtracted. Each operation keeps its own rule.

## Why the separated rules matter

Cartesian expansion of a high power is long and hides rotation. Polar form makes the scale and direction independently checkable.

## Reactivate the exact prerequisite for this lesson

Compute modulus and one argument with the correct quadrant. Begin with the concrete case Write $1-i$ in polar form. and keep every root, modulus, argument, and domain statement explicit.

content.markdown:
Compute $(1-i)^8$ exactly using polar form and verify its modulus.

### Target

Apply De Moivre's law to modulus and argument separately.

### Strategy

Use $1-i=\sqrt2e^{-i\pi/4}$, raise the modulus to the eighth power, and multiply the argument by eight.

### Hypotheses

The base is nonzero and the exponent is an integer.

### Complete solution

$(1-i)^8=(\sqrt2)^8e^{-2\pi i}=16$. The modulus check is $|1-i|^8=(\sqrt2)^8=16$, agreeing with $|16|$.

### Boundary check

Multiplying the modulus by eight instead of raising it to the eighth power would give the wrong scale.

content.markdown:
## Week 4 substantial problem

Five-part problem, 90 minutes; feedback follows each attempt.

### Shared stem

Let $\omega=e^{2i\pi/5}$. Study the regular pentagon with vertices $1,\omega,\omega^2,\omega^3,\omega^4$.

data.markdown: Likely issue: the geometric-sum proof divided before establishing $\omega\ne1$, or the barycenter argument did not use rotational invariance. First repair: state the nonzero divisor, then write the separate fixed-barycenter equation.

Likely issue: $\omega^2+\omega^{-2}$ was not expressed consistently in $t$, causing the wrong quadratic. First repair: square the definition of $t$, isolate the reciprocal-square sum, and substitute once.

Likely issue: the algebraic root was selected without an angle-sign argument, or the half-angle sign was left ambiguous. First repair: locate both angles on the circle before choosing each sign and then check the quadratic.

Likely issue: the diagonal-to-side quotient was simplified without factoring the complex difference, or the modulus sign was mishandled. First repair: factor the diagonal difference, cancel only positive lengths, and interpret the remaining modulus geometrically.

Likely issue: the conjugate roots were paired incorrectly or rotation was claimed to preserve lengths without identifying it as a unit-modulus multiplication. First repair: list the two conjugate pairs, build their quadratics, then justify distance preservation.

activities.title: Part 1 · Cyclotomic identity and symmetry
activities.promptMarkdown: Prove $1+\omega+\omega^2+\omega^3+\omega^4=0$ first as a geometric sum and then from rotational symmetry of the barycenter. Explain why division by $\omega-1$ is legal.

rubric.label: Method and dependency
rubric.description: Select and justify the result needed from the preceding part.

rubric.label: Verified result
rubric.description: Complete the calculation or proof and state the verified conclusion.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Since $\omega^5=1$ and $\omega\ne1$, $(\omega^5-1)/(\omega-1)=0$. If $B$ is the barycenter, rotation gives $\omega B=B$; because $\omega\ne1$, this forces $B=0$. The geometric argument is independent of the geometric-series calculation and therefore checks the same identity structurally. It also explains why the center is fixed.

activities.title: Part 2 · Reduce to a quadratic
activities.promptMarkdown: Divide by $\omega^2$, set $t=\omega+\omega^{-1}$, and express $\omega^2+\omega^{-2}$ in terms of $t$. Derive the quadratic equation for $t$ and find both roots.

rubric.label: Method and dependency
rubric.description: Select and justify the result needed from the preceding part.

rubric.label: Verified result
rubric.description: Complete the calculation or proof and state the verified conclusion.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Division gives $\omega^2+\omega+1+\omega^{-1}+\omega^{-2}=0$. Since $t^2=\omega^2+2+\omega^{-2}$, obtain $t^2+t-1=0$, hence $t=(-1\pm\sqrt5)/2$. Both algebraic roots remain possible until the location of $2\pi/5$ supplies the missing sign information. This is the decisive geometric input.

activities.title: Part 3 · Exact trigonometric values
activities.promptMarkdown: Select the correct root for $t$, deduce $\cos(2\pi/5)$ and $\cos(\pi/5)$, justify every sign from the angle locations, and verify the resulting values in the defining quadratic.

rubric.label: Method and dependency
rubric.description: Select and justify the result needed from the preceding part.

rubric.label: Verified result
rubric.description: Complete the calculation or proof and state the verified conclusion.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: $t=2\cos(2\pi/5)>0$, so $t=(\sqrt5-1)/2$ and $\cos(2\pi/5)=(\sqrt5-1)/4$. The positive half-angle gives $\cos(\pi/5)=(1+\sqrt5)/4$. Substitution into $4c^2+2c-1=0$ provides a direct check of $c=\cos(2\pi/5)$. The angle range rules out the negative root.

activities.title: Part 4 · Diagonal-to-side ratio
activities.promptMarkdown: Express a side and a diagonal as moduli, reduce their ratio to $|1+\omega|$, and prove that $\varphi=(1+\sqrt5)/2$ satisfies $\varphi^2=\varphi+1$. Explain its geometric meaning.

rubric.label: Method and dependency
rubric.description: Select and justify the result needed from the preceding part.

rubric.label: Verified result
rubric.description: Complete the calculation or proof and state the verified conclusion.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: A side is $|\omega-1|$ and a diagonal is $|\omega^2-1|=|\omega-1||\omega+1|$. Their ratio is $|1+\omega|=2\cos(\pi/5)=\varphi$. Direct calculation gives $\varphi^2=\varphi+1$, matching the similar-triangle decomposition of a pentagram diagonal. The factorization $\omega^2-1=(\omega-1)(\omega+1)$ is legitimate and preserves the nonzero side length. Thus the ratio loses no admissible case.

activities.title: Part 5 · Real factorization and rotation
activities.promptMarkdown: Factor $X^4+X^3+X^2+X+1$ over $\mathbb R$ using $t$. Identify each conjugate pair and explain why multiplication by $\omega$ preserves every side and diagonal.

rubric.label: Method and dependency
rubric.description: Select and justify the result needed from the preceding part.

rubric.label: Verified result
rubric.description: Complete the calculation or proof and state the verified conclusion.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: The pair $\omega,\omega^{-1}$ gives $X^2-tX+1$. The pair $\omega^2,\omega^3$ has sum $-(1+t)$ and gives $X^2+(1+t)X+1$. Their product is the stated polynomial because $t^2+t=1$. Multiplication by $\omega$ is a rotation through $2\pi/5$, so it preserves all distances. Multiplying the two quadratics and using $t^2+t=1$ checks every coefficient, not only the roots. Conjugation guarantees real coefficients throughout.

Compute $(\sqrt3+i)^6$ by supplying the missing polar conversion.

### Target

Recover modulus and argument, then apply the sixth-power law.

### Strategy

The reference angle and quadrant must be supplied before the power.

### Hypotheses

The base is nonzero and the exponent is an integer.

### Complete solution

$|\sqrt3+i|=2$ and an argument is $\pi/6$, so $\sqrt3+i=2e^{i\pi/6}$. Therefore $(\sqrt3+i)^6=2^6e^{i\pi}=-64$.

### Boundary check

Using argument $-\pi/6$ would conjugate the base and change the power's direction before reduction.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: The roots have modulus $2$ and arguments $\pi/6+k\pi/3$ for $k=0,\ldots,5$. Thus they are $2e^{i(\pi/6+k\pi/3)}$. lessons.title: Week 5, Day 1 · Preserve signs in real-order arguments
lessons.summary: Define Real numbers · Order, solve signed inequalities, and identify operations that reverse or destroy an inequality.
objectives: Define Real numbers · Order, solve signed inequalities, and identify operations that reverse or destroy an inequality.

content.markdown:
# Order arguments carry sign hypotheses

Every multiplication, division, reciprocal, square, or square-root step has a domain and a monotonicity rule. Today those rules remain visible rather than being hidden inside algebra.

## Why sign control matters

A formally neat inequality can be false after one unlicensed multiplication by an unknown-sign quantity. Concours proofs reward the short line that names the sign before the transformation.

## Reactivate the number line

Addition preserves order. Multiplication by a positive number preserves order, while multiplication by a negative number reverses it.

## Real numbers · Order

An order argument uses comparisons that remain valid under the stated operations; multiplication or division requires the sign of the factor.

An order proof records which operation is monotone on the current domain. Reciprocal and square functions are not globally increasing, so positivity or interval restrictions must precede their use.

content.markdown:
Solve $(x-1)(x+2)\le0$ on $\mathbb R$.

### Target

Locate zeros, determine the product sign on each interval, and include equality cases.

### Strategy

Order the critical points $-2<1$ and track the sign of each factor.

### Hypotheses

Both factors are defined for every real $x$.

### Complete solution

The factors vanish at $-2$ and $1$. For $x<-2$ both factors are negative, so the product is positive. For $-2<x<1$ the factors have opposite signs, so the product is negative. For $x>1$ both are positive. Equality holds at both zeros, hence the solution is $[-2,1]$.

### Boundary check

Testing only one point without separating at both zeros can miss a sign change.

lessons.title: Week 5, Day 2 · Prove a least upper bound
lessons.summary: Define Real numbers · Supremum, distinguish it from a maximum, and prove a candidate is least by defeating every smaller upper bound.
objectives: Define Real numbers · Supremum, distinguish it from a maximum, and prove a candidate is least by defeating every smaller upper bound.

content.markdown:
# A supremum has two proof obligations

First prove the candidate bounds the set. Then prove that every smaller real number fails to be an upper bound.

## Why membership is a separate question

A set may approach a boundary forever without containing it. The supremum records the sharp boundary; a maximum additionally requires membership.

## Reactivate quantified comparisons

To say that $M$ is an upper bound of $A$ means $x\le M$ for every $x\in A$. One favorable element cannot establish this universal statement.

**Reference path:** $3$ is an upper bound because every $x\in(0,3)$ satisfies $x<3$. The number $2$ is not: for example $5/2\in A$ and $5/2>2$.

content.markdown:
## Real numbers · Supremum

The supremum of a nonempty set bounded above is an upper bound no larger than any other upper bound.

For a candidate $s$, the usable characterization is: every element is at most $s$, and for every $u<s$ some element of the set exceeds $u$. The second clause is the constructive form of leastness.

content.markdown:
Let $A=\{1-1/n:n\in\mathbb N,\ n\ge1\}$. Prove that $\sup A=1$ and decide whether $A$ has a maximum.

### Target

Prove the candidate is an upper bound, prove leastness using an Archimedean choice, and decide membership.

### Strategy

Given $u<1$, choose an integer index large enough that the missing gap $1/n$ is smaller than $1-u$.

### Hypotheses

The set is nonempty, its indices satisfy $n\ge1$, and the Archimedean property supplies arbitrarily large integers.

### Complete solution

For every $n\ge1$, one has $1-1/n<1$, so $1$ is an upper bound of $A$. To prove it is the least upper bound, let $u<1$. Choose an integer $n>1/(1-u)$, which is possible by the Archimedean property. Then $1/n<1-u$, so

$$1-\frac1n>u.$$

Thus no number smaller than $1$ is an upper bound, and $\sup A=1$. Because $1-1/n$ is strictly less than $1$ for every finite $n$, the supremum does not belong to $A$. Therefore $A$ has no maximum.

### Boundary check

An upper bound is not automatically the supremum. For instance, $2$ bounds $A$ but is not least. Conversely, the supremum need not be a member of the set, so writing “maximum $=1$” would be false here.

## Supremum does not imply maximum

A maximum is an element of the set. A supremum is a least upper bound and may lie outside the set.

content.markdown:
## Transfer to a set defined by an inequality

A sharp-bound proof must use the defining inequality for every element and construct elements arbitrarily close to the candidate.

content.title: Identify a quadratic supremum
content.introMarkdown: Prove that $\sup A=\sqrt2$ and decide whether the supremum belongs to $A$.

data.markdown:
### Repair guide for “Identify a quadratic supremum”

Use this guide only after reading Forge’s assessment of your submitted answer.

For **Identify a quadratic supremum**, compare your response with the task-specific reference path below.

**Task:** Let $A=\{x\in\mathbb R:x\ge0\text{ and }x^2<2\}$.

**Reference path:** Every $x\in A$ is nonnegative with $x^2<2$, so $x<\sqrt2$ and $\sqrt2$ is an upper bound. For any $u<\sqrt2$, if $u<0$ then $0\in A$ exceeds $u$. If $0\le u<\sqrt2$, choose $x=(u+\sqrt2)/2$; then $u<x<\sqrt2$, and monotonicity of squaring on nonnegative numbers gives $x^2<2$, so $x\in A$. Thus no smaller number is an upper bound. Since $(\sqrt2)^2=2$, the supremum is not in $A$.

For **Identify a quadratic supremum**, the first mismatch that blocks “Prove that $\sup A=\sqrt2$ and decide whether the supremum belongs to $A$.” is your repair point.

Without correcting **Identify a quadratic supremum**, this required evidence remains unsupported: Prove that $\sup A=\sqrt2$ and decide whether the supremum belongs to $A$.

# Four boundary notions answer different questions

Supremum and infimum concern sharp bounds; maximum and minimum additionally require membership.

## Why the vocabulary matters

A correct value with the wrong status can invalidate the conclusion of an optimization or convergence argument.

## Reactivate upper and lower comparisons

Upper bounds sit above every set element; lower bounds sit below every set element.

content.markdown:
Let $A=\{1/n:n\ge1\}$. Find its infimum and minimum.

### Target

Prove the lower bound is greatest and decide attainment.

### Strategy

Use positivity and choose $n$ larger than the reciprocal of a proposed positive lower bound.

### Hypotheses

Indices are positive integers.

### Complete solution

Every $1/n$ is positive, so $0$ is a lower bound. If $v>0$, choose $n>1/v$; then $1/n<v$, so $v$ is not a lower bound. Hence $\inf A=0$. Since $1/n\ne0$ for every finite $n$, the set has no minimum.

### Boundary check

The first term $1$ is the maximum, not the minimum.

## Week 5 substantial problem

Five-part problem, 90 minutes; feedback follows each attempt.

### Shared stem

Let A and B be nonempty subsets of the real line, both bounded above. Write $a=\sup A$ and $b=\sup B$, and define $A+B=\{x+y:x \in A and y \in B\}$.

content.title: Part 1 · Construct the candidate upper bound

data.markdown: Likely issue: nonemptiness and boundedness were asserted together without witnesses or separate upper-bound inequalities. First repair: choose one element of each set, then prove the candidate bound for an arbitrary sum element.

content.title: Part 2 · Prove sharpness from epsilon witnesses

data.markdown: Likely issue: each supremum witness used the full $\varepsilon$, leaving no strict margin after addition. First repair: split the tolerance between the two sets and add the resulting strict inequalities.

Likely issue: equality of suprema was concluded from an upper bound alone, or maximum attainment was proved in only one direction. First repair: combine upper-bound and epsilon-witness arguments, then prove both implications for attainment.
Likely issue: subtraction was treated like addition without reversing the bounds for the second set. First repair: express $A-B$ as a sum with $-B$ and derive the extrema of $-B$ before substituting.

content.title: Part 5 · All scalar and affine images

data.markdown: Likely issue: the negative-scalar case kept the order of supremum and infimum unchanged. First repair: separate the three signs of $\lambda$ and build an epsilon witness from the opposite extremum when $\lambda<0$.

activities.title: Part 1 · Construct the candidate upper bound
activities.promptMarkdown: Prove that $A+B$ is nonempty and bounded above, and that $a+b$ is an upper bound. State exactly where nonemptiness and the two boundedness assumptions enter.

rubric.label: Method and dependency
rubric.description: Select and justify the result needed from the preceding part.

rubric.label: Verified result
rubric.description: Complete the calculation or proof and state the verified conclusion.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Choose $x_{0}$ in A and $y_{0}$ in B; then $x_{0}+y_{0}$ belongs to $A+B$, so the sum set is nonempty. Since $x\le a$ for every x in A and $y\le b$ for every y in B, every element $x+y$ of $A+B$ satisfies $x+y\le a+b$. Boundedness above supplies the finite numbers a and b; nonemptiness makes their suprema and the sum set meaningful.

activities.title: Part 2 · Prove sharpness from epsilon witnesses
activities.promptMarkdown: Given $\varepsilon>0$, construct one element of $A+B$ larger than $a+b-\varepsilon$. Justify why the supremum property supplies both witnesses even when neither supremum belongs to its set.

rubric.label: Method and dependency
rubric.description: Select and justify the result needed from the preceding part.

rubric.label: Verified result
rubric.description: Complete the calculation or proof and state the verified conclusion.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Because $a=\sup A$, the number $a-\varepsilon/2$ is not an upper bound of A, so some x in A satisfies $a-\varepsilon/2<x\le a$. Likewise choose y in B with $b-\varepsilon/2<y\le b$. Then $x+y>a+b-\varepsilon$. This uses approximation from below and does not require a in A or b in B.

activities.title: Part 3 · Supremum and attainment
activities.promptMarkdown: Conclude that $\sup (A+B) = a+b$. Then prove that $A+B$ has maximum $a+b$ exactly when A has maximum a and B has maximum b.

rubric.label: Method and dependency
rubric.description: Select and justify the result needed from the preceding part.

rubric.label: Verified result
rubric.description: Complete the calculation or proof and state the verified conclusion.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Part $1$ makes $a+b$ an upper bound, while Part $2$ shows every smaller number fails to be one; hence $\sup (A+B) = a+b$. If a belongs to A and b belongs to B, their sum is the maximum. Conversely, if $x+y=a+b$ with x in A and y in B, then $x\le a$ and $y\le b$. Any strict inequality in either coordinate would make $x+y<a+b$, so $x=a$ and $y=b$. Thus both suprema must be attained.

activities.title: Part 4 · Infima and difference sets
activities.promptMarkdown: Now assume A and B are also bounded below. Prove $\inf (A+B) = \inf A + \inf B$, and then derive exact formulas for $\sup (A-B)$ and $\inf (A-B)$, where $A-B=\{x-y:x \in A,y \in B\}$.

rubric.label: Method and dependency
rubric.description: Select and justify the result needed from the preceding part.

rubric.label: Verified result
rubric.description: Complete the calculation or proof and state the verified conclusion.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Let $\alpha=\inf A$ and $\beta=\inf B$. Every $x+y$ is at least $\alpha+\beta$, and epsilon witnesses $x<\alpha+\varepsilon/2$, $y<\beta+\varepsilon/2$ show that no larger lower bound works; hence $\inf (A+B) = \alpha+\beta$. Negation reverses order: -$\inf B$ is the least upper bound of -B and -$\sup B$ is its greatest lower bound, as the same epsilon witnesses verify. Since $A-B=A+(-B)$, we obtain $\sup (A-B) = \sup A - \inf B$ and $\inf (A-B) = \inf A - \sup B$.

activities.title: Part 5 · All scalar and affine images
activities.promptMarkdown: For a nonempty bounded set A and real $\lambda$, determine both $\sup (\lambda A)$ and $\inf (\lambda A)$ in the cases $\lambda>0$, $\lambda<0$, and $\lambda=0$. Deduce formulas for the affine image $\lambda A+c$ and prove the negative-scalar case with an epsilon witness rather than only citing order reversal.

rubric.label: Method and dependency
rubric.description: Select and justify the result needed from the preceding part.

rubric.label: Verified result
rubric.description: Complete the calculation or proof and state the verified conclusion.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: If $\lambda>0$, order is preserved, so $\sup (\lambda A) = \lambda \sup A$ and $\inf (\lambda A) = \lambda \inf A$. If $\lambda<0$, order reverses, so $\sup (\lambda A) = \lambda \inf A$ and $\inf (\lambda A) = \lambda \sup A$. For sharpness of the first negative formula, choose x in A with $\inf A ≤ x<\inf A + \varepsilon/|\lambda|$; then $\lambda x>\lambda \inf A - \varepsilon$. If $\lambda=0$, $\lambda A=\{0\}$, so both extrema are $0$. Translation adds c to every bound, giving the corresponding formulas for $\lambda A+c$.

Let $A=\{n/(n+2):n\ge1\}$. Prove the missing leastness line in the claim $\sup A=1$.

### Target

Supply the index choice that places a set element above an arbitrary $u<1$.

### Strategy

Rewrite $n/(n+2)=1-2/(n+2)$.

### Hypotheses

The index is a positive integer and $1-u>0$.

### Complete solution

Every element is below $1$. Given $u<1$, choose $n$ with $n+2>2/(1-u)$. Then $2/(n+2)<1-u$, so $n/(n+2)=1-2/(n+2)>u$. Thus $1$ is the least upper bound.

### Boundary check

Showing only that all elements are below $1$ proves upper boundedness, not leastness.

## Sequences · Convergence

$(u_n)$ converges to $\ell$ when, for every $\varepsilon>0$, some $N$ makes $|u_n-\ell|<\varepsilon$ for all $n\ge N$.

Prove that $1/n\to0$ as $n\to\infty$.

### Target

Construct a threshold for an arbitrary positive tolerance.

### Strategy

Solve $1/n<\varepsilon$ for the positive integer $n$.

### Hypotheses

Indices satisfy $n\ge1$ and $\varepsilon>0$.

### Complete solution

Let $\varepsilon>0$. Choose an integer $N>1/\varepsilon$. For every $n\ge N$, positivity gives $0<1/n\le1/N<\varepsilon$. Thus $|1/n-0|<\varepsilon$, proving $1/n\to0$.

### Boundary check

The threshold depends on $\varepsilon$; choosing one fixed $N$ for all positive tolerances is impossible.

content.markdown:
For $n\ge0$, let $u_n=n/(n+1)$. Prove that $(u_n)$ is increasing and bounded above, and determine its limit.

### Target

Prove definition, monotonicity, upper boundedness, and the numerical limit in the correct order.

### Strategy

Compute the consecutive difference, rewrite the sequence relative to the proposed bound, then identify the limit.

### Hypotheses

Indices satisfy $n\ge0$, so all denominators are positive.

### Complete solution

The terms are defined because $n+1>0$. Their consecutive difference is

$$u_{n+1}-u_n=\frac{n+1}{n+2}-\frac{n}{n+1}=\frac{1}{(n+1)(n+2)}>0.$$

Hence the sequence is strictly increasing. Also $u_n=1-1/(n+1)<1$, so it is bounded above by $1$. The monotone convergence theorem gives convergence to a finite limit. Finally, $1/(n+1)\to0$, so

$$u_n=1-\frac1{n+1}\longrightarrow1.$$

### Boundary check

Increasing does not mean convergent without an upper bound. The sequence $v_n=n$ satisfies $v_{n+1}>v_n$ for every $n$ but diverges to $+\infty$.

# Limit laws compress error estimates

Each algebraic law rests on a bound for the new error and the hypotheses that make products or quotients safe.

## Why the proofs matter

Memorized limit laws can be misapplied to a zero denominator or an unbounded factor. The proof reveals the missing hypothesis immediately.

## Reactivate the triangle inequality

To control a sum error, split it into two errors and allocate part of the tolerance to each.

Assume $u_n\to a$ and $v_n\to b$. Prove $u_n+v_n\to a+b$.

### Target

Choose a common tail threshold and control the combined error.

### Strategy

Apply each convergence definition with tolerance $\varepsilon/2$ and take the larger threshold.

### Hypotheses

Both sequences converge to finite real limits.

### Complete solution

Let $\varepsilon>0$. Choose $N_1$ so $|u_n-a|<\varepsilon/2$ for $n\ge N_1$ and $N_2$ so $|v_n-b|<\varepsilon/2$ for $n\ge N_2$. For $n\ge\max(N_1,N_2)$, the triangle inequality gives $|(u_n+v_n)-(a+b)|<\varepsilon$.

### Boundary check

Using only $N_1$ may leave the second sequence outside its controlled tail.

## Week 6 substantial problem

Five-part problem, 90 minutes; feedback follows each attempt.

### Shared stem

Let $u_{0}>0$ and $u_{n+1}=(u_{n}+3/u_{n})/2$. Study this Newton sequence for $\sqrt{3}$.

content.title: Part 1 · Positivity and the first overshoot

data.markdown: Likely issue: positivity was used before it was propagated, or the first-step lower bound lacks an equality audit. First repair: prove the denominator and numerator signs by induction, then derive the overshoot from one exact nonnegative expression.

content.title: Part 2 · Invariant half-line and exact error

data.markdown: Likely issue: invariance was inferred from the fixed point, or the error recurrence lost its denominator. First repair: evaluate the update relative to $\sqrt3$ exactly and keep the positive denominator through the bound.

Likely issue: the sign of $u_{n+1}-u_n$ was decided before using the invariant half-line, or index $0$ was included without proof. First repair: factor the difference and apply the Part 2 bound only for the justified indices.

Likely issue: convergence was claimed from monotonicity alone, or the negative fixed point was discarded circularly. First repair: name the monotone convergence theorem with its lower bound, then use positivity after solving the limit equation.

Likely issue: the fractional error transformation was simplified without checking its nonzero denominator, or the squaring law was not iterated exactly. First repair: compute the transformed next term as one fraction, then solve that recurrence before reconstructing $u_n$.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: If $u_{n}>0$, then $u_{n}$ and $3/u_{n}$ are positive, so their average $u_{n+1}$ is positive. Moreover $u_{n+1}-\sqrt{3}=(u_{n}-\sqrt{3})^{2}/(2u_{n})\ge 0$. Applied at $n=0$, this gives $u_{1}\ge \sqrt{3}$, with equality exactly when $u_{0}=\sqrt{3}$. This is also the AM-GM inequality for $u_{0}$ and $3/u_{0}$.

activities.title: Part 2 · Invariant half-line and exact error
activities.promptMarkdown: Prove that $[\sqrt3,\infty)$ is invariant. For $e_n=u_n-\sqrt3$, derive the exact recurrence for $e_{n+1}$, including its denominator, and obtain a quadratic upper bound for $n\ge1$.

rubric.label: Method and dependency
rubric.description: Select and justify the result needed from the preceding part.

rubric.label: Verified result
rubric.description: Complete the calculation or proof and state the verified conclusion.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Part $1$ sends every positive input into $[\sqrt3,\infty)$. Direct subtraction gives $e_{n+1}=(u_n-\sqrt3)^2/(2u_n)=e_n^2/(2u_n)$. For $n\ge1$, $u_n\ge\sqrt3$, hence $0\le e_{n+1}\le e_n^2/(2\sqrt3)$. The denominator cannot be discarded before positivity is known.

activities.title: Part 3 · Monotonicity after the overshoot
activities.promptMarkdown: Compute $u_{n+1}-u_{n}$ and prove that the sequence is nonincreasing from index $1$. Determine all equality cases and explain why no monotonicity claim about the initial step is needed.

rubric.label: Method and dependency
rubric.description: Select and justify the result needed from the preceding part.

rubric.label: Verified result
rubric.description: Complete the calculation or proof and state the verified conclusion.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: We have $u_{n+1}-u_{n}=(3-u_{n}^{2})/(2u_{n})$. For $n\ge 1$, $u_{n}\ge \sqrt{3}$ and $u_{n}>0$, so the difference is nonpositive. Equality occurs exactly when $u_{n}=\sqrt{3}$, after which every later term equals $\sqrt{3}$. The step from $u_{0}$ to $u_{1}$ may rise or fall depending on $u_{0}$; convergence uses monotonicity only on the tail beginning at $u_{1}$.

activities.title: Part 4 · Convergence and identification
activities.promptMarkdown: Use a named convergence theorem to prove that $u_{n}$ has a finite limit. Pass to the limit with every nonzero condition justified, identify the limit, and rule out the negative fixed point without circular reasoning.

rubric.label: Method and dependency
rubric.description: Select and justify the result needed from the preceding part.

rubric.label: Verified result
rubric.description: Complete the calculation or proof and state the verified conclusion.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: From Part $3$, $(u_{n})_{n\ge 1}$ is nonincreasing, and Part $2$ bounds it below by $\sqrt{3}$. The monotone convergence theorem gives a limit $\ell\ge \sqrt{3}>0$. Continuity of x↦$(x+3/x)/2$ on the positive half-line gives $\ell=(\ell+3/\ell)/2$, hence $\ell^{2}=3$. The lower bound forces $\ell=\sqrt{3}$, independently of the fixed-point calculation's negative root.

activities.title: Part 5 · Closed error formula
activities.promptMarkdown: Define $r_{n}=(u_{n}-\sqrt{3})/(u_{n}+\sqrt{3})$. Prove $r_{n+1}=r_{n}^{2}$, solve this recurrence exactly, reconstruct $u_{n}$ from $r_{n}$, and use the formula to explain quantitatively why the number of correct digits roughly doubles near the limit.

rubric.label: Method and dependency
rubric.description: Select and justify the result needed from the preceding part.

rubric.label: Verified result
rubric.description: Complete the calculation or proof and state the verified conclusion.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Writing $s=\sqrt{3}$ and $u'=(u+3/u)/2=(u^{2}+s^{2})/(2u)$, we obtain $(u'-s)/(u'+s)=(u-s)^{2}/(u+s)^{2}$. Thus $r_{n+1}=r_{n}^{2}$ and $r_{n}=r_{0}^{2^{n}}$. Since $u_{n}=s(1+r_{n})/(1-r_{n})$, the error is $u_{n}-s=2sr_{n}/(1-r_{n})$. For $u_{0}>0$, $|r_{0}|<1$, so the exponent $2^{n}$ makes the transformed error square at each step. Once the error is small, its decimal exponent approximately doubles.

# A subsequence selects terms without changing their order

Its index map is strictly increasing, so selected indices eventually pass every original tail threshold.

## Why the index map is mathematical data

A list of familiar terms is not enough. Strict increase proves that the selection moves forward and supports inherited convergence.

## Reactivate tail thresholds

If $u_n\to\ell$, every index beyond a fixed threshold gives a term inside the requested tolerance.

## Sequences · Subsequence

A subsequence has the form $(u_{\varphi(n)})$, where $\varphi:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N$ is strictly increasing.

Strict increase of $\varphi$ implies $\varphi(n)\ge n$ after the initial indexing convention, so selected indices tend to infinity. Repetition or backward movement would not define a subsequence.

Assume $u_n\to\ell$ and $\varphi:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N$ is strictly increasing. Prove $u_{\varphi(k)}\to\ell$.

### Target

Transfer an arbitrary original threshold through the lower bound on selected indices.

### Strategy

Use $\varphi(k)\ge k$ and choose $k$ beyond the original threshold.

### Hypotheses

The original sequence converges and the selection map is strictly increasing.

### Complete solution

Let $\varepsilon>0$. Choose $N$ such that $n\ge N$ implies $|u_n-\ell|<\varepsilon$. Strict increase gives $\varphi(k)\ge k$, so for every $k\ge N$, $\varphi(k)\ge N$. Hence $|u_{\varphi(k)}-\ell|<\varepsilon$, proving the subsequence converges to $\ell$.

### Boundary check

A map that repeatedly selects one early index does not eventually enter the controlled tail.

# Selected limits and recurrence stability answer different questions

Cluster values describe limits visible along subsequences; recurrence analysis first proves that every term remains defined.

## Why fixed points are only candidates

A fixed-point equation can identify a possible limit, but stability and an actual convergence mechanism must precede passage to the limit.

## Reactivate selected-limit logic

A convergent full sequence gives the same limit along every subsequence; two different cluster values therefore rule out full convergence.

## Sequences · Recurrence

A recurrence defines later terms from earlier ones; its analysis must first prove that every term is defined and remains in a stable set.

A recurrence proof separates existence and stability of the orbit from asymptotic analysis. A fixed point becomes a limit only after convergence is established or a contraction error is proved.

content.markdown:
Let $u_0\in[0,2]$ and define $u_{n+1}=(u_n+1)/2$. Prove that every term is defined, that $[0,2]$ is stable, and that $u_n\to1$.

### Target

Prove definition and stability, identify the fixed point, derive the exact contraction error, and conclude.

### Strategy

Establish the invariant interval by induction before subtracting the fixed point.

### Hypotheses

The initial value lies in $[0,2]$.

### Complete solution

If $u_n\in[0,2]$, then $(u_n+1)/2\in[1/2,3/2]\subset[0,2]$. Since $u_0\in[0,2]$, induction proves that every term is defined and remains in that interval. Subtracting the fixed point $1$ gives

$$u_{n+1}-1=\frac{u_n-1}{2}.$$

A second induction yields $u_n-1=2^{-n}(u_0-1)$. Because $2^{-n}\to0$, the right-hand side tends to zero and therefore $u_n\to1$.

### Boundary check

The equation $\ell=(\ell+1)/2$ identifies the only possible limit, namely $1$, but it does not prove convergence. Stability and the contraction identity are the steps that justify taking a limit.

# Cluster classification has existence and exclusion halves

Each claimed value needs a witnessing subsequence; every other candidate must be ruled out.

## Why listing visible patterns is incomplete

A sequence can have a hidden continuum of selected limits. Proof requires control of all possible selections.

## Reactivate witness structure

A cluster claim names a strict index map and proves the selected terms converge.

content.title: Write a complete witness
content.introMarkdown: Witness the cluster value $-1$.

data.markdown:

Use this guide only after reading Forge’s assessment of your submitted answer.

For **Write a complete witness**, compare your response with the task-specific reference path below.

**Task:** Let $u_n=\cos(n\pi)$.

**Reference path:** Take $\varphi(k)=2k+1$. It is strictly increasing and $u_{\varphi(k)}=\cos((2k+1)\pi)=-1$, so the selected sequence converges to $-1$.

For **Write a complete witness**, the first mismatch that blocks “Witness the cluster value $-1$.” is your repair point.

content.markdown:
Find all cluster values of $u_n=(-1)^n+1/n$.

### Target

Witness both parity limits and exclude every other selected limit.

### Strategy

Separate any selected indices by parity and use the vanishing reciprocal.

### Hypotheses

Indices satisfy $n\ge1$.

### Complete solution

Even terms are $1+1/(2k)\to1$, and odd terms are $-1+1/(2k+1)\to-1$, so both values occur. Any subsequence contains either infinitely many even or infinitely many odd indices; selecting that parity again yields a sub-subsequence tending to $1$ or $-1$. If the original selected sequence converged, every sub-subsequence would share its limit, so no other cluster value is possible.

### Boundary check

Witnessing two values does not by itself exclude a third; the parity exhaustion supplies that step.

content.introMarkdown: Prove it has an infinite even or infinite odd selection.

Every subsequence inherits the full limit, while the full sequence is itself selected by the identity map.

For a finite-period sequence, each residue class supplies one constant subsequence and exhausts all indices.
