## Week 7 substantial problem

Five-part problem, 90 minutes; feedback follows each attempt.

### Shared stem

Analyze two genuinely nonlinear recurrences. A: $u_{0}$ in $(0,1)$, $u_{n+1}=u_{n}(2-u_{n})$. B: $v_{0}>0$, $v_{n+1}=2v_{n}/(1+v_{n})$.

content.title: Part 1 · Recurrence A: invariant interval and error law

data.markdown: Likely issue: invariance checks only one endpoint, or the error recurrence was guessed from the fixed point. First repair: bound $x(2-x)$ on the whole interval and compute $1-f(x)$ exactly.

content.title: Part 2 · Recurrence A: exact solution and speed

data.markdown: Likely issue: repeated squaring was converted to the wrong exponent, or the logarithmic iteration bound reverses an inequality. First repair: write the first three error terms, identify the exponent pattern, and solve the tolerance inequality with sign-aware logarithms.

Likely issue: the reciprocal substitution was made before proving positivity, or the affine recurrence was solved with the wrong fixed point. First repair: establish nonvanishing by induction, derive the recurrence for $w_n$, and verify the reconstructed denominator.

content.title: Part 4 · Recurrence B: invariant sides and convergence

data.markdown: Likely issue: the sign of the increment was not factored around $1$, so crossing and monotonicity were conflated. First repair: factor $v_{n+1}-v_n$, then treat initial values below, equal to, and above $1$ separately.

content.title: Part 5 · Compare the two convergence mechanisms

data.markdown: Likely issue: convergence rates were compared in the original variables rather than their exact transformed errors. First repair: write both transformed recurrences side by side and derive each iteration count from its own tolerance inequality.

## Further reading

Use the page card for “Week 7, Day 4 · Extract convergence from bounded sequences.”

Reference pages: 14–19.

## What is now established

Every bounded real sequence has a convergent subsequence; boundedness plus one cluster value forces full convergence only with an exclusion argument. Day 5 retrieves earlier structures.

activities.title: Part 1 · Recurrence A: invariant interval and error law
activities.promptMarkdown: Prove that $(0,1)$ is invariant under $f(x)=x(2-x)$. Derive an exact recurrence for $e_{n}=1-u_{n}$, and explain why proving only that $1$ is a fixed point would not establish convergence.

rubric.label: Method and dependency
rubric.description: Select and justify the result needed from the preceding part.

rubric.label: Verified result
rubric.description: Complete the calculation or proof and state the verified conclusion.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: For $0<x<1$, $f(x)>0$ and $1-f(x)=1-2x+x^{2}=(1-x)^{2}$ lies in $(0,1)$, so $0<f(x)<1$. Hence $e_{n+1}=e_{n}^{2}$ with $0<e_{0}<1$. A fixed-point equation identifies possible limits only; invariance and the solved error recurrence supply the actual convergence argument.

activities.title: Part 2 · Recurrence A: exact solution and speed
activities.promptMarkdown: Solve the error recurrence exactly, deduce monotonicity and the limit of $(u_n)$, and determine the smallest $n$ that guarantees $1-u_n\le\varepsilon$ in terms of $e_0$ and $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$.

rubric.label: Method and dependency
rubric.description: Select and justify the result needed from the preceding part.

rubric.label: Verified result
rubric.description: Complete the calculation or proof and state the verified conclusion.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Iteration gives $e_n=e_0^{2^n}$, so $u_n=1-e_0^{2^n}$. Also $u_{n+1}-u_n=u_n(1-u_n)>0$, so $u_n\to1$. The condition is $2^n\ge\log(\varepsilon)/\log(e_0)$. Thus $n\ge\left\lceil\log_2[\log(\varepsilon)/\log(e_0)]\right\rceil$, with $n=0$ allowed when the initial error already meets the tolerance.

activities.title: Part 3 · Recurrence B: reciprocal linearization
activities.promptMarkdown: Prove positivity of every $v_{n}$, set $w_{n}=1/v_{n}$, and derive and solve the affine recurrence for $w_{n}$. Reconstruct an explicit formula for $v_{n}$ and state why its denominator never vanishes.

rubric.label: Method and dependency
rubric.description: Select and justify the result needed from the preceding part.

rubric.label: Verified result
rubric.description: Complete the calculation or proof and state the verified conclusion.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Positive $v_{n}$ gives positive $v_{n+1}$, so reciprocals are defined. We have $w_{n+1}=(1+v_{n})/(2v_{n})=(w_{n}+1)/2$, hence $w_{n}=1+2^{-n}(w_{0}-1)$. Therefore $v_{n}=1/[1+2^{-n}(1/v_{0}-1)]$. The bracket is a convex combination of $1/v_{0}>0$ and $1$, so it remains positive and never vanishes.

activities.title: Part 4 · Recurrence B: invariant sides and convergence
activities.promptMarkdown: Determine the sign of $v_{n+1}-v_{n}$, prove that a term starting below $1$ never crosses above $1$ and a term starting above $1$ never crosses below, and conclude convergence without relying only on the explicit formula.

rubric.label: Method and dependency
rubric.description: Select and justify the result needed from the preceding part.

rubric.label: Verified result
rubric.description: Complete the calculation or proof and state the verified conclusion.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Direct calculation gives $v_{n+1}-v_{n}=v_{n}(1-v_{n})/(1+v_{n})$. Also $v_{n+1}-1=(v_{n}-1)/(1+v_{n})$, so the sign relative to $1$ is preserved. Thus a start below $1$ produces an increasing sequence bounded above by $1$, while a start above $1$ produces a decreasing sequence bounded below by $1$. Monotone convergence gives a positive limit, and the fixed-point equation forces that limit to be $1$.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: For A, $e_{n+1}=e_{n}^{2}$, so $e_{n}=\delta^{2^{n}}$; the error exponent doubles and the convergence is quadratic. For B, $d_{n}=w_{n}-1$ satisfies $d_{n+1}=d_{n}/2$, so $|d_{n}|=\delta2^{-n}$; this is linear convergence with ratio $1/2$. The first needs $2^{n}\ge \log(\varepsilon)/\log(\delta)$, while the second needs $n\ge \log_{2}(\delta/\varepsilon)$. The different growth laws make the quadratic iteration eventually much faster.

Find the cluster values of $u_n=\cos(n\pi/2)$.

### Target

Supply the residue-class values and exclusion argument.

### Strategy

Evaluate one full period of length four.

### Hypotheses

Indices are integers.

### Complete solution

For residues $0,1,2,3$ modulo four, the values are $1,0,-1,0$. Thus $1$, $0$, and $-1$ each have constant witnessing subsequences. Every index has one of these residues, so any convergent selected sequence has a further constant-residue selection with one of these values. Hence the exact cluster set is $\{-1,0,1\}$.

### Boundary check

The value $0$ occurs in two residue classes but is one cluster value, not two.

## Why oscillation need not destroy continuity

An oscillating factor can be controlled by a shrinking amplitude. The estimate, not a graphing impression, decides the point behavior.

content.markdown:
Define $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ by $f(0)=0$ and $f(x)=x\sin(1/x)$ for $x\ne0$. Prove that $f$ is continuous at $0$.

### Target

Match the nearby limit to the assigned value using a squeeze estimate.

### Strategy

Bound the oscillating sine factor before taking the limit.

### Hypotheses

The piecewise definition assigns $f(0)=0$.

### Complete solution

Continuity at $0$ requires $f(x)\to f(0)=0$ as $x\to0$. For $x\ne0$, the bound $|\sin(1/x)|\le1$ gives

$$|f(x)-f(0)|=|x\sin(1/x)|\le|x|.$$

The right-hand side tends to zero. By the squeeze theorem, $f(x)\to0=f(0)$, so $f$ is continuous at $0$. The oscillation of $\sin(1/x)$ causes no problem because the multiplying factor $x$ controls its size.

### Boundary check

If the same formula for $x\ne0$ were paired with $f(0)=1$, the limit would still be $0$ but would not equal the assigned value. A finite limit at a point is not continuity unless the function is defined there with that limit value.

# Continuity fills the values between endpoint images

The domain must be an interval connecting the two inputs; the theorem proves existence of a preimage.

## Why sign changes find roots

If a continuous function moves from negative to positive, it must take the intermediate value zero somewhere between.

content.markdown:
Prove that $x^3+x-1=0$ has a solution in $(0,1)$.

### Target

Verify continuity, endpoint inequalities, and the interval conclusion.

### Strategy

Apply the intermediate value theorem to zero.

### Hypotheses

Polynomials are continuous on real intervals.

### Complete solution

Set $f(x)=x^3+x-1$. The function is continuous on $[0,1]$, with $f(0)=-1$ and $f(1)=1$. Since $0$ lies between these values, the intermediate value theorem gives $c\in(0,1)$ with $f(c)=0$.

### Boundary check

The theorem supplies existence; strict increase of $f$ would be a separate uniqueness proof.

content.markdown:
## Week 8 substantial problem

Five-part problem, 90 minutes; feedback follows each attempt.

### Shared stem

### Compact-extrema model before the problem

A continuous real-valued function on a closed bounded interval attains both a minimum and a maximum. For example, on $[0,1]$, $g(x)=x(1-x)=\tfrac14-(x-\tfrac12)^2$. Therefore $g$ attains its maximum $1/4$ at $x=1/2$ and its minimum $0$ at the endpoints. On the open interval $(0,1)$ the infimum $0$ is not attained, which shows why the compact-domain hypothesis matters. In Part 1, first identify the compact interval and the attained extrema; only then use strict increase and the endpoint signs to locate the zero.

For a parameter $\lambda>0$, study $f_\lambda(x)=x^{3}+\lambda x-1$.

First repair: state why $f_\lambda$ attains its extrema on $[0,1]$, identify them from strict increase, then use the endpoint signs for existence and the factorization for uniqueness.

content.title: Part 2 · Order the roots by the parameter

Likely issue: both bounds were derived from the same side of the root equation, so one limiting regime is unsupported. First repair: use $0<a_\lambda<1$ once to bound the linear term and once to compare the cubic and linear terms.

Likely issue: the subtraction identity has a sign error or its denominator was bounded in the wrong direction. First repair: factor the cubic difference before isolating the root difference, then apply only positive lower bounds to the denominator.

activities.promptMarkdown: On the compact interval $[0,1]$, first justify that $f_\lambda$ attains a minimum and a maximum and identify both from strict increase. Then prove that it has a unique zero $a_\lambda$ in $(0,1)$ for every $\lambda>0$, without differentiating, by factoring $f_\lambda(y)-f_\lambda(x)$.

rubric.label: Method and dependency
rubric.description: Select and justify the result needed from the preceding part.

rubric.label: Verified result
rubric.description: Complete the calculation or proof and state the verified conclusion.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: The polynomial $f_\lambda$ is continuous on the compact interval $[0,1]$, so the extreme value theorem guarantees an attained minimum and maximum. If $y>x$, then $f_\lambda(y)-f_\lambda(x)=(y-x)(y^{2}+xy+x^{2}+\lambda)>0$ because $\lambda>0$; hence $f_\lambda$ is strictly increasing. Its minimum is $f_\lambda(0)=-1$ and its maximum is $f_\lambda(1)=\lambda>0$. The intermediate value theorem therefore gives a zero in $(0,1)$, and strict increase makes that zero unique.

activities.title: Part 2 · Order the roots by the parameter
activities.promptMarkdown: For $0<\lambda<\mu$, compare $a_\lambda$ and $a_\mu$ in two independent ways: by evaluating one function at the other's root, and by subtracting the two root equations. Preserve the strict inequality.

rubric.label: Method and dependency
rubric.description: Select and justify the result needed from the preceding part.

rubric.label: Verified result
rubric.description: Complete the calculation or proof and state the verified conclusion.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: First, $f_\mu(a_\lambda)=f_\lambda(a_\lambda)+(\mu-\lambda)a_\lambda>0$, while $f_\mu$ is increasing and vanishes at $a_\mu$; hence $a_\mu<a_\lambda$. Alternatively, subtracting $a_\lambda^{3}+\lambda a_\lambda=1$ and $a_\mu^{3}+\mu a_\mu=1$ gives $(a_\lambda-a_\mu)(a_\lambda^{2}+a_\lambda a_\mu+a_\mu^{2}+\lambda)=(\mu-\lambda)a_\mu>0$. The bracket is positive, so again $a_\lambda>a_\mu$.

activities.title: Part 3 · Global two-sided bounds
activities.promptMarkdown: Derive explicit upper and lower bounds for $a_\lambda$ using only $0<a_\lambda<1$ and the root equation. Use them to prove both $a_\lambda\to 0$ as $\lambda\to+\infty$ and $a_\lambda\to 1$ as $\lambda$ tends to $0$ from above.

rubric.label: Method and dependency
rubric.description: Select and justify the result needed from the preceding part.

rubric.label: Verified result
rubric.description: Complete the calculation or proof and state the verified conclusion.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: From $\lambda a_\lambda=1-a_\lambda^{3}<1$ we get $a_\lambda<1/\lambda$. Since $a_\lambda^{3}<a_\lambda$, the equation gives $1=\lambda a_\lambda+a_\lambda^{3}<(\lambda+1)a_\lambda$, so $a_\lambda>1/(\lambda+1)$. For large $\lambda$ both bounds tend to $0$. For $\lambda\to 0$, the upper bound $a_\lambda<1$ combines with $1-a_\lambda^{3}=\lambda a_\lambda\le \lambda$ to give $a_\lambda^{3}\ge 1-\lambda$, hence $a_\lambda\to 1$.

activities.title: Part 4 · Quantitative parameter comparison
activities.promptMarkdown: Starting from the subtraction identity in Part $2$, derive an exact formula for $a_\lambda-a_\mu$ when $0<\lambda<\mu$. Obtain a simple upper bound in terms of $\mu-\lambda$ and $\lambda$, and explain what the bound proves about parameter stability away from $\lambda=0$.

rubric.label: Method and dependency
rubric.description: Select and justify the result needed from the preceding part.

rubric.label: Verified result
rubric.description: Complete the calculation or proof and state the verified conclusion.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: The exact identity is $a_\lambda-a_\mu=(\mu-\lambda)a_\mu/[a_\lambda^{2}+a_\lambda a_\mu+a_\mu^{2}+\lambda]$. The denominator is at least $\lambda$, and $0<a_\mu<1$, so $0<a_\lambda-a_\mu<(\mu-\lambda)/\lambda$. On any parameter interval $\lambda\ge \lambda_{0}>0$, this gives a Lipschitz bound $|a_\lambda-a_\mu|\le |\lambda-\mu|/\lambda_{0}$ after ordering the pair, so the root depends continuously and stably on the parameter there.

activities.title: Part 5 · First corrections in both regimes
activities.promptMarkdown: Prove the refined limits $\lambda a_\lambda\to 1$ and $\lambda^{4}(a_\lambda-1/\lambda)\to -1$ as $\lambda\to+\infty$. Then prove $(1-a_\lambda)/\lambda\to 1/3$ as $\lambda$ tends to $0$ from above. Every normalization must come from an exact identity.

rubric.label: Method and dependency
rubric.description: Select and justify the result needed from the preceding part.

rubric.label: Verified result
rubric.description: Complete the calculation or proof and state the verified conclusion.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: The root equation gives $\lambda a_\lambda=1-a_\lambda^{3}$; Part $3$ gives $a_\lambda\to 0$, hence $\lambda a_\lambda\to 1$. Also $a_\lambda-1/\lambda=-a_\lambda^{3}/\lambda$, so $\lambda^{4}(a_\lambda-1/\lambda)=-(\lambda a_\lambda)^{3}\to -1$. For $\lambda\to 0$, factor $1-a_\lambda^{3}=(1-a_\lambda)(1+a_\lambda+a_\lambda^{2})=\lambda a_\lambda$. Since $a_\lambda\to 1$, $(1-a_\lambda)/\lambda=a_\lambda/(1+a_\lambda+a_\lambda^{2})\to 1/3$.

Explain why nested sign-changing intervals of lengths tending to zero isolate a zero of a continuous function.

### Target

Supply the common-point and continuity steps.

### Strategy

Use nested compact intervals and endpoint sequences.

### Hypotheses

The function is continuous and each interval has endpoint values of opposite signs.

### Complete solution

Nested closed intervals with lengths tending to zero have one common point $c$. Their left and right endpoints both converge to $c$. Continuity makes their function values converge to $f(c)$. Since the left values are nonpositive and the right values nonnegative, their common limit satisfies $f(c)\le0$ and $f(c)\ge0$, hence $f(c)=0$.

### Boundary check

Without continuity, endpoint signs can persist while the common point carries a jump.

# A derivative is a limit of local slopes

The increment tends to zero through nonzero values, and the function must be defined near the base point.

## Why the quotient is local

The derivative records the first-order response near one point. Cancelling the increment is legal only before taking its punctured limit.

## Reactivate punctured limits

The difference quotient is evaluated for $h\ne0$ and only then is its limit taken as $h\to0$.

content.markdown:
Compute the derivative of $f(x)=1/x$ at $a\ne0$ from the definition.

### Target

Simplify the quotient, control its denominator near $a$, and take the limit.

### Strategy

Combine the two reciprocal terms before dividing by $h$.

### Hypotheses

$a\ne0$ and $h$ is small enough that $a+h\ne0$.

### Complete solution

For $h\ne0$, $[1/(a+h)-1/a]/h=[a-(a+h)]/[a(a+h)h]=-1/[a(a+h)]$. As $h\to0$, the denominator tends to $a^2\ne0$, so the quotient tends to $-1/a^2$. Thus $f'(a)=-1/a^2$.

### Boundary check

The formula is not a derivative at $a=0$ because the original function is not defined there.

If $f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$, differentiable on $(a,b)$, and $f(a)=f(b)$, then some $c\in(a,b)$ satisfies $f'(c)=0$.

content.markdown:
Apply Rolle's theorem to $f(x)=x^2-4x+3$ on $[1,3]$ and identify every point whose existence the theorem guarantees.

### Target

Verify all hypotheses, invoke the theorem, and solve the derivative equation inside the interval.

### Strategy

Check polynomial regularity and endpoint equality before differentiating.

### Hypotheses

The interval is $[1,3]$ with nonempty interior.

### Complete solution

The polynomial $f$ is continuous on $[1,3]$ and differentiable on $(1,3)$. Its endpoint values are

$$f(1)=0,\qquad f(3)=0,$$

so all hypotheses of Rolle's theorem hold. The theorem gives a point $c\in(1,3)$ with $f'(c)=0$. Since $f'(x)=2x-4$, the equation $2c-4=0$ has the unique solution $c=2$. Thus the guaranteed point is $2$, and it lies in the required open interval.

### Boundary check

The function $g(x)=|x|$ on $[-1,1]$ is continuous and has equal endpoint values, but it is not differentiable at $0$. Rolle's theorem cannot be invoked, and indeed there is no point in $(-1,1)$ where its derivative equals zero.

Subtracting the secant line creates equal endpoint values and reduces the theorem to Rolle.

## Real functions · Mean value theorem

The mean value theorem gives $f'(c)=[f(b)-f(a)]/(b-a)$ for some $c\in(a,b)$ under continuity and differentiability hypotheses.

Under the same continuity and differentiability domains as Rolle, some interior derivative equals the secant slope. The theorem asserts existence, not the location or uniqueness of the point.

content.markdown:
Derive the mean value theorem from Rolle's theorem.

### Target

Verify the auxiliary function hypotheses and translate its zero derivative.

### Strategy

Subtract the secant line from $f$.

### Hypotheses

$f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$, differentiable on $(a,b)$, and $a<b$.

### Complete solution

Let $m=[f(b)-f(a)]/(b-a)$ and $g(x)=f(x)-m(x-a)$. Then $g$ is continuous on $[a,b]$, differentiable on $(a,b)$, and $g(a)=g(b)=f(a)$. Rolle gives $c\in(a,b)$ with $g'(c)=0$. Since $g'(c)=f'(c)-m$, one has $f'(c)=m$.

### Boundary check

If the function is not differentiable at an interior point, the auxiliary function inherits the same defect.

## Week 9 substantial problem

Five-part problem, 90 minutes; feedback follows each attempt.

### Shared stem

Starting from Rolle's theorem, derive the mean value theorem and use it to analyze the fixed-point equation $x=e^{-x}$ without invoking convexity or Taylor expansion.

data.markdown: Likely issue: the proof invokes Fermat at an endpoint or omits the constant-function case. First repair: separate constant and nonconstant cases, use compactness to obtain extrema, and identify an interior extremum before differentiating.

content.title: Part 2 · Derive the mean value theorem

data.markdown: Likely issue: the auxiliary function does not have equal endpoint values, or its derivative loses the secant slope. First repair: recompute the affine correction from the endpoint difference and verify both endpoint and derivative identities.

Likely issue: existence and uniqueness were blended, leaving either the sign change or strict increase unjustified. First repair: complete the intermediate-value argument first, then apply the mean value theorem to two hypothetical zeros using the sign of $h'$.

Likely issue: interval invariance checks only one bound, or the derivative maximum was taken at the wrong endpoint. First repair: bound the image of both endpoints and then maximize $e^{-x}$ over the stated interval before checking the constant is below one.

Likely issue: the one-step contraction estimate was not iterated correctly, or the a posteriori bound lacks the geometric tail. First repair: prove the $q^n$ estimate by induction, then sum the successive-increment bounds from index $n$ onward.

activities.title: Part 1 · Prove Rolle's theorem
activities.promptMarkdown: Let $f$ be continuous on $[a,b]$, differentiable on $(a,b)$, and satisfy $f(a)=f(b)$. Prove that some $c\in(a,b)$ satisfies $f'(c)=0$, separating the constant and nonconstant cases.

rubric.label: Method and dependency
rubric.description: Select and justify the result needed from the preceding part.

rubric.label: Verified result
rubric.description: Complete the calculation or proof and state the verified conclusion.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: If $f$ is constant, every $c\in(a,b)$ works. Otherwise the extreme-value theorem gives a global maximum and a global minimum on $[a,b]$. Because the endpoint values agree while $f$ is not constant, at least one of those two extremal values differs from the common endpoint value. A point where that value is attained must therefore lie in $(a,b)$. It is a local extremum, so Fermat's theorem gives $f'(c)=0$. The extreme-value theorem gives attained global minimum and maximum values. Because the function is nonconstant while its endpoint values agree, at least one attained extremal value differs from the common endpoint value, so every point attaining that value lies in the open interval.

activities.title: Part 2 · Derive the mean value theorem
activities.promptMarkdown: For $f$ continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$, construct an auxiliary function for Part $1$ and prove $f(b)-f(a)=f'(c)(b-a)$ for some $c\in(a,b)$.

rubric.label: Method and dependency
rubric.description: Select and justify the result needed from the preceding part.

rubric.label: Verified result
rubric.description: Complete the calculation or proof and state the verified conclusion.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Set $m=[f(b)-f(a)]/(b-a)$ and $g(x)=f(x)-m(x-a)$. Then $g$ is continuous on $[a,b]$, differentiable inside, and $g(a)=f(a)=g(b)$. Rolle's theorem gives $g'(c)=0$, hence $f'(c)=m$. Multiplying by $b-a$ gives the required identity. This auxiliary function subtracts the secant line, making its endpoint values equal before Rolle is applied.

activities.title: Part 3 · Existence and uniqueness
activities.promptMarkdown: Apply the intermediate value theorem to $h(x)=x-e^{-x}$ on $[0,1]$ to prove existence of a zero $\alpha$. Then use Part $2$ and the sign of $h'$ to prove uniqueness.

rubric.label: Method and dependency
rubric.description: Select and justify the result needed from the preceding part.

rubric.label: Verified result
rubric.description: Complete the calculation or proof and state the verified conclusion.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: $h(0)=-1<0$ and $h(1)=1-e^{-1}>0$, so continuity gives $\alpha\in(0,1)$ with $h(\alpha)=0$. Also $h'(x)=1+e^{-x}>0$. If two distinct zeros existed, the mean value theorem would give $0=h(y)-h(x)=h'(c)(y-x)>0$, a contradiction. Strict positivity of $h'$ is used through the mean value theorem, not asserted from a graph.

activities.title: Part 4 · Build a contraction
activities.promptMarkdown: For $\varphi(x)=e^{-x}$, prove that $I=[e^{-1},1]$ is invariant. Use Part $2$ to show $|\varphi(x)-\varphi(y)|\le e^{-e^{-1}}|x-y|$ on $I$, and check that the constant is below $1$.

rubric.label: Method and dependency
rubric.description: Select and justify the result needed from the preceding part.

rubric.label: Verified result
rubric.description: Complete the calculation or proof and state the verified conclusion.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: If $x\in I$, then $e^{-1}\le e^{-x}\le e^{-e^{-1}}<1$, so $\varphi(I)\subset I$. The mean value theorem gives $|\varphi(x)-\varphi(y)|=e^{-c}|x-y|$ for some $c$ between $x$ and $y$. Since $c\ge e^{-1}$, this is at most $q|x-y|$ with $q=e^{-e^{-1}}<1$. The interval estimate is uniform because the same constant $q<1$ works for every pair in $I$.

activities.title: Part 5 · Control the iteration
activities.promptMarkdown: Let $u_0\in I$ and $u_{n+1}=e^{-u_n}$. Prove $|u_n-\alpha|\le q^n|u_0-\alpha|$, deduce convergence, and derive $|u_n-\alpha|\le q|u_n-u_{n-1}|/(1-q)$ for $n\ge1$. Name the induction and geometric-tail estimates you use.

rubric.label: Method and dependency
rubric.description: Select and justify the result needed from the preceding part.

rubric.label: Verified result
rubric.description: Complete the calculation or proof and state the verified conclusion.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Part $4$ and $\varphi(\alpha)=\alpha$ give $|u_{n+1}-\alpha|\le q|u_n-\alpha|$, hence induction yields $|u_n-\alpha|\le q^n|u_0-\alpha|\to0$. Successive increments also shrink by at most $q$. Summing the geometric tail from $u_n$ to the limit gives $|u_n-\alpha|\le q|u_n-u_{n-1}|/(1-q)$. The geometric-tail estimate is valid because successive increments are bounded by $q^k$ times the first omitted increment.

Assume $|f'|\le M$ on $(a,b)$. Prove $|f(b)-f(a)|\le M(b-a)$ using a partition and local mean-value estimates.

### Target

Apply the theorem on each subinterval, sum absolute bounds, and telescope.

### Strategy

Use arbitrary partition points and the triangle inequality.

### Hypotheses

$f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$, differentiable on $(a,b)$, and $a<b$.

### Complete solution

On each $[x_k,x_{k+1}]$, the mean value theorem gives $|f(x_{k+1})-f(x_k)|\le M(x_{k+1}-x_k)$. Telescoping and the triangle inequality yield $|f(b)-f(a)|\le\sum_k|f(x_{k+1})-f(x_k)|\le M\sum_k(x_{k+1}-x_k)=M(b-a)$.

### Boundary check

The continuity and differentiability hypotheses must hold on every subinterval; the partition does not repair a singular point.

# Convexity places the graph below every chord

The weights are nonnegative and sum to one, so the input is an interval point between the two endpoints.

## Why shape becomes algebra

The chord inequality converts a geometric picture into a proof that can be manipulated, differentiated, and generalized.

## Reactivate derivative behavior

A derivative records tangent slope; convexity will require these slopes to increase with the base point.

## Real functions · Convexity

$f$ is convex on an interval when $f(tx+(1-t)y)\le tf(x)+(1-t)f(y)$ for $0\le t\le1$.

For $t\in[0,1]$, the point $tx+(1-t)y$ lies between $x$ and $y$. Convexity compares the function at that mixed input with the same weighted mix of endpoint values.

Prove $f(x)=|x|$ is convex on $\mathbb R$.

### Target

Apply the triangle inequality to an arbitrary convex combination.

### Strategy

Treat the weights as nonnegative scalars.

### Hypotheses

$x,y\in\mathbb R$ and $0\le t\le1$.

### Complete solution

$|tx+(1-t)y|\le|tx|+|(1-t)y|=t|x|+(1-t)|y|$ because both weights are nonnegative. This is exactly the convexity inequality, so absolute value is convex.

### Boundary check

Differentiability is not required by the definition; the cusp at zero is compatible with convexity.

objectives: Apply the convexity definition to a quadratic, isolate the nonnegative chord gap, and distinguish derivative sign from convexity.

content.markdown:
# Direct convexity proofs expose a nonnegative gap

Subtract the graph value from the chord value and factor the result.

## Why the gap matters

The exact gap measures how far the chord lies above the graph and makes equality cases visible.

## Reactivate weight conditions

Both $t$ and $1-t$ are nonnegative exactly when $t\in[0,1]$.

content.markdown:
Prove directly from the defining chord inequality that $f(x)=x^2$ is convex on $\mathbb R$.

### Target

Expand the chord gap, factor it, and use all domain hypotheses.

### Strategy

Subtract the mixed square from the weighted endpoint squares.

### Hypotheses

$x,y\in\mathbb R$ and $t\in[0,1]$.

### Complete solution

Take real numbers $x,y$ and $t\in[0,1]$. The difference between the right and left sides of the convexity inequality is

$$tx^2+(1-t)y^2-\bigl(tx+(1-t)y\bigr)^2=t(1-t)(x-y)^2.$$

Both factors $t$ and $1-t$ are nonnegative, and a square is nonnegative. Therefore the difference is at least zero, which is exactly

$$f(tx+(1-t)y)\le tf(x)+(1-t)f(y).$$

Since $x,y,t$ were arbitrary in the required domains, $f$ is convex on $\mathbb R$.

### Boundary check

A nonnegative derivative proves monotonicity, not convexity. For example, $g(x)=1-e^{-x}$ has $g'(x)>0$ but $g''(x)<0$, so it is concave rather than convex.

Convexity needs increasing derivative or a nonnegative second derivative when those criteria apply.

lessons.title: Week 10, Day 3 · Order secant and tangent slopes
lessons.summary: Derive increasing-slope and supporting-tangent properties of differentiable convex functions.
objectives: Derive increasing-slope and supporting-tangent properties of differentiable convex functions.

content.markdown:
# Convexity orders slopes from left to right

A chord through farther-right points cannot have smaller slope than a chord nested to its left.

## Why slope order is powerful

It turns a two-variable chord inequality into derivative tests and tangent-line estimates.

## Reactivate a secant slope

For $x<y$, the slope is $[f(y)-f(x)]/(y-x)$ with positive denominator.

content.title: Compute two secant slopes
content.introMarkdown: Compare the slopes on $[0,1]$ and $[1,2]$.

**Task:** For $f(x)=x^2$, use points $0,1,2$.

**Reference path:** The first slope is $(1-0)/(1-0)=1$ and the second is $(4-1)/(2-1)=3$, so the slopes increase.

For **Compute two secant slopes**, the first mismatch that blocks “Compare the slopes on $[0,1]$ and $[1,2]$.” is your repair point.

Without correcting **Compute two secant slopes**, this required evidence remains unsupported: Compare the slopes on $[0,1]$ and $[1,2]$.

content.markdown:
For convex $f$ and $x<y<z$, prove $[f(y)-f(x)]/(y-x)\le[f(z)-f(x)]/(z-x)\le[f(z)-f(y)]/(z-y)$.

### Target

Write $y$ as a convex combination of $x$ and $z$ and rearrange.

### Strategy

Use weight $(z-y)/(z-x)$ on $x$.

### Hypotheses

$f$ is convex on an interval containing $x<y<z$.

### Complete solution

Since $y=[(z-y)/(z-x)]x+[(y-x)/(z-x)]z$, convexity gives $(z-x)f(y)\le(z-y)f(x)+(y-x)f(z)$. Rearranging once yields the left slope inequality and rearranging equivalently yields the right one.

### Boundary check

All denominators are positive because the points are strictly ordered.

activities.title: Oral preparation · Convexity definitions
activities.promptMarkdown: State convexity by chords and the tangent characterization for a differentiable function.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Convexity means $f((1-s)x+sy)\le (1-s)f(x)+sf(y)$ for $0\le s\le 1$. If f is differentiable on an interval, convexity is equivalent to $f(y)\ge f(x)+f'(x)(y-x)$ for all x,y in that interval.

content.markdown:
## Week 10 substantial problem

Five-part problem, 90 minutes; feedback follows each attempt.

### Shared stem

For $p>1$, study $F_p(x)=x^p-px+p-1$ on the positive real axis.

data.markdown: Likely issue: the sign of $F_p''$ was discussed at zero although the domain is open, or the case $1<p<2$ was rejected because of a boundary singularity. First repair: factor the derivative signs for $x>0$ and state exactly where convexity is being proved.

content.title: Part 2 · Global minimum and tangent inequality

data.markdown: Likely issue: a critical point was called a global minimum without using strict convexity, or equality was read only from a sketch. First repair: connect the unique critical point to strict convexity, then derive equality from uniqueness of the zero minimum.

Likely issue: the zero boundary case was divided away, or the scaling leaves an uncancelled power of $b$. First repair: settle zero inputs first, then write every exponent after substitution and verify the conjugacy identity before cancellation.

Likely issue: equality for a zero input was merged with the positive-input condition, or the equivalence with the Part 2 equality was one-way. First repair: separate boundary and positive cases, then prove the power equality in both directions.

Likely issue: the conjugate exponents or powered inputs were chosen inconsistently, so Young's two power terms do not become the weighted terms. First repair: compute both powered inputs explicitly, then audit interior and endpoint weight equality cases separately.

## What is now established

activities.title: Part 1 · Curvature with parameter hypotheses
activities.promptMarkdown: Compute the first two derivatives of $F_{p}$ on $(0,\infty)$. Prove strict convexity for every real $p>1$, including the case $1<p<2$ where $x^{p-2}$ is singular at zero, and explain why the open domain is sufficient.

rubric.label: Method and dependency
rubric.description: Select and justify the result needed from the preceding part.

rubric.label: Verified result
rubric.description: Complete the calculation or proof and state the verified conclusion.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: We have $F_{p}'(x)=p(x^{p-1}-1)$ and $F_{p}''(x)=p(p-1)x^{p-2}$. For $x>0$ and $p>1$, every factor is positive, so $F_{p}''(x)>0$ and $F_{p}$ is strictly convex on $(0,\infty)$. When $1<p<2$ the second derivative grows near zero, but it exists and remains positive at every point of the open domain; no value at zero is needed for this conclusion.

activities.title: Part 2 · Global minimum and tangent inequality
activities.promptMarkdown: Locate the unique critical point, prove it is the global minimum, and derive $x^{p}\ge px-(p-1)$ for $x>0$. State and prove the equality case rather than inferring it only from a graph.

rubric.label: Method and dependency
rubric.description: Select and justify the result needed from the preceding part.

rubric.label: Verified result
rubric.description: Complete the calculation or proof and state the verified conclusion.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: The equation $F_{p}'(x)=0$ is $x^{p-1}=1$, hence $x=1$. Strict convexity makes this critical point the unique global minimum, and $F_{p}(1)=0$. Thus $F_{p}(x)\ge 0$, which rearranges to $x^{p}\ge px-(p-1)$. Equality means $F_{p}(x)=0$; uniqueness of the minimum forces $x=1$, which indeed gives equality.

activities.title: Part 3 · Scale to Young's inequality
activities.promptMarkdown: Let $q=p/(p-1)$, so $1/p+1/q=1$. First prove Young's inequality when $a=0$ and $b\ge0$. Then, for $a>0$ and $b>0$, choose the positive scaling substitution that yields $ab\le a^p/p+b^q/q$, showing every exponent cancellation.

rubric.label: Method and dependency
rubric.description: Select and justify the result needed from the preceding part.

rubric.label: Verified result
rubric.description: Complete the calculation or proof and state the verified conclusion.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: If $a=0$, then $ab=0\le b^q/q$; this boundary is settled before any division. For $a,b>0$, Part $2$ is $x\le x^p/p+1/q$. Put $x=a/b^{q-1}>0$ and multiply by $b^q>0$. The left side is $ab$, and the power term is $a^pb^{q-p(q-1)}/p=a^p/p$ because $p(q-1)=q$. The last term is $b^q/q$.

activities.title: Part 4 · Boundary and equality audit
activities.promptMarkdown: Extend Young's inequality to $a=0$ or $b=0$, and prove that equality for nonnegative $a,b$ occurs exactly when $a^p=b^q$. Connect this condition to equality $x=1$ in Part $2$.

rubric.label: Method and dependency
rubric.description: Select and justify the result needed from the preceding part.

rubric.label: Verified result
rubric.description: Complete the calculation or proof and state the verified conclusion.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: If $a=0$ or $b=0$, equality occurs only when both are zero. For $a,b>0$, equality requires $a/b^{q-1}=1$, so $a=b^{q-1}$. Raising to $p$ gives $a^p=b^{p(q-1)}=b^q$ because $p(q-1)=q$. The converse reverses these steps.

activities.title: Part 5 · Weighted AM-GM synthesis
activities.promptMarkdown: For $0<\alpha<1$ and x,$y\ge 0$, derive $x^\alpha y^{1-\alpha}\le \alpha x+(1-\alpha)y$ from Young's inequality by choosing conjugate exponents and inputs. Determine equality and reconcile the endpoint weights $\alpha=0$ and $\alpha=1$.

rubric.label: Method and dependency
rubric.description: Select and justify the result needed from the preceding part.

rubric.label: Verified result
rubric.description: Complete the calculation or proof and state the verified conclusion.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Choose $p=1/\alpha$ and $q=1/(1-\alpha)$, and apply Young to $a=x^\alpha$ and $b=y^{1-\alpha}$. Then $ab=x^\alpha y^{1-\alpha}$, $a^{p}/p=\alpha x$, and $b^{q}/q=(1-\alpha)y$. Equality requires $a^{p}=b^{q}$, hence $x=y$ when both are positive; if one is zero and $0<\alpha<1$, equality forces both to be zero, again $x=y$. At $\alpha=0$ or $1$ the inequality becomes respectively $y\le y$ or $x\le x$, so it extends continuously with equality for all x,y.

content.markdown:
Prove $f(x)=e^x+x^2$ is strictly convex on $\mathbb R$ and derive its tangent bound at zero.

### Target

Use exact curvature, then state the global tangent inequality and equality case.

### Strategy

Compute the second derivative and tangent data.

### Hypotheses

The function is twice differentiable on $\mathbb R$.

### Complete solution

$f''(x)=e^x+2>0$, so $f$ is strictly convex. At zero, $f(0)=1$ and $f'(0)=1$, so the supporting tangent is $1+x$. Therefore $e^x+x^2\ge1+x$ for every real $x$, with equality only at $x=0$ by strict convexity.

### Boundary check

Strict positivity of the second derivative supplies the uniqueness of the tangent contact.

content.markdown:
# A local expansion records both polynomial data and precision

The remainder is part of the statement; it says how small the unrecorded terms are relative to the last retained power.

## Why the order matters

A tangent approximation captures first-order behavior. Higher-order coefficients reveal curvature and make difficult limits algebraic.

## Reactivate first-order linearization

Differentiability at $a$ means $f(a+h)=f(a)+f'(a)h+o(h)$.

content.markdown:
## Taylor expansions · Local expansions

A Taylor expansion separates a function near a point into a polynomial determined by derivatives and a controlled remainder.

A local polynomial is centered at the expansion point and ordered by powers of the increment. Writing $o(h^n)$ means the remainder divided by $h^n$ tends to zero; it is not an unspecified exact zero.

content.markdown:
Expand $(1+h)^4$ through order four at $h=0$.

### Target

Identify every coefficient and the exact remainder.

### Strategy

Use the binomial theorem and compare with the local-expansion format.

### Hypotheses

$h$ is real and tends to zero.

### Complete solution

$(1+h)^4=1+4h+6h^2+4h^3+h^4$ exactly. Thus the order-four local expansion has these coefficients and zero remainder; zero is in particular $o(h^4)$.

### Boundary check

Stopping at order two would require retaining $4h^3+h^4$ inside a remainder of order $O(h^3)$, not claiming exact equality with the quadratic.

content.markdown:
# Taylor–Young converts derivative data into a local polynomial

Each derivative contributes one factorial-scaled coefficient, and the theorem controls the remainder relative to the final power.

## Why factorials appear

Differentiating $h^k$ exactly $k$ times produces $k!$, so dividing by the factorial makes the coefficient recover the derivative value.

## Reactivate derivative cycles and factorials

List derivative values at the expansion point before writing any polynomial term.

content.markdown:
## Taylor expansions · Young

Taylor–Young states that $n$ derivatives at $a$ give $f(a+h)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}f^{(k)}(a)h^k/k!+o(h^n)$.

The theorem is centered at a point $a$ and uses derivatives through order $n$ there. Its $o(h^n)$ remainder is relative to the increment $h=x-a$ and therefore states local precision.

content.markdown:
Use Taylor–Young at $0$ to obtain the expansion of $\sin h$ through order $3$ as $h\to0$.

### Target

List derivatives at zero, apply factorial scaling, simplify zero coefficients, and preserve the remainder.

### Strategy

Use the four-term derivative cycle of sine.

### Hypotheses

Sine has derivatives of every order near zero.

### Complete solution

The derivatives of $\sin$ at $0$ are $0$, $1$, $0$, and $-1$ through order $3$. Taylor–Young therefore gives

$$\sin h=0+h+0\cdot\frac{h^2}{2}-\frac{h^3}{6}+o(h^3).$$

Hence

$$\sin h=h-\frac{h^3}{6}+o(h^3).$$

The remainder statement means that after division by $h^3$, the unrecorded part tends to zero. It is part of the conclusion and controls the precision of the expansion.

### Boundary check

Replacing $o(h^3)$ by zero turns an asymptotic statement into a false exact identity. The polynomial $h-h^3/6$ approximates $\sin h$ near zero but does not equal it for every nonzero $h$.

# Expansion algebra is ordinary algebra plus order bookkeeping

Discard a term only after proving its order is beyond the requested precision.

## Why bookkeeping is mathematical

A correct leading term can coexist with a wrong next coefficient if cross-products or remainder orders are dropped too early.

## Reactivate powers and retained order

When multiplying two series, every pair of retained terms can contribute to the requested total degree.

content.markdown:
Find the expansion of $1/(1+h)$ through order three.

### Target

Choose coefficients so multiplication by $1+h$ gives $1$ through the requested order.

### Strategy

Use a geometric-series ansatz.

### Hypotheses

$h\to0$, so $1+h\ne0$ locally.

### Complete solution

$(1+h)(1-h+h^2-h^3)=1-h^4$. Therefore $1/(1+h)=1-h+h^2-h^3+O(h^4)$, and in particular the remainder is $o(h^3)$ when the expansion is written through order three.

### Boundary check

The alternating signs are forced by cancellation; using all positive signs fails already at order one.

content.markdown:
## Week 11 substantial problem

Five-part problem, 90 minutes; feedback follows each attempt.

### Shared stem

For $x$ near $0$, study $g(x)=\log(1+x)/x$, extended by $g(0)=1$.

content.title: Part 1 · Choose and execute the required order

data.markdown: Likely issue: the logarithm was expanded only to degree four before division, or the remainder order was not reduced with the powers. First repair: plan one extra numerator degree, divide every term and remainder by $x$, then justify the continuous value.

content.title: Part 2 · Read derivatives from the extension

data.markdown: Likely issue: Taylor coefficients were copied directly as derivatives without factorials. First repair: make a degree-by-degree table pairing each coefficient with $g^{(k)}(0)/k!$ before evaluating derivatives.

Likely issue: inverse coefficients were solved out of order or the product was not checked through degree four. First repair: multiply the two formal series, set each successive nonconstant coefficient to zero, and verify the truncated product.

Likely issue: the wrong terms were subtracted before normalization, or nonvanishing of the logarithmic quotient was assumed. First repair: establish that $g$ stays nonzero near zero, then expose the first surviving term in each numerator before dividing.

content.title: Part 5 · Local sign and remainder discipline

data.markdown: Likely issue: a negative leading quadratic term was treated as sign-definite without controlling its remainder, or an insufficient logarithm order was used. First repair: factor the quadratic scale with its $1+o(1)$ multiplier and trace which numerator order is needed after inversion.

## What is now established

The denominator scale determines the minimal expansion order, and the first surviving coefficient determines the limit. Day 5 retrieves three earlier proof structures.

activities.title: Part 1 · Choose and execute the required order
activities.promptMarkdown: To control g through degree four, determine how far $\log (1+x)$ must be expanded before division. Write the complete expansion with its remainder, divide by x, and justify the extension $g(0)=1$.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Division by x lowers every degree by one, so $\log (1+x)$ is needed through degree five: $\log (1+x) = x-x^{2}/2+x^{3}/3-x^{4}/4+x^{5}/5+o(x^{5})$. Therefore $g(x)=1-x/2+x^{2}/3-x^{3}/4+x^{4}/5+o(x^{4})$. The expansion tends to $1$, so defining $g(0)=1$ gives the unique continuous extension. Dividing the remainder $o(x^5)$ by $x$ gives $o(x^4)$ for nonzero $x$, completing the order audit.

activities.title: Part 2 · Read derivatives from the extension
activities.promptMarkdown: Assuming the Taylor-Young regularity supplied by the logarithm expansion, determine $g'(0)$, $g''(0)$, $g'''(0)$, and $g^{(4)}(0)$. Explain the factorial conversion between coefficients and derivatives.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: A Taylor coefficient $c_k$ equals $g^{(k)}(0)/k!$. Therefore $g'(0)=-1/2$, $g''(0)=2!/3=2/3$, $g'''(0)=3!(-1/4)=-3/2$, and $g^{(4)}(0)=4!/5=24/5$. Each derivative is recovered by multiplying the corresponding coefficient by its factorial; no regularity is inferred from notation alone.

activities.title: Part 3 · Invert through degree four
activities.promptMarkdown: Write $1/g(x)=1+a_1x+a_2x^2+a_3x^3+a_4x^4+o(x^4)$. Multiply by the expansion in Part $1$, solve the four coefficient equations in order, and verify the product through degree four.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Cancellation gives $a_1=1/2$, $a_2=-1/12$, $a_3=1/24$, and $a_4=-19/720$. Hence $1/g(x)=1+x/2-x^2/12+x^3/24-19x^4/720+o(x^4)$. Multiplication by the Part $1$ expansion cancels coefficients of degrees one through four. A final multiplication gives coefficients $0$ at degrees one, two, three, and four, checking the inversion.

activities.title: Part 4 · Two renormalized limits
activities.promptMarkdown: Use Part $3$ to compute $\lim_{x\to0}[x/\log(1+x)-1-x/2]/x^2$ and $\lim_{x\to0}[x/\log(1+x)-1-x/2+x^2/12]/x^3$. Explain why the quotient is defined near zero and how each leading coefficient determines its limit.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Because $g(x)\to1$, it is nonzero near zero. The first numerator is $-x^2/12+x^3/24+o(x^3)$, so the first limit is $-1/12$. After adding $x^2/12$, the numerator is $x^3/24+o(x^3)$, so the second limit is $1/24$. The nonzero-near-zero claim follows from continuity and the limit $g(x)\to1$, not from cancelling $x$ at zero.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: The difference is $-x^2/12+o(x^2)=-(x^2/12)[1+o(1)]$, which is negative for small nonzero $x$ and is equivalent to $-x^2/12$. A degree-two expansion of $\log(1+x)$ determines $g$ only through degree one, so it cannot determine the decisive quadratic coefficient after inversion. The sign conclusion uses the nonzero quadratic coefficient together with a remainder strictly smaller in relative order.

# Friday joins tangent geometry, pointwise limits, and legal quotient algebra

Together they explain coefficients, remainder meaning, and the validity of asymptotic division.

## Why the older skills remain visible

Taylor expansions refine tangents, are limit statements at a point, and must obey the same denominator restrictions as exact quotients.

## Reactivate coefficient meaning

The constant, linear, and quadratic coefficients encode value, slope, and half the second derivative.

content.markdown:
Expand $\log(1+h)/(e^h-1)$ through order one and determine its limit.

### Target

Use numerator and denominator expansions, factor the common increment, and invert the remaining denominator.

### Strategy

Retain both source expansions through order two before division.

### Hypotheses

$h\to0$ through values where the quotient is defined.

### Complete solution

$\log(1+h)=h-h^2/2+o(h^2)$ and $e^h-1=h+h^2/2+o(h^2)$. Factoring $h$ gives $(1-h/2+o(h))/(1+h/2+o(h))$. Since the denominator tends to $1$, its reciprocal is $1-h/2+o(h)$. Multiplication gives $1-h+o(h)$, so the quotient tends to $1$.

### Boundary check

Cancelling $h$ is legal only for nonzero increments; the limit is taken on that punctured domain.

# A primitive is verified by differentiation

Today every proposed primitive is checked on a stated interval. The additive constant describes all solutions only after the connected domain is fixed.

## Why the interval belongs in the answer

The formula for a primitive can change across a singular point, and a disconnected domain can carry different constants on different components. Domain and derivative are part of the mathematical object.

## Reactivate differentiation as a verification tool

Differentiate term by term and simplify before comparing with the target function.

content.markdown:
## Integration · Antiderivatives

A primitive of $f$ on an interval is a differentiable function $F$ with $F'=f$ there.

On one interval, any two primitives of the same function differ by a constant. Verification therefore has two parts: differentiate the candidate and state the interval where both functions are defined.

content.markdown:
Find every primitive of $f(x)=3x^2-4$ on $\mathbb R$.

### Target

Construct one primitive and prove that the additive-constant family is complete.

### Strategy

Integrate each term, then compare any other primitive with the constructed one.

### Hypotheses

The domain $\mathbb R$ is an interval, and every candidate is differentiable there.

### Complete solution

One primitive is $F_0(x)=x^3-4x$. For every $C\in\mathbb R$, $F_C=F_0+C$ has derivative $3x^2-4$. Conversely, if $G'=f$, then $(G-F_0)'=0$ on the interval $\mathbb R$, so $G-F_0$ is constant. Therefore all primitives are $x^3-4x+C$.

### Boundary check

Writing only $x^3-4x$ gives one primitive, not the complete family requested.

On $\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}$, the negative and positive half-lines are separate components. A primitive of $1/x$ may carry one constant on each component.

# A differential-equation answer is a verified family

Today the derivative equation, characteristic roots, real basis, and dimension all remain visible. Substitution verifies every proposed member.

## Why a family needs a completeness argument

Checking one formula proves that it is a solution. It does not prove that every solution has been found; the equation's order and independent basis functions close that gap.

## Reactivate the derivative and primitive mechanism

A first-order homogeneous exponential is verified by differentiation, and the product derivative behind an integrating factor is recovered by taking a primitive.

content.markdown:
Find every real-valued solution of $y''+4y=0$ on an interval of the real line, and verify the resulting family.

### Target

Derive the complete real family from the characteristic roots and verify it by substitution.

### Strategy

Solve the characteristic polynomial, convert the conjugate exponentials into a sine-cosine basis, and differentiate twice.

### Hypotheses

The equation is homogeneous, has real constant coefficients, and is posed on a real interval.

### Complete solution

The characteristic polynomial is $r^2+4$, whose complex roots are $2i$ and $-2i$. The corresponding real solution family is

$$y(x)=A\cos(2x)+B\sin(2x),\qquad A,B\in\mathbb R.$$

Differentiating twice gives $y''(x)=-4A\cos(2x)-4B\sin(2x)=-4y(x)$, so every member satisfies the equation. The roots are distinct and the equation has order two, so the two independent solutions $\cos(2x)$ and $\sin(2x)$ span the full real solution space.

### Boundary check

For a repeated characteristic root $r$, the two functions $e^{rx}$ and $e^{rx}$ are not independent. The missing second solution is $xe^{rx}$; omitting it leaves only a one-dimensional family for a second-order equation.

# An integrating factor creates an exact derivative

Today the factor, product derivative, primitive, and final division remain on separate lines so that each equivalence can be checked.

## Why substitution closes the method

A sign error in the factor can still produce a plausible exponential formula. Substitution into the untouched differential equation is the decisive final check.

## Reactivate the product derivative behind integrating factors

Choose the exponential factor so that its derivative supplies the coefficient of $y$.

content.markdown:
Solve $y'+y=e^x$ on $\mathbb R$.

### Target

Derive the complete family and verify it in the original equation.

### Strategy

Multiply by $e^x$, integrate the product derivative, and divide by the nonzero factor.

### Hypotheses

All coefficients and the right-hand side are continuous on $\mathbb R$.

### Complete solution

Multiplying by $e^x$ gives $(e^xy)'=e^{2x}$. Hence $e^xy=\tfrac12e^{2x}+C$, so $y=\tfrac12e^x+Ce^{-x}$. Conversely, $y'=\tfrac12e^x-Ce^{-x}$, and therefore $y'+y=e^x$.

### Boundary check

The constant is introduced when taking a primitive, not after dividing by the integrating factor.

content.markdown:
# Linear structure distinguishes homogeneous freedom from forcing

Today constants, particular solutions, and homogeneous corrections are separated explicitly before a variable coefficient is handled.

## Why superposition needs the right equation

Sums and scalar multiples preserve a homogeneous equation. For an inhomogeneous equation, adding two particular solutions doubles the forcing unless a homogeneous correction is used.

## Reactivate exponential differentiation

The derivative of $Ce^{-ax}$ supplies exactly the negative multiple needed in a constant-coefficient homogeneous equation.

content.markdown:
For constants $a\ne0$ and $b$, solve $y'+ay=b$ on $\mathbb R$.

### Target

Find a particular solution, add the complete homogeneous family, and verify.

### Strategy

Try a constant particular solution before solving the associated homogeneous equation.

### Hypotheses

$a$ and $b$ are real constants with $a\ne0$.

### Complete solution

The constant $y_p=b/a$ satisfies $y_p'+ay_p=b$. The homogeneous equation has family $Ce^{-ax}$, so every candidate is $y=b/a+Ce^{-ax}$. Its derivative is $-aCe^{-ax}$, hence $y'+ay=-aCe^{-ax}+b+aCe^{-ax}=b$. Conversely, subtracting $b/a$ from any solution gives a homogeneous solution, proving completeness.

### Boundary check

If $a=0$, division by $a$ is illegal and the equation becomes $y'=b$, with family $bx+C$.

**Reference correction.** Multiplication by $e^{-2x}$ gives $(e^{-2x}y)'=x$. Hence $e^{-2x}y=x^2/2+C$. The initial condition gives $C=1$, so $y=e^{2x}(1+x^2/2)$. Differentiation yields $y'-2y=xe^{2x}$ and $y(0)=1$.

Integration gives $\mu y=B+C$, where $B$ is a primitive of $\mu b$, hence $y=e^{-A}(B+C)$. Differentiation verifies the family.

# Divisibility is an integer-existence statement

Today every symbol $a\mid b$ is translated into an integer witness $b=ak$. Closure proofs keep those witnesses explicit.

## Why quotient language is not enough

A real quotient always exists when the divisor is nonzero. Divisibility requires that quotient to be an integer, so the witness and its domain carry the proof.

## Activate integer multiplication as evidence

To establish a divisibility claim, exhibit the multiplier and verify the product.

content.markdown:
Prove that $a\mid b$ and $b\mid c$ imply $a\mid c$.

### Target

Compose the two integer witnesses without dividing.

### Strategy

Write one witness equation for each hypothesis and substitute.

### Hypotheses

$a,b,c$ are integers.

### Complete solution

Since $a\mid b$, there is $k\in\mathbb Z$ with $b=ak$. Since $b\mid c$, there is $\ell\in\mathbb Z$ with $c=b\ell$. Substitution gives $c=a(k\ell)$, and $k\ell\in\mathbb Z$. Therefore $a\mid c$.

### Boundary check

The proof remains valid when one of the integers is zero because it uses witness equations, not illegal division.

# A gcd becomes useful when it is a certificate

Today Euclidean remainders are back-substituted into an explicit Bézout identity, which then proves a prime-divisor theorem.

## Why a computed gcd is not the end

The number $\gcd(a,b)$ records common divisibility. Its expression $ua+vb$ is the operational certificate that solves congruences and transfers prime divisibility to a factor.

## Activate the Euclidean remainder invariant

Replacing $(a,b)$ by $(b,a-qb)$ preserves the common divisors and therefore preserves the positive gcd.

## Integer arithmetic · Bézout identity

Bézout's identity states that $\gcd(a,b)$ is an integer combination $ua+vb$.

The extended Euclidean algorithm computes the gcd and back-substitutes it as an integer linear combination. The special certificate $ua+vb=1$ is equivalent to coprimality.

## Integer arithmetic · Primes

A prime is an integer $p\ge2$ whose only positive divisors are $1$ and $p$.

If a prime $p$ does not divide $a$, then $\gcd(p,a)=1$. A Bézout certificate for that coprimality proves Euclid's lemma: $p\mid ab$ forces $p\mid b$.

content.markdown:
Let $p$ be a prime integer and let $a\in\mathbb Z$. Prove that $p\mid a^2$ implies $p\mid a$.

### Target

Apply Euclid's lemma to the product $a\cdot a$ and isolate the role of primality.

### Strategy

Rewrite the square as a product and invoke the prime-divisor alternative.

### Hypotheses

$p$ is prime, $a$ is an integer, and $p\mid a^2$.

### Complete solution

The hypothesis $p\mid a^2$ is the same as $p\mid a\cdot a$. Because $p$ is prime, Euclid's lemma applies and gives $p\mid a$ or $p\mid a$. Both alternatives have the same conclusion, so $p\mid a$. The primality hypothesis is the decisive reason the divisibility of a product can be transferred to one factor.

### Boundary check

The conclusion fails for a composite divisor. For example, $6\mid 2\cdot3$, but $6$ divides neither $2$ nor $3$. Euclid's lemma cannot be used after replacing “prime” by “positive integer.”

# Back-substitution turns remainders into certificates

Today each Euclidean line is preserved so the gcd can be written as a linear combination and reused in an equation.

## Why one solution is not every solution

A Bézout certificate gives a particular integer pair. The homogeneous difference between solutions supplies the parameterization, and divisibility by the gcd decides whether any pair exists.

## Activate common-divisor control

A common divisor of two coefficients divides every integer linear combination.

content.markdown:
Compute $\gcd(84,30)$ and one Bézout identity.

### Target

Run the Euclidean algorithm and back-substitute the last nonzero remainder.

### Strategy

Record every quotient and express each remainder from the preceding line.

### Hypotheses

$84$ and $30$ are positive integers.

### Complete solution

$84=2\cdot30+24$, $30=1\cdot24+6$, and $24=4\cdot6$. Hence the gcd is $6$. Back-substitution gives $6=30-24=30-(84-2\cdot30)=3\cdot30-84$. Thus $6=(-1)84+3\cdot30$.

### Boundary check

Stopping after the gcd omits the coefficients needed for Diophantine and congruence problems.

# Congruence is divisibility of a difference

Today every modular manipulation can be translated back to a divisibility statement, and cancellation occurs only after invertibility is proved.

## Why cancellation has a hypothesis

Multiplication modulo a composite number can collapse distinct residue classes. A Bézout inverse is the certificate that a factor may be cancelled safely.

## Activate coprimality with a prime modulus

A nonzero residue modulo a prime is coprime to that prime and therefore has a Bézout inverse.

## Integer arithmetic · Congruences

$a\equiv b\pmod n$ means that $n$ divides $a-b$.

Congruence is compatible with addition and multiplication because divisibility of differences is preserved. Cancellation requires the factor to be coprime to the modulus.

Solve $3x\equiv4\pmod7$.

### Target

Construct an inverse, multiply both sides, and state the complete residue class.

### Strategy

Use the Bézout certificate $3\cdot5-2\cdot7=1$.

### Hypotheses

$\gcd(3,7)=1$, so an inverse exists.

### Complete solution

Since $3\cdot5\equiv1\pmod7$, multiply by $5$: $x\equiv20\equiv6\pmod7$. Conversely, $3\cdot6=18\equiv4\pmod7$, so the complete solution is $x=6+7k$ with $k\in\mathbb Z$.

### Boundary check

Multiplying by an inverse is reversible. Cancelling a noninvertible factor need not preserve the solution set.

Explain how a Bézout identity for $(a,n)$ solves $ax\equiv b\pmod n$ when $\gcd(a,n)=1$.

### Target

Connect the integer certificate, modular inverse, and solution verification.

### Strategy

Reduce the Bézout identity modulo $n$ and multiply by $b$.

### Hypotheses

$a,n,b$ are integers, $n\ge2$, and $\gcd(a,n)=1$.

### Complete solution

Choose $u,v$ with $ua+vn=1$. Modulo $n$, this gives $ua\equiv1$, so $u$ is an inverse of $a$. Multiplying by $b$ gives $a(ub)\equiv b$, hence $x\equiv ub\pmod n$. Substitution verifies the residue.

### Boundary check

If the gcd is not one, an inverse need not exist; solvability must instead be checked against divisibility of the target.

Solve $x+2y=5$ and $3x-y=4$ by elimination.

### Target

Create a pivot, eliminate one unknown, back-substitute, and verify.

### Strategy

Use the first equation as pivot and replace the second by $R_2-3R_1$.

### Hypotheses

The system is over $\mathbb R$.

### Complete solution

$R_2\leftarrow R_2-3R_1$ gives $-7y=-11$, so $y=11/7$. The first equation then gives $x=5-22/7=13/7$. Substitution yields $13/7+22/7=5$ and $39/7-11/7=4$, so the unique solution is $(13/7,11/7)$.

### Boundary check

The division by $-7$ is legal because the pivot is nonzero.

content.markdown:
Determine whether the system $x+y=2$ and $2x+2y=5$ is consistent over $\mathbb R$. Justify the answer by comparing ranks.

### Target

Reduce the coefficient and augmented matrices together and compare their ranks.

### Strategy

Replace the second row by $R_2-2R_1$.

### Hypotheses

The system is over $\mathbb R$.

### Complete solution

The coefficient and augmented matrices are

$$A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\2&2\end{pmatrix},\qquad [A\mid b]=\begin{pmatrix}1&1&2\\2&2&5\end{pmatrix}.$$

Replacing the second row by $R_2-2R_1$ leaves a zero row in $A$ but gives $(0,0,1)$ in the augmented matrix. Hence $\operatorname{rank}(A)=1$ and $\operatorname{rank}([A\mid b])=2$. The ranks differ, so the consistency criterion says that the system has no solution. Equivalently, the equations would require both $2x+2y=4$ and $2x+2y=5$.

### Boundary check

Counting equations and unknowns does not determine the number of solutions. Two equations in two unknowns can be dependent, inconsistent as above, or independent with one solution; the rank comparison distinguishes the cases.

# Equivalence is a two-direction proof

Today each row replacement is shown reversible before it is used computationally.

## Why obtaining the right answer is not the proof

A transformed system may be easier, but it is valid only when every old solution is new and every new solution recovers the old equations.

## Activate equation linear combinations

A solution satisfies every scalar multiple and sum of equations it already satisfies.

content.markdown:
Prove that replacing $E_2$ by $E_2+\lambda E_1$ preserves the solution set.

### Target

Prove both solution-set inclusions.

### Strategy

Use direct addition forward and the inverse replacement backward.

### Hypotheses

$E_1,E_2$ are linear equations over $\mathbb R$ and $\lambda\in\mathbb R$.

### Complete solution

Any solution of $E_1,E_2$ satisfies $E_2+\lambda E_1$, so it solves the transformed system. Conversely, a solution of $E_1$ and $E_2+\lambda E_1$ also satisfies $(E_2+\lambda E_1)-\lambda E_1=E_2$. Hence the solution sets are equal.

### Boundary check

Both directions use the unchanged first equation; discarding it would invalidate the reverse implication.

Classify $x+y=1$ and $x+ay=2$ for real $a$.

### Target

Expose the pivot $a-1$ and solve both branches.

### Strategy

Replace the second row by $R_2-R_1$.

### Hypotheses

### Complete solution

Elimination gives $(a-1)y=1$. If $a\ne1$, then $y=1/(a-1)$ and $x=(a-2)/(a-1)$, giving one solution. If $a=1$, the new row is $0=1$, so the system is inconsistent.

### Boundary check

The rational formula belongs only to $a\ne1$ and cannot be evaluated at the singular branch.

An echelon augmented matrix has rows $(1,0,2\mid3)$, $(0,1,-1\mid4)$, and $(0,0,0\mid0)$.

### Target

Count pivots, identify the free variable, and parameterize the complete solution set.

### Strategy

Let the nonpivot variable be the parameter and solve the pivot equations.

### Hypotheses

The variables are $(x,y,z)\in\mathbb R^3$.

### Complete solution

There are two coefficient pivots and no contradictory row, so one variable is free. Let $z=t$. Then $x=3-2t$ and $y=4+t$. Thus every solution is $(3-2t,4+t,t)$ for $t\in\mathbb R$.

### Boundary check

The zero row contributes no pivot and no constraint; replacing it by $(0,0,0\mid1)$ would make the system inconsistent.

Today every division is certified by both the identity $A=BQ+R$ and the strict remainder-degree bound.

## Why matching leading terms is not enough

Long division is complete only when the remainder is too small to divide again. The identity and degree bound make the answer checkable.

## Activate coefficient arithmetic and factor evaluation

## Polynomials · Division

For polynomials $A,B$ with $B\ne0$, Euclidean division gives unique $Q,R$ with $A=BQ+R$ and $\deg R<\deg B$.

content.markdown:
Divide $2x^3+3x^2-x+5$ by $x^2+1$ over $\mathbb R[x]$.

### Target

Find $Q$ and $R$, then certify both the identity and degree condition.

### Strategy

Cancel the leading cubic term, then cancel the leading quadratic term of the intermediate remainder.

### Hypotheses

The divisor $x^2+1$ is nonzero and coefficients lie in the field $\mathbb R$.

### Complete solution

The first quotient term $2x$ leaves $3x^2-3x+5$. The next term is $3$; subtracting $3(x^2+1)$ leaves $-3x+2$. Thus $Q=2x+3$ and $R=-3x+2$. Indeed $(x^2+1)(2x+3)+(-3x+2)=2x^3+3x^2-x+5$, and $\deg R=1<2=\deg(x^2+1)$.

### Boundary check

Stopping at $3x^2-3x+5$ would be premature because its degree still equals the divisor degree.

# Common polynomial factors emerge as last nonzero remainders

Today factor evaluation, Euclidean division, and monic normalization form one verifiable algorithm.

## Why the monic convention matters

Over a field, nonzero scalar multiples divide the same polynomials. Normalizing the leading coefficient to one selects a unique gcd.

## Activate evaluation and exact division

A common linear factor gives a common root, and a zero Euclidean remainder proves exact divisibility.

content.markdown:
## Polynomials · Roots

$\alpha$ is a root of $P$ exactly when $P(\alpha)=0$, equivalently when $x-\alpha$ divides $P$.

For a scalar $a$, division by $x-a$ has constant remainder $P(a)$. Therefore $P(a)=0$ exactly when $x-a$ divides $P$.

content.markdown:
## Polynomials · Greatest common divisors

A polynomial gcd is a greatest common divisor normalized to be monic; it is obtained by the Euclidean algorithm.

The Euclidean algorithm preserves common divisors because $A=BQ+R$ implies that a polynomial divides both $A,B$ exactly when it divides both $B,R$. The last nonzero remainder is normalized to be monic.

content.markdown:
Over a field, compute the monic greatest common divisor of $P(x)=x^3-1$ and $Q(x)=x^2-1$ by the Euclidean algorithm.

### Target

Execute every Euclidean remainder step and state the unique monic gcd.

### Strategy

Divide the cubic by the quadratic, then divide the quadratic by the first remainder.

### Hypotheses

The coefficient ring is a field, so nonzero leading coefficients are invertible.

### Complete solution

The first Euclidean division gives

$$P-xQ=(x^3-1)-x(x^2-1)=x-1.$$

Next,

$$Q=(x+1)(x-1),$$

so the remainder after dividing $Q$ by $x-1$ is zero. The last nonzero remainder is $x-1$, which is already monic. Therefore

$$\gcd(P,Q)=x-1.$$

The factor indeed divides both polynomials, and the zero remainder shows that every common divisor divides it.

### Boundary check

Before normalization, any nonzero scalar multiple of $x-1$ is also a greatest common divisor. Naming the monic representative is what makes the answer unique over a field.

# Multiplicity leaves a derivative trace

Today the factor theorem and product rule turn a repeated factor into a common-root criterion.

## Why repeated roots need a structural test

A graph or numerical approximation can hide multiplicity. The pair $P,P'$ gives an exact algebraic certificate.

## Activate simple and repeated factors

A multiplicity-two root contributes the square $(x-a)^2$, while a simple root contributes only one factor.

Assume $P=(x-a)^2Q$. Prove that $P(a)=P'(a)=0$.

### Target

Differentiate the factorization and retain every factor needed at $a$.

### Strategy

Use the product rule before substituting $x=a$.

### Hypotheses

$P,Q$ are polynomials over a characteristic-zero field and $a$ is a scalar.

Today coefficients are solved by an identity, while the final equality is stated only away from the original poles.

## Why poles and multiplicities cannot be ignored

A missing repeated-factor term makes the coefficient system unsolvable, and a correct numerator identity still does not define values at excluded points.

Decompose $1/(x^2-1)$ into real simple fractions.

### Target

Derive coefficients by clearing denominators and verify the numerator identity.

### Strategy

Write $A/(x-1)+B/(x+1)$ and evaluate the cleared identity at the two roots.

### Hypotheses

$x\in\mathbb R\setminus\{-1,1\}$.

### Complete solution

Clearing denominators gives $1=A(x+1)+B(x-1)$. At $x=1$, $A=1/2$; at $x=-1$, $B=-1/2$. Therefore $1/(x^2-1)=\frac12(1/(x-1)-1/(x+1))$ on the common domain. The numerator reconstructs as $((x+1)-(x-1))/2=1$.

### Boundary check

The identity does not assign values at $x=\pm1$, where both the original expression and at least one decomposed term have poles.

# A polynomial certificate has several independent checks

Today transformations preserve roots, substitution verifies candidates, and a derivative test separates simple from repeated roots.

## Why one successful check is insufficient

Finding a root does not establish multiplicity or exhaust all roots. Factor degree, derivative evidence, and reconstruction jointly close the argument.

## Activate the factor theorem and degree count

Each extracted linear factor consumes one degree, counted with multiplicity.

Classify $P(x)=x^3-3x+2$ by testing a root, dividing, and checking multiplicity.

### Target

Produce a factorization, a derivative certificate, and a degree-based exhaustion argument.

### Strategy

Verify $P(1)=0$, divide by $x-1$, factor the quotient, then compare with $P'$.

### Hypotheses

$P\in\mathbb R[x]$ is monic of degree three.

### Complete solution

$P(1)=0$, and division gives $P=(x-1)(x^2+x-2)=(x-1)^2(x+2)$. Moreover $P'=3x^2-3=3(x-1)(x+1)$, confirming that one is repeated while minus two is simple. The factor degrees sum to three, so no roots are missing over $\mathbb C$.

### Boundary check

The derivative common-root test establishes repetition; evaluation of $P$ alone would not.

content.markdown:
Show that the set $\mathcal F(\mathbb R,\mathbb R)$ of real-valued functions is closed under linear combinations.

### Target

Define the operations pointwise and verify that the output remains a real-valued function.

### Strategy

Take arbitrary functions and scalars, then evaluate their linear combination at an arbitrary input.

### Hypotheses

$f,g:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ and $\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb R$.

### Complete solution

Define $h=\alpha f+\beta g$ by $h(x)=\alpha f(x)+\beta g(x)$. For every real $x$, both function values and scalars are real, so $h(x)\in\mathbb R$. Thus $h$ is again a function from $\mathbb R$ to $\mathbb R$; the remaining vector-space identities hold pointwise because they hold in $\mathbb R$.

### Boundary check

The pointwise rule is essential: an unspecified or incompatible operation does not inherit the real-number axioms automatically.

content.markdown:
Prove that $F=\{(x,y,z)\in\mathbb R^3:x+y+z=0\}$ is a vector subspace of $\mathbb R^3$.

### Target

Verify zero membership and arbitrary linear-combination closure.

### Strategy

Apply the defining coordinate-sum equation to two arbitrary members and combine the resulting equalities.

### Hypotheses

The ambient vector space is $\mathbb R^3$ over $\mathbb R$.

### Complete solution

The zero vector belongs to $F$ because $0+0+0=0$. Take $u=(x_1,y_1,z_1)$ and $v=(x_2,y_2,z_2)$ in $F$, and let $\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb R$. Then

$$\alpha(x_1+y_1+z_1)+\beta(x_2+y_2+z_2)=0.$$

This is the sum of the coordinates of $\alpha u+\beta v$, so $\alpha u+\beta v\in F$. The set contains zero and is closed under every linear combination; therefore it is a subspace.

### Boundary check

The parallel plane $x+y+z=1$ does not contain the zero vector and is not closed under scalar multiplication. It is an affine set, not a vector subspace.

# A direct sum adds uniqueness to existence

Today $F+G$ supplies decompositions, while $F\cap G=\{0\}$ determines whether those decompositions are unique.

## Why spanning the ambient space is only half the claim

Many pairs of subspaces generate every vector but overlap, allowing several representations of the same vector.

## Activate subspace sums and intersections

The sum contains all $f+g$, and the intersection contains vectors eligible for both roles.

## Vector spaces · Direct sums

$V=E\oplus F$ means every $v\in V$ has a unique decomposition $v=e+f$ with $e\in E$ and $f\in F$.

The notation $E=F\oplus G$ means both $E=F+G$ and $F\cap G=\{0\}$. Equivalently, every vector of $E$ has exactly one decomposition $f+g$.

In $\mathbb R^3$, let $F=\{(x,y,0)\}$ and $G=\{(0,0,z)\}$. Prove $\mathbb R^3=F\oplus G$.

### Target

Construct every decomposition and prove the intersection is zero.

### Strategy

Split the first two coordinates from the third coordinate.

### Hypotheses

$F$ and $G$ carry the inherited real vector-space operations.

### Complete solution

Every $(x,y,z)$ equals $(x,y,0)+(0,0,z)$ with the first term in $F$ and the second in $G$, so $F+G=\mathbb R^3$. If a vector lies in both, its third coordinate is zero because it lies in $F$, and its first two coordinates are zero because it lies in $G$. Thus the intersection is $\{0\}$ and the sum is direct.

### Boundary check

Showing the displayed decomposition proves existence; the separate intersection argument proves uniqueness.

content.markdown:
Assume $E=F+G$. Prove that decompositions are unique exactly when $F\cap G=\{0\}$.

### Target

Prove both implications with arbitrary decompositions and an arbitrary intersection vector.

### Strategy

Subtract representations in one direction; use $0=h+(-h)$ in the other.

### Hypotheses

$F,G$ are subspaces of $E$ and every vector of $E$ has at least one $F+G$ decomposition.

### Complete solution

If the intersection is zero and $f_1+g_1=f_2+g_2$, then $f_1-f_2=g_2-g_1$ lies in the intersection, hence is zero; thus $f_1=f_2$ and $g_1=g_2$. Conversely, if decompositions are unique and $h\in F\cap G$, then $0=0+0=h+(-h)$ are two decompositions with terms in $F$ and $G$. Uniqueness gives $h=0$, so the intersection is zero.

### Boundary check

The assumption $E=F+G$ supplies existence; the equivalence concerns the additional uniqueness property.

Let $E$ and $O$ be the even and odd polynomials in $\mathbb R_3[x]$. Prove $\mathbb R_3[x]=E\oplus O$.

### Target

Establish subspaces, construct the decomposition, and prove zero intersection.

### Strategy

Use $(P(x)+P(-x))/2$ and $(P(x)-P(-x))/2$, then compare both parity equations.

### Hypotheses

Scalars are real and polynomial degree is at most three.

### Complete solution

Parity is preserved by linear combinations, so $E$ and $O$ are subspaces. Every $P$ equals $P_e+P_o$ with $P_e=(P(x)+P(-x))/2$ even and $P_o=(P(x)-P(-x))/2$ odd. If $H$ is both, then $H(-x)=H(x)=-H(x)$, hence $H=0$. Therefore the sum is direct.

### Boundary check

The construction proves coverage; the both-parities argument separately proves uniqueness.

### 1. Definition sheet

**Prompt.** Prepare exact statements of the vector-space axioms, the subspace test, and the equivalent criteria for $E=F\oplus G$.

**Reference correction.** Let $E$ be a set over a field $K$. The eight vector-space axioms are: addition is associative and commutative; there is an additive zero; every vector has an additive inverse; $\lambda(x+y)=\lambda x+\lambda y$; $(\lambda+\mu)x=\lambda x+\mu x$; $(\lambda\mu)x=\lambda(\mu x)$; and $1_Kx=x$. A nonempty subset $F$ is a subspace when $\lambda x+\mu y\in F$ for all $x,y\in F$ and $\lambda,\mu\in K$. Finally, $E=F\oplus G$ means $E=F+G$ and $F\cap G=\{0\}$, equivalently every vector has a unique decomposition $f+g$.

**Scoring.** 7 points: The mathematical statement, calculation, proof, and boundary conditions are correct. 3 points: The exposition names the plan, uses stable notation, and reaches the conclusion without a hidden step.
