## Open the record after retrieval

**Definition to compare:** A Poisson variable with parameter $\lambda>0$ has $P(X=k)=e^{-\lambda}\lambda^k/k!$.

**Worked example to compare:** Its expectation and variance both equal $\lambda$.

**Boundary to compare:** A Poisson variable has unbounded countable support, unlike a binomial variable.

### Week 53 — Parameter-dependent integrals · Integral

**Definition.** Continuity of a parameter integral follows by combining pointwise continuity in the parameter with an integrable local domination.

**Example.** $F(x)=\int_0^1e^{-xt}dt$ is continuous for $x\ge0$ by domination with $1$.

**Boundary.** Pointwise continuity of the integrand is not enough on an improper domain without domination.

**Proof target.** Prove continuity of a parameter integral using a stated domination theorem.

**Decisive proof route.** If $f(t,x)$ is continuous in $t$ and dominated by an integrable $g(x)$ near $t_0$, then $f(t,x)\to f(t_0,x)$ pointwise. Dominated convergence moves the limit through the integral, proving continuity.

### Week 51 — Vector-valued functions · Taylor

**Definition.** Taylor's formula for a vector-valued function applies componentwise with a vector remainder estimate.

**Example.** $r(t+h)=r(t)+hr'(t)+O(h^2)$ for a twice differentiable plane curve.

**Boundary.** A componentwise expansion needs one remainder control valid for the chosen vector norm.

**Proof target.** Prove that the derivative of a constant-norm curve is orthogonal to the position vector.

**Decisive proof route.** Differentiate $\langle\gamma(t),\gamma(t)\rangle=c^2$. The product rule gives $2\langle\gamma'(t),\gamma(t)\rangle=0$, so velocity is orthogonal to position.

### Week 46 — Numerical series · Remainder

**Definition.** The remainder after $n$ terms is the tail $R_n=\sum_{k>n}u_k$, estimated with a theorem suited to the terms.

**Example.** For a positive decreasing function, integral comparison bounds the series tail by neighboring improper integrals.

**Boundary.** A remainder estimate must control the full infinite tail, not only the next term unless an alternating-series theorem applies.

**Proof target.** Prove an integral-comparison bound for a positive decreasing series.

**Decisive proof route.** For positive decreasing $f$ with $u_n=f(n)$, compare each rectangle with the integrals on $[n,n+1]$. Summing gives the two-sided bounds between the series tail and adjacent improper-integral tails.

### Week 38 — Linear maps · Kernel decomposition

**Definition.** If coprime polynomials $P_i$ satisfy $\prod P_i(T)=0$, the space decomposes as the direct sum of the kernels $\ker P_i(T)$.

**Example.** Distinct eigenvalue factors give the direct sum of their generalized eigenspaces.

**Boundary.** Coprimality is essential; overlapping factors do not give the same direct-sum conclusion.

**Proof target.** Prove the two-factor kernel decomposition when the annihilating factors are coprime.

**Decisive proof route.** If $P$ and $Q$ are coprime and $P(T)Q(T)=0$, choose $A P+B Q=1$. Then every $x$ decomposes as $B(T)Q(T)x+A(T)P(T)x$, lying in $\ker P(T)$ and $\ker Q(T)$ respectively. Their intersection is zero by the same identity.

content.title: Week 55, day 1: Build the foundation
content.markdown: You are in **MP**. This page follows the week 55 syllabus requirement: Independent families, expectation, variance, and covariance.

## Today's learning goal

By the end of this page, you can state the defining conditions for Probability · Independent families, verify the supplied example, and identify why the boundary case fails.

## Why this matters

Definitions control every later method. Naming each condition now prevents familiar notation from concealing a false assumption.

## What you need first

The exact current definition is: A family is mutually independent when every finite subfamily has product probabilities for all corresponding events. The scheduled prerequisite statements are: Week 54: A countable discrete law assigns nonnegative masses to countably many values whose total is $1$. Week 52: An improper integral is defined as a limit of proper integrals near an infinite endpoint or singularity. Week 47: Uniform convergence means one index works for every point: $\sup_x|f_n(x)-f(x)|\to0$. Week 39: The adjoint $u^*$ is defined by $\langle u(x),y\rangle=\langle x,u^*(y)\rangle$ for all $x,y$. If any statement or symbol is unfamiliar, stop and open the linked concept before attempting the checkpoint.

## Define the objects in independent families, expectation, variance, and covariance

A family is mutually independent when every finite subfamily has product probabilities for all corresponding events.

### A complete first example

Independent coordinate variables on a product probability space form an independent family.

The example works because it meets the definition above. Name each condition before calculating; this prevents a familiar-looking expression from being used outside its domain.

### Boundary case to remember

Pairwise independence does not generally imply mutual independence.

content.title: Week 55, day 2: Follow the method
content.markdown: You are in **MP**. This page follows the week 55 syllabus requirement: Independent families, expectation, variance, and covariance.

## Today's learning goal

By the end of this page, you can apply a definition-first method to a complete Probability · First absolute moment verification and check its boundary.

## Why this matters

A stable route lets you decide what to do before calculation begins. The same route will support tomorrow's proof and the later timed transfer.

## What you need first

The exact current definition is: $L^1$ consists of integrable random variables with $E[|X|]<\infty$. The scheduled prerequisite statements are: Week 54: A countable discrete law assigns nonnegative masses to countably many values whose total is $1$. Week 52: An improper integral is defined as a limit of proper integrals near an infinite endpoint or singularity. Week 47: Uniform convergence means one index works for every point: $\sup_x|f_n(x)-f(x)|\to0$. Week 39: The adjoint $u^*$ is defined by $\langle u(x),y\rangle=\langle x,u^*(y)\rangle$ for all $x,y$. If any statement or symbol is unfamiliar, stop and open the linked concept before attempting the checkpoint.

## Follow a reliable method



**Deliberate method replay.** The definition is repeated exactly so that every decision in the new worked problem can be checked against it. The worked problem, formative checkpoint, and exit task are three different mathematical cases.

Use this route before trying shortcuts:

1. Name the objects, domains, and requested conclusion.

2. Write the definition or theorem that can produce that conclusion.

3. Check its hypotheses against the data.

4. Calculate one justified line at a time.

5. Test the result against a simple or boundary case.

### Exact definition or theorem: Probability · First absolute moment

$L^1$ consists of integrable random variables with $E[|X|]<\infty$.

### Complete worked problem

Let $X$ be a real random variable with $E[X^2]=9$. Prove that $X\in L^1$ and give a numerical bound for $E[|X|]$.

### Complete worked derivation

Apply Cauchy–Schwarz to the random variables $|X|$ and $1$:

$$E[|X|]=E[|X|\cdot1]\le\sqrt{E[X^2]}\sqrt{E[1^2]}.$$

Because $E[X^2]=9$ and $E[1]=1$, this gives

$$E[|X|]\le3<\infty.$$

Thus $X$ is absolutely integrable and belongs to $L^1$. The second-moment hypothesis supplies more than a merely formal signed expectation.

### Boundary and failed hypothesis

Symmetric cancellation does not prove integrability. Normalize probabilities proportional to $1/n^2$ at both $n$ and $-n$ for $n\ge1$. Symmetric truncated signed sums cancel, but $E[|X|]$ contains a divergent harmonic sum, so the integrable expectation $E[X]$ is not defined.

The solution and the boundary check concern different mathematical cases. The solution above is the fully displayed model; the checkpoint below asks you to begin a new case rather than repeat it.

The formative checkpoint asks only for the first justified check on that different case. After feedback, the exit activity asks you to repair and verify it completely.

## Open the record after retrieval

**Definition to compare:** $L^2$ consists of square-integrable random variables with $E[X^2]<\infty$.

**Worked example to compare:** Variance is finite for every $L^2$ variable.

**Boundary to compare:** Being in $L^1$ does not imply being in $L^2$.

### Week 54 — Probability · Countable

**Definition.** A countable discrete law assigns nonnegative masses to countably many values with total $1$.

**Example.** $P(X=k)=2^{-k}$ for $k\ge1$ is a law because the geometric sum equals $1$.

**Boundary.** Point masses whose series diverges or sums below $1$ do not define the stated full law.

**Proof target.** Prove that the geometric masses sum to one.

**Decisive proof route.** For geometric law $P(X=k)=p(1-p)^{k-1}$ on $k\ge1$, the total mass is $p\sum_{j\ge0}(1-p)^j=p/p=1$ because $0<p\le1$.

### Week 52 — Improper integrals · Parts

**Definition.** Integration by parts for an improper integral is performed on finite truncations before passing to the limit.

**Example.** $\int_1^R(\log x)/x^2dx$ is integrated by parts first, then $R\to\infty$.

**Boundary.** The limiting boundary term must exist; formal endpoint notation cannot replace that check.

**Proof target.** Prove the $p$-integral convergence criterion by evaluating finite truncations.

**Decisive proof route.** For $p\ne1$, $\int_1^R x^{-p}dx=(R^{1-p}-1)/(1-p)$, whose limit is finite exactly when $p>1$. For $p=1$, the truncation is $\log R\to\infty$.

### Week 47 — Sequences of functions · Uniform

**Definition.** $f_n\to f$ uniformly when $\sup_x|f_n(x)-f(x)|\to0$.

**Example.** $x/n\to0$ uniformly on $[0,1]$ because the supremum error is $1/n$.

**Boundary.** Pointwise convergence to a discontinuous limit on a compact interval cannot be uniform when all $f_n$ are continuous.

**Proof target.** Prove that a uniform limit of continuous functions is continuous.

**Decisive proof route.** Given $f_n\to f$ uniformly and $x\to a$, choose $n$ so $\|f-f_n\|_\infty<\varepsilon/3$, then use continuity of $f_n$ at $a$. The triangle inequality splits $|f(x)-f(a)|$ into three terms below $\varepsilon/3$.

### Week 39 — Euclidean spaces · Isometry

**Definition.** A linear isometry preserves norms, equivalently inner products in a real Euclidean space.

**Example.** Reflections and rotations are linear isometries.

**Boundary.** A general affine isometry may include a translation and therefore need not be linear.

**Proof target.** Prove that a linear map is an isometry exactly when $u^*u=I$.

**Decisive proof route.** The norm identity $\|ux\|^2=\langle u^*ux,x\rangle$ shows that $u^*u=I$ implies isometry. Conversely, preserving norms and polarizing gives $\langle ux,uy\rangle=\langle x,y\rangle$, hence $u^*u=I$.

## Task-specific reference for Probability · Second moment

**Definition.** $L^2$ consists of square-integrable random variables with $E[X^2]<\infty$.

**Valid case.** Variance is finite for every $L^2$ variable.

**Boundary.** Being in $L^1$ does not imply being in $L^2$.

**Scheduled review answer key.**

### Week 54 — Probability · Countable

**Definition.** A countable discrete law assigns nonnegative masses to countably many values with total $1$.

**Example.** $P(X=k)=2^{-k}$ for $k\ge1$ is a law because the geometric sum equals $1$.

**Boundary.** Point masses whose series diverges or sums below $1$ do not define the stated full law.

**Proof target.** Prove that the geometric masses sum to one.

**Decisive proof route.** For geometric law $P(X=k)=p(1-p)^{k-1}$ on $k\ge1$, the total mass is $p\sum_{j\ge0}(1-p)^j=p/p=1$ because $0<p\le1$.

### Week 52 — Improper integrals · Parts

**Definition.** Integration by parts for an improper integral is performed on finite truncations before passing to the limit.

**Example.** $\int_1^R(\log x)/x^2dx$ is integrated by parts first, then $R\to\infty$.

**Boundary.** The limiting boundary term must exist; formal endpoint notation cannot replace that check.

**Proof target.** Prove the $p$-integral convergence criterion by evaluating finite truncations.

**Decisive proof route.** For $p\ne1$, $\int_1^R x^{-p}dx=(R^{1-p}-1)/(1-p)$, whose limit is finite exactly when $p>1$. For $p=1$, the truncation is $\log R\to\infty$.

### Week 47 — Sequences of functions · Uniform

**Definition.** $f_n\to f$ uniformly when $\sup_x|f_n(x)-f(x)|\to0$.

**Example.** $x/n\to0$ uniformly on $[0,1]$ because the supremum error is $1/n$.

**Boundary.** Pointwise convergence to a discontinuous limit on a compact interval cannot be uniform when all $f_n$ are continuous.

**Proof target.** Prove that a uniform limit of continuous functions is continuous.

**Decisive proof route.** Given $f_n\to f$ uniformly and $x\to a$, choose $n$ so $\|f-f_n\|_\infty<\varepsilon/3$, then use continuity of $f_n$ at $a$. The triangle inequality splits $|f(x)-f(a)|$ into three terms below $\varepsilon/3$.

### Week 39 — Euclidean spaces · Isometry

**Definition.** A linear isometry preserves norms, equivalently inner products in a real Euclidean space.

**Example.** Reflections and rotations are linear isometries.

**Boundary.** A general affine isometry may include a translation and therefore need not be linear.

**Proof target.** Prove that a linear map is an isometry exactly when $u^*u=I$.

**Decisive proof route.** The norm identity $\|ux\|^2=\langle u^*ux,x\rangle$ shows that $u^*u=I$ implies isometry. Conversely, preserving norms and polarizing gives $\langle ux,uy\rangle=\langle x,y\rangle$, hence $u^*u=I$.

# One power series can encode an entire discrete law

For an $\mathbb N$-valued variable, the coefficient of $t^k$ is the probability of the value $k$. The same series can also calculate moments, but a derivative at the boundary $t=1$ is legitimate only when the corresponding moment is finite.

## Why encode the law

Convolutions of independent laws become products of generating functions. This replaces a long sum over all decompositions of an integer by one algebraic multiplication, while the coefficients still retain the full law.

## Reactivate independence through a product expectation

This Week 55 prerequisite is the exact mechanism behind the product formula for generating functions of independent sums.

content.markdown:
## Probability · Probability-generating functions

The probability generating function of a nonnegative integer-valued variable is $G_X(s)=E[s^X]$ on its domain.

Let $X$ take values in $\mathbb N$. For $|t|\le1$, the series $G_X(t)=\sum_{k\ge0}P(X=k)t^k$ converges absolutely because $\sum P(X=k)=1$; its radius is therefore at least $1$. The coefficient of $t^k$ recovers $P(X=k)$, so $G_X$ determines the law. If $E[X]<\infty$, then $G_X'(1)=E[X]$. If $E[X^2]<\infty$, then $G_X''(1)=E[X(X-1)]$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X)=G_X''(1)+G_X'(1)-G_X'(1)^2$. For a complete first model, if $P(X=0)=1-p$ and $P(X=2)=p$, then $G_X(t)=1-p+pt^2$, $G_X'(1)=2p$, and $G_X''(1)+G_X'(1)-G_X'(1)^2=4p(1-p)$.

Let $X=B_1+B_2+B_3$, where the $B_i$ are independent Bernoulli variables with common parameter $p$.

### Target

Build a binomial generating function and recover both moments

### Strategy

Derive $G_X$, then use its first two derivatives at $1$ to calculate $E[X]$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X)$.

### Hypotheses

Let $X=B_1+B_2+B_3$, where the $B_i$ are independent Bernoulli variables with common parameter $p$.

Each factor has generating function $1-p+pt$. Independence gives $G_X(t)=(1-p+pt)^3$. Thus $G_X'(1)=3p$. Also $G_X''(1)=6p^2$, so $\operatorname{Var}(X)=6p^2+3p-(3p)^2=3p(1-p)$.

# Tail bounds begin with a pointwise comparison

Markov turns the inequality $a\mathbf 1_{\{Y\ge a\}}\le Y$ into a probability bound. The comparison works because $Y$ is nonnegative. Chebyshev is the same argument after the nonnegative variable is chosen to be a squared centered deviation.

## Why moments can control tails

A distribution may be unknown even when its expectation or variance is easy to calculate. Markov and Chebyshev convert those limited numerical summaries into guaranteed upper bounds without assuming a density or a named law.

## Reactivate product moments before bounding a sum

This prerequisite calculation supplies the exact moments that the new inequalities will consume.

## Probability · Markov

For a nonnegative random variable, Markov's inequality is $P(X\ge a)\le E[X]/a$ for $a>0$.

Let $Y$ be nonnegative almost surely and integrable, and let $a>0$. The pointwise inequality $a\mathbf 1_{\{Y\ge a\}}\le Y$ holds everywhere. Taking expectations gives $aP(Y\ge a)\le E[Y]$, hence $P(Y\ge a)\le E[Y]/a$. Both hypotheses matter: nonnegativity supplies the pointwise order, and integrability makes the right side finite. For a complete first model, if $Y\ge0$ and $E[Y]=12$, then $P(Y\ge60)\le12/60=1/5$.

content.markdown:
## Probability · Chebyshev

Chebyshev's inequality is $P(|X-E[X]|\ge t)\le\operatorname{Var}(X)/t^2$.

Let $X\in L^2$ and let $t>0$. Then $E[X]$ is finite and $Y=(X-E[X])^2$ is nonnegative and integrable, with $E[Y]=\operatorname{Var}(X)$. Moreover, $\{|X-E[X]|\ge t\}=\{Y\ge t^2\}$. Markov applied to $Y$ at the positive threshold $t^2$ gives $P(|X-E[X]|\ge t)\le\operatorname{Var}(X)/t^2$. This is Chebyshev's inequality, derived rather than quoted. For example, variance $4$ and $t=6$ give a tail bound $1/9$.

A random variable has mean $10$ and variance $9$. Use Chebyshev's inequality to bound the probability that it differs from its mean by at least $6$.

### Target

Convert a stated mean and variance into a guaranteed two-sided tail bound and its complementary central-probability bound.

### Strategy

Check that the stated finite variance places the variable in $L^2$, match the deviation threshold to Chebyshev's $t$, divide the variance by $t^2$, and take a complement only after preserving the inequality direction.

### Hypotheses

The variable has finite mean $10$ and finite variance $9$, so its squared centered deviation is integrable. The threshold is $6>0$. No distributional shape or independence assumption is needed.

### Complete solution

Chebyshev's inequality applies because the variance is finite. With $t=6$,

$$P(|X-10|\ge6)\le\frac{\operatorname{Var}(X)}{6^2}=\frac9{36}=\frac14.$$

Taking complements also gives

$$P(|X-10|<6)\ge\frac34.$$

The conclusion is a guaranteed bound derived only from the first two moments; no distributional shape has been assumed.

### Boundary check

The number $1/4$ is an upper bound, not necessarily the exact tail probability. Writing an equality would claim information that Chebyshev's inequality does not provide.

content.markdown:
# The strategic step is the choice of variable

Markov is short once the correct nonnegative integrable variable has been selected. Squaring a centered deviation produces Chebyshev. Taking an absolute power produces a moment tail bound. Taking a positive part repairs a signed-variable mistake.

## Why prove the inequality again

A memorized formula does not reveal whether it applies to a new event. Reconstructing the indicator proof makes the nonnegativity, integrability, and positive-threshold requirements available for transfer.

## Reactivate the exact Markov and independence boundary

This retrieval reactivates independence, product expectations, and yesterday's Markov statement before the proof is rebuilt.

content.markdown:
Let $Y$ be a nonnegative integrable random variable and let $a>0$. Thus $E[Y]$ is finite, and the threshold is strictly positive.

### Target

Prove Markov from the indicator inequality

### Strategy

Prove $P(Y\ge a)\le E[Y]/a$ from a pointwise inequality, naming where nonnegativity and integrability enter.

### Hypotheses

Let $Y$ be a nonnegative integrable random variable and let $a>0$. Thus $E[Y]$ is finite, and the threshold is strictly positive.

### Complete solution

For every outcome, $a\mathbf1_{\{Y\ge a\}}\le Y$: on $\{Y\ge a\}$ this is $a\le Y$, and outside it the left side is $0\le Y$, using nonnegativity. Both sides are integrable because $Y\in L^1$. Monotonicity and linearity of expectation give $aP(Y\ge a)\le E[Y]$. Since $a>0$, division yields Markov's inequality.

### Boundary check

The complete proof model exposes the theorem's mechanism and the exact role of each assumption.

lessons.summary: Define Probability · Weak law of large numbers. State the weak law with independent identical distribution and finite variance, derive the $\sigma^2/(n\varepsilon^2)$ bound, and calculate sample sizes from it.
objectives: Define Probability · Weak law of large numbers. State the weak law with independent identical distribution and finite variance, derive the $\sigma^2/(n\varepsilon^2)$ bound, and calculate sample sizes from it.

content.markdown:
# Averaging shrinks variance

For independent variables with common variance $\sigma^2$, the sum has variance $n\sigma^2$. Dividing the sum by $n$ divides its variance by $n^2$, leaving $\sigma^2/n$. Chebyshev then turns this shrinking variance into convergence in probability.

## Why the weak law matters

The weak law gives a mathematical basis for the stabilization of empirical averages. It also shows exactly which available ingredients do the work: independence removes covariance terms, identical distribution supplies common moments, and finite variance makes Chebyshev available.

## Recover variance additivity and Chebyshev before averaging

This prerequisite activation isolates the calculation that the weak-law definition will convert into a limit statement.

### Repair guide for “Recover variance additivity and Chebyshev before averaging”

The rate $1/n$ is the bridge from finite variance to concentration.

content.markdown:
## Probability · Weak law of large numbers

The weak law states that sample averages converge in probability to the common mean under suitable independence and variance hypotheses.

Let $(X_k)_{k\ge1}$ be independent and identically distributed with finite variance $\sigma^2$ and common mean $m$. Put $S_n=\sum_{k=1}^nX_k$ and $\overline X_n=S_n/n$. Linearity gives $E[\overline X_n]=m$. Independence gives $\operatorname{Var}(S_n)=n\sigma^2$, and variance scaling gives $\operatorname{Var}(\overline X_n)=\sigma^2/n$. For every $\varepsilon>0$, Chebyshev yields $P(|\overline X_n-m|\ge\varepsilon)\le\sigma^2/(n\varepsilon^2)\to0$. This proves convergence in probability. For a complete first model, if $\sigma^2=4$ and $\varepsilon=1/2$, the bound is $16/n$.

Let $B_1,\ldots,B_n$ be independent Bernoulli variables with common parameter $p$, and let $F_n=n^{-1}\sum_{k=1}^nB_k$.

### Target

Prove concentration of a Bernoulli empirical frequency

### Strategy

Calculate the exact mean and variance of $F_n$, derive a concentration bound, and state the convergence-in-probability conclusion.

### Hypotheses

Let $B_1,\ldots,B_n$ be independent Bernoulli variables with common parameter $p$, and let $F_n=n^{-1}\sum_{k=1}^nB_k$.

### Complete solution

$E[F_n]=p$. Since $\operatorname{Var}(B_k)=p(1-p)$ and the variables are independent, $\operatorname{Var}(F_n)=p(1-p)/n$. Thus for every $\varepsilon>0$, $P(|F_n-p|\ge\varepsilon)\le p(1-p)/(n\varepsilon^2)\to0$. Hence $F_n$ converges in probability to $p$.

### Boundary check

The complete model connects the official weak law to the empirical frequency interpretation of probability.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Independence gives $\operatorname{Var}(\sum_{k=1}^nX_k)=n\sigma^2$. Scaling by $1/n$ multiplies variance by $1/n^2$, so $\operatorname{Var}(n^{-1}\sum X_k)=n\sigma^2/n^2=\sigma^2/n$. Because the variables have finite variance, Chebyshev applies and gives $P(|n^{-1}\sum X_k-m|\ge\varepsilon)\le\sigma^2/(n\varepsilon^2)$.

Solve the resulting inequality for the smallest integer $n$ certified by this bound, and explain why the answer is sufficient rather than necessary.

For “Choose a sample size from a weak-law guarantee”, success means: Solve the resulting inequality for the smallest integer $n$ certified by this bound, and explain why the answer is sufficient rather than necessary.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Chebyshev gives $P(|\overline X_n-m|\ge0.2)\le9/(n\cdot0.2^2)=225/n$. Requiring $225/n\le0.05$ gives $n\ge4500$. Thus $n=4500$ is the smallest integer certified by this bound. A smaller sample may work for a particular law because Chebyshev may be loose.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: A Poisson variable has mean and variance $\lambda<\infty$. Independence gives $E[\overline X_n]=\lambda$ and $\operatorname{Var}(\overline X_n)=\lambda/n$. Therefore, for every $\varepsilon>0$, Chebyshev gives $P(|\overline X_n-\lambda|\ge\varepsilon)\le\lambda/(n\varepsilon^2)\to0$. Hence $\overline X_n$ converges in probability to $\lambda$.

content.markdown:
Let $B_1,\ldots,B_n$ be independent Bernoulli variables with parameter $p$, and set $T_n=\sum B_k$.

### Target

Use a product generating function to obtain moments, then derive concentration of the empirical frequency directly from Markov.

### Strategy

Multiply the Bernoulli generators, differentiate at $1$ to recover the sum's mean and variance, and apply Markov to $(T_n-np)^2$ at $n^2\varepsilon^2$.

### Hypotheses

The variables are independent, $\mathbb N$-valued, and bounded, so the generating-function product is valid and all required moments are finite. The deviation threshold satisfies $\varepsilon>0$.

### Complete solution

$G_{T_n}(t)=(1-p+pt)^n$. Thus $E[T_n]=np$ and $\operatorname{Var}(T_n)=np(1-p)$. The variable $Y=(T_n-np)^2$ is nonnegative and integrable. Since $\{|T_n/n-p|\ge\varepsilon\}=\{Y\ge n^2\varepsilon^2\}$, Markov gives $P(|T_n/n-p|\ge\varepsilon)\le p(1-p)/(n\varepsilon^2)$, which tends to zero.

### Boundary check

The proof gives convergence in probability. It does not prove almost-sure convergence, and the displayed probability is bounded above rather than calculated exactly.

content.markdown:
# Fix the mathematical universe before solving

Throughout this week, $\mathbb K$ is $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, $I\subset\mathbb R$ is one interval, and $E$ is a finite-dimensional $\mathbb K$-vector space of dimension $n$. After choosing a basis of $E$, a system is written $Y'=A(t)Y+B(t)$ with $A:I\to M_n(\mathbb K)$ and $B:I\to\mathbb K^n$. The coordinate matrix depends on the basis; the solution vector in $E$ does not.

## Uniqueness creates linear algebra

Assume $A$ and $B$ are continuous on the whole interval $I$. The linear Cauchy theorem gives exactly one $C^1$ solution on $I$ through each pair $(t_0,y_0)$ with $t_0\in I$. For the homogeneous equation, this means that evaluation at one time remembers the entire solution. That bijection transfers the finite-dimensional structure of $E$ to a space of functions.

## Translate a vector derivative into one chosen basis

Week 18 basis coordinates and Week 51 vector differentiation are the exact prerequisites for reading a vector differential system.

## Differential equations · Linear systems

A linear system has the form $Y'=A(t)Y+B(t)$; its homogeneous solution set is a vector space.

Let $A\in C^0(I,\mathcal L(E))$ and $b\in C^0(I,E)$. A solution is a $C^1$ map $x:I\to E$ satisfying $x'(t)=A(t)x(t)+b(t)$ for every $t\in I$. The associated homogeneous equation has $b=0$. Its solution set $\mathcal S_h$ is a vector subspace of $C^1(I,E)$ because the differential operator $x\mapsto x'-Ax$ is linear. For any $t_0\in I$, uniqueness makes $\operatorname{ev}_{t_0}:\mathcal S_h\to E$, $x\mapsto x(t_0)$, injective; existence makes it surjective. Hence it is a linear isomorphism and $\dim_{\mathbb K}\mathcal S_h=\dim_{\mathbb K}E=n$. If $x_p$ is one solution of the forced equation, its complete solution set is the affine space $x_p+\mathcal S_h$. Continuity on one interval is the stated global hypothesis; the lesson makes no claim for discontinuous coefficients or across a gap in the domain.

On $I=\mathbb R$ over $\mathbb R$, consider $Y'=A(t)Y+B(t)$ with $A(t)=\operatorname{diag}(t,-1)$ and $B(t)=(e^{t^2/2},0)^T$, using the standard basis and initial time $t_0=0$.

### Target

Prove explicitly that evaluation at one time identifies a homogeneous two-dimensional solution space with its state space, then obtain the associated affine forced family.

### Strategy

Separate the diagonal homogeneous equations, read evaluation at zero through the two constants, construct its inverse, find one forced solution by a moving scalar coefficient, and translate the homogeneous space.

### Hypotheses

The field is $\mathbb R$, the interval is all of $\mathbb R$, the standard basis is fixed, $A$ and $B$ are continuous, and solutions are $C^1$ vector functions on the same interval.

### Complete solution

The homogeneous equations are $y_1'=ty_1$ and $y_2'=-y_2$, so $Y_h(t)=(c_1e^{t^2/2},c_2e^{-t})^T$. Evaluation at $0$ sends $Y_h$ to $(c_1,c_2)^T$; it is linear and bijective, with inverse $(u,v)\mapsto(ue^{t^2/2},ve^{-t})^T$. Hence the homogeneous space has dimension $2$. For a particular solution, write $y_1=u(t)e^{t^2/2}$; then $u'e^{t^2/2}=e^{t^2/2}$, so $u=t$ works, while $y_2=0$. Thus $Y_p(t)=(te^{t^2/2},0)^T$, and every inhomogeneous solution is exactly $Y_p+Y_h$. This last set is an affine translate, not a vector subspace because $B\ne0$.

### Boundary check

The forced family is affine and does not contain zero because $B\ne0$. The evaluation argument would fail without both existence and uniqueness on the complete interval.

## Day 1 synthesis

For continuous coefficients on one interval, evaluation at any time is an isomorphism from the homogeneous solution space to the state space. This proves dimension $n$ without solving explicitly. activities.title: Translate a vector derivative into one chosen basis
activities.promptMarkdown:

content.markdown:
# Put a solution basis into columns

Fix $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, an interval $I$, a continuous $A:I\to M_n(\mathbb K)$, and one fixed basis of the state space. A matrix function $\Phi\in C^1(I,M_n(\mathbb K))$ satisfies $\Phi'=A\Phi$ exactly when each column is a homogeneous solution. The numerical Wronskian $\det\Phi$ changes by a nonzero constant when the state basis or the solution basis changes, but the property “Wronskian nowhere zero” is basis-independent.

## Invertibility is the whole basis question

The columns form a basis of the homogeneous solution space precisely when their values at one time form a basis of $\mathbb K^n$. Thus $\Phi$ is fundamental exactly when $\det\Phi(t_0)\ne0$ at one time; uniqueness then prevents its determinant from becoming zero elsewhere on the interval.

## Reactivate column coordinates and determinant independence

The prerequisite block reconnects basis coordinates and vector derivatives before any determinant is called a Wronskian.

content.markdown:
Solve the homogeneous system $Y'=AY$ for $A=\operatorname{diag}(2,-1)$ and $Y=(y_1,y_2)^T$.

### Target

Solve a diagonal constant-coefficient system for arbitrary initial data, identify the resulting diagonal fundamental matrix, and verify the full two-dimensional homogeneous family.

### Strategy

Use the standard eigenbasis in which the coefficient matrix is diagonal, solve the two scalar equations, place the canonical initial-data solutions into columns, and differentiate the complete vector family.

### Hypotheses

The field is $\mathbb R$, the coefficient matrix is constant and diagonal in the stated fixed basis, the interval is all of $\mathbb R$, and both exponential diagonal entries are nonzero at every time.

### Complete solution

Because $A$ is diagonal, the vector equation separates into

$$y_1'=2y_1,\qquad y_2'=-y_2.$$

The scalar solutions are $y_1(t)=C_1e^{2t}$ and $y_2(t)=C_2e^{-t}$. Hence every solution is

$$Y(t)=\begin{pmatrix}C_1e^{2t}\\C_2e^{-t}\end{pmatrix},\qquad C_1,C_2\in\mathbb R.$$

Differentiation gives $Y'=(2C_1e^{2t},-C_2e^{-t})^T=AY$, which verifies the full family.

Putting the solutions with initial data $(1,0)^T$ and $(0,1)^T$ into columns gives $\Phi(t)=\operatorname{diag}(e^{2t},e^{-t})$. It satisfies $\Phi'=A\Phi$, $\Phi(0)=I_2$, and $W(t)=\det\Phi(t)=e^t\ne0$, so it is fundamental. More generally, Liouville's formula for a continuous coefficient matrix gives $\det\Psi(t)=\det\Psi(t_0)\exp(\int_{t_0}^t\operatorname{tr}A(s)\,ds)$. Thus a matrix solution that is invertible at one time cannot acquire an isolated singular time on the same interval.

### Boundary check

Coordinatewise scalar equations arise here because the matrix is diagonal in the chosen basis. A nondiagonal matrix couples the coordinates, so solving only its diagonal entries would omit terms. The value of a Wronskian depends on the chosen state and solution bases, but its nonvanishing does not. A matrix whose columns solve the system is fundamental only after this invertibility condition is checked.

## Exact course reference

This lesson follows the named syllabus section below. The linked locator identifies the exact external passage used for the definitions, hypotheses, and methods in this lesson.

Exact locator: [source document](https://www.education.gouv.fr/bo/21/Hebdo31/ESRS2111702A.htm); page 25–26/28, section b and section c · evaluation isomorphism, dimension, matrix exponential, and invertible solution matrices in “Programme de mathématiques MP/MP*, annexe 1, Bulletin officiel no. 31 of 26 August 2021”.

## Day 2 synthesis

A fundamental matrix is a matrix solution whose columns form a basis of the homogeneous solution space. One nonzero Wronskian value is enough on a connected interval, and normalization at $t_0$ gives the evolution matrix $\Phi(t)\Phi(t_0)^{-1}$. Day 3 computes that matrix for constant coefficients, including a genuinely non-diagonalizable case.

content.markdown:
# The exponential is the evolution operator

For $A\in M_n(\mathbb K)$ constant on an interval and initial time $t_0$, the unique solution of $Y'=AY$, $Y(t_0)=y_0$, is $Y(t)=e^{(t-t_0)A}y_0$. The series defining $e^A$ is valid over $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$ in finite dimension and is independent of the matrix norm used to prove convergence.

## Reduction changes the calculation, not the theorem

If $A=PDP^{-1}$ is diagonalizable over the chosen field, then $e^{tA}=Pe^{tD}P^{-1}$. If it is not diagonalizable, a nilpotent part supplies polynomial factors. A real matrix may be diagonalizable over $\mathbb C$ but not over $\mathbb R$, so the field must be stated before choosing an eigenbasis.

## Reactivate a basis change in a constant system

The basis-change calculation is the exact prerequisite for treating a diagonalizable coefficient matrix.

Over $\mathbb R$, let $A=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\0&2\end{pmatrix}=2I+N$ with $N^2=0$, and solve $Y'=AY$ for arbitrary $Y(0)=(a,b)^T$.

### Target

Compute the evolution operator for a constant non-diagonalizable Jordan block and prove the complete arbitrary-initial-data solution family.

### Strategy

Split the matrix into a scalar part and a nilpotent part, verify commutation, truncate the nilpotent exponential, multiply by arbitrary initial data, and check both coupled component equations.

### Hypotheses

The field is $\mathbb R$, the interval is all of $\mathbb R$, the standard basis is fixed, the coefficient matrix is constant, $N^2=0$, and $2I$ commutes with $N$.

### Complete solution

Because $2I$ and $N$ commute, $e^{tA}=e^{2tI}e^{tN}$. Since $N^2=0$, $e^{tN}=I+tN$, so

$$e^{tA}=e^{2t}\begin{pmatrix}1&t\\0&1\end{pmatrix}.$$

Therefore

$$Y(t)=e^{2t}\begin{pmatrix}a+tb\\b\end{pmatrix}.$$

Differentiating gives $y_2'=2y_2$ and $y_1'=2e^{2t}(a+tb)+e^{2t}b=2y_1+y_2$. At $t=0$ the vector is $(a,b)^T$. The term $tb e^{2t}$ is essential whenever $b\ne0$ and records the non-diagonalizable Jordan coupling.

### Boundary check

The polynomial factor cannot be removed unless the initial vector lies in the eigenspace. Exponential factorization is justified here by commutation and is not a general identity for arbitrary summands.

content.markdown:
# Let the coefficient vector move

Let $A\in C^0(I,M_n(\mathbb K))$, $B\in C^0(I,\mathbb K^n)$, and let $\Phi$ be a fundamental matrix for $Y'=AY$ on the same interval. For $t_0\in I$, every Cauchy solution of $Y'=AY+B$ is

$$Y(t)=\Phi(t)\left(\Phi(t_0)^{-1}y_0+\int_{t_0}^t\Phi(s)^{-1}B(s)\,ds\right).$$

## The formula is a product-rule argument

Write $Y=\Phi C$. Since $\Phi'=A\Phi$, differentiation cancels the homogeneous part and leaves $C'=\Phi^{-1}B$. The inverse is pointwise and multiplies the column vector on the left. No commutation between $A(t)$ at different times is required because the already-constructed fundamental matrix carries the homogeneous evolution.

## Differentiate a matrix-vector product before cancelling

This prerequisite reactivates Week 51 vector differentiation and Day 2 invertibility before the new method is used.

content.markdown:
On $I=\mathbb R$, consider $Y'=AY+B(t)$ with $A=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)$, $B(t)=(e^t,1)^T$, and $Y(0)=0$ over $\mathbb R$.

### Target

Derive vector variation of constants with a pointwise-invertible fundamental matrix and solve one forced diagonal Cauchy problem completely.

### Strategy

Use the matrix-vector product rule, cancel the homogeneous term, multiply by the inverse on the left, integrate from the initial time, reconstruct the state, and verify both coordinates.

### Hypotheses

The field is $\mathbb R$, the interval is all of $\mathbb R$, the standard basis is fixed, $A$ and $B$ are continuous, and the chosen fundamental matrix has nonzero determinant everywhere.

### Complete solution

Take $\Phi(t)=\operatorname{diag}(e^t,e^{-t})$, which is invertible for every $t$. If $Y=\Phi C$, then $Y'=\Phi'C+\Phi C'=A\Phi C+\Phi C'$. Comparing with $AY+B$ gives $\Phi C'=B$, hence

$$C'(t)=\Phi(t)^{-1}B(t)=(1,e^t)^T.$$

The initial condition gives $C(0)=0$, so $C(t)=(t,e^t-1)^T$. Therefore

$$Y(t)=(te^t,1-e^{-t})^T.$$

Indeed, $y_1'=e^t(t+1)=y_1+e^t$ and $y_2'=e^{-t}=-y_2+1$, with $Y(0)=0$.

### Boundary check

The inverse order is essential for column vectors. The formula uses a genuine fundamental matrix and does not assume that variable coefficient matrices commute at different times.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: The product rule gives $(\Phi C)'=\Phi'C+\Phi C'=A\Phi C+\Phi C'$. Since $AY=A\Phi C$, the forced equation is equivalent to $\Phi C'=B$. Pointwise invertibility gives $C'=\Phi^{-1}B$. The alternative $B\Phi^{-1}$ is not a column vector product in this convention.

The matrix $\Phi$ is fundamental and $\Phi^{-1}(s)=\operatorname{diag}(e^{-2s},e^{2s})$. The product-rule argument gives $C'=\Phi^{-1}B$ and $C(0)=y_0$. Therefore

$$Y(t)=\Phi(t)\left(y_0+\int_0^t\Phi(s)^{-1}B(s)\,ds\right).$$

The integrand is continuous. Differentiating with the fundamental theorem of calculus gives

$$Y'=\Phi'\left(y_0+\int_0^t\Phi^{-1}B\right)+\Phi\Phi^{-1}B=AY+B,$$

and at $t=0$, $\Phi(0)=I$, so $Y(0)=y_0$. Uniqueness makes this the only solution.

Complete oral model over $\mathbb R$: on $I=\mathbb R$, solve $Y'=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)Y+(e^t,1)^T$ with $Y(0)=0$, and organize the derivation around a fundamental matrix.

### Target

Present a complete forced-system solution in a sequence that makes the field, interval, continuity, basis, fundamental-matrix inverse, affine structure, and final verification audible.

### Strategy

State the Cauchy hypotheses, choose the normalized diagonal fundamental matrix, derive $C'=\Phi^{-1}B$, integrate from the actual initial time, reconstruct $Y$, and close by differentiating both coordinates.

### Hypotheses

The field is $\mathbb R$, the standard basis is fixed, the interval is all of $\mathbb R$, the constant matrix and forcing are continuous, and $\Phi(t)=\operatorname{diag}(e^t,e^{-t})$ has determinant $1$ for every $t$.

### Complete solution

The linear Cauchy theorem gives one global $C^1$ solution through the prescribed data. For the homogeneous system, $\Phi(t)=\operatorname{diag}(e^t,e^{-t})$ satisfies $\Phi'=A\Phi$, $\Phi(0)=I$, and $\det\Phi=1$, so it is fundamental. Write $Y=\Phi C$. Then $C'=\Phi^{-1}B=(1,e^t)^T$ and $C(0)=0$, hence $C(t)=(t,e^t-1)^T$. Therefore

$$Y(t)=(te^t,1-e^{-t})^T.$$

Verification gives $y_1'=e^t(t+1)=y_1+e^t$, $y_2'=e^{-t}=-y_2+1$, and $Y(0)=0$. All forced solutions without fixed initial data would form this particular solution plus the two-dimensional homogeneous solution space.

### Boundary check

No timed oral score is claimed. The ordinary matrix exponential is used because $A$ is constant. For a general continuous $A(t)$, use a genuine fundamental matrix; the shortcut $\exp(\int A)$ needs pairwise commutation. The determinant check cannot be omitted because variation of constants uses $\Phi^{-1}$.

# The interval and leading coefficient come before the formula

Fix $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ and an interval $I\subset\mathbb R$. For $a_2y''+a_1y'+a_0y=b$, the order-two Cauchy theorem applies on a region where $a_2$ never vanishes and the normalized coefficients $a_1/a_2$, $a_0/a_2$, and $b/a_2$ are continuous. Initial data are $(y(t_0),y'(t_0))\in\mathbb K^2$ at $t_0\in I$.

## Why Week 58 is more general than Week 12

Week 12 verified constant-coefficient families. Here the same derivative discipline is placed inside the linear Cauchy theorem: the homogeneous solution set is a vector space, the inhomogeneous set is an affine translate, and a zero of the leading coefficient can split the legal analysis into different intervals.

## Translate an order-two equation into a system

This prerequisite activation connects primitives, scalar normalization, power-operation discipline, and the Week 57 system theorem without yet asserting a solution formula.

## Differential equations · General scalar equations

A scalar linear differential equation has the unknown and its derivatives appearing linearly with coefficient functions on a stated interval.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $a_0,\ldots,a_n,b:I\to\mathbb K$ be continuous with $a_n(t)\ne0$ for every $t\in I$. After division by $a_n$, the scalar equation $a_ny^{(n)}+\cdots+a_0y=b$ is equivalent on this same interval to a first-order system with continuous coefficients. The linear Cauchy theorem gives one $C^n$ solution for each $t_0\in I$ and each initial vector $(y(t_0),\ldots,y^{(n-1)}(t_0))\in\mathbb K^n$. Consequently the homogeneous solution space has dimension $n$, and every forced solution is one particular solution plus that space.

**Complete boundary model.** For $t y''+y'=0$, division by $t$ is valid on $(-\infty,0)$ and $(0,\infty)$ but not across $0$. The general theorem therefore gives separate Cauchy problems on those components; it does not license one normalized formula through the singular point.

Over $\mathbb K=\mathbb R$ on $I=\mathbb R$, determine the full solution space of $y''-y=0$ and relate it to the data $(y(0),y'(0))$.

### Target

Determine the complete real solution space, prove that its displayed functions form a basis, and identify the exact initial-data isomorphism at zero.

### Strategy

Verify the two exponentials, calculate their Wronskian, then match arbitrary Cauchy data and use uniqueness to prove that the resulting linear combination equals every solution.

### Hypotheses

The field is $\mathbb R$, the interval is $\mathbb R$, the normalized coefficients are continuous, the leading coefficient equals one, and solutions belong to $C^2(\mathbb R)$.

### Complete solution

The coefficient functions are continuous on $I$ and the leading coefficient is $1$, so each pair $(u_0,u_1)\in\mathbb R^2$ determines one $C^2$ solution. The functions $e^x$ and $e^{-x}$ solve the equation and have Wronskian $-2$, hence they are independent. For an arbitrary solution, choose $A=(y(0)+y'(0))/2$ and $B=(y(0)-y'(0))/2$. Then $Ae^x+Be^{-x}$ has the same two initial data as $y$; uniqueness makes the functions equal. Thus $S=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb R}\{e^x,e^{-x}\}$ and $\dim S=2$.

### Boundary check

Two verified solutions do not by themselves prove completeness. Independence needs the Wronskian, and exhaustion of all solutions needs the order-two Cauchy theorem.

content.markdown:
# Formal algebra and analytic legitimacy are two stages

For $y'+a(x)y=b(x)$ on an interval of continuous real or complex coefficients, variation of constants follows from a nonvanishing integrating factor. For $y=\sum a_n(x-x_0)^n$, coefficient comparison is legal only after termwise operations are justified on an open radius, or else remains a formal calculation awaiting convergence proof.

## Why the integration base point and radius must be visible

The base point stores the initial value in the variation formula. The convergence radius stores the domain on which a coefficient recurrence defines a differentiable function. Omitting either boundary turns a correct symbolic line into an unsupported solution claim.

## Reactivate the integrating-factor identity

The activation rebuilds the Week 12 product derivative under the general interval and field hypotheses needed today.

### Repair guide for “Reactivate the integrating-factor identity”

Use this guide only after reading Forge’s assessment of your submitted answer.

For **Reactivate the integrating-factor identity**, repair the first missing chain-rule factor $A'$ or unsupported division by the integrating factor.

Variation of constants is an equivalence only because the chosen factor is differentiable and nowhere zero on the whole interval.

For **Reactivate the integrating-factor identity**, derive $A'=a$, apply both differentiation rules, and state the nonvanishing property before integrating.

content.markdown:
## Differential equations · Variation of constants

Variation of constants replaces a homogeneous constant parameter by a function chosen to produce the forcing term.

Let $I$ be an interval, $a,b\in C^0(I,\mathbb K)$, $x_0\in I$, and $y(x_0)=y_0$. Put $A(x)=\int_{x_0}^x a(s)\,ds$ and $\mu=e^A$, which never vanishes. Then $(\mu y)'=\mu(y'+ay)=\mu b$, so

$$y(x)=e^{-A(x)}\left(y_0+\int_{x_0}^x e^{A(t)}b(t)\,dt\right).$$

Every step is reversible on $I$, and substitution verifies the equation and datum. **Complete analogous model.** For $y'+2xy=x$ on $\mathbb R$ with $y(0)=3$, $\mu=e^{x^2}$ and $\int_0^x te^{t^2}dt=(e^{x^2}-1)/2$, hence $y=1/2+(5/2)e^{-x^2}$; direct differentiation gives the original equation.

content.markdown:
## Differential equations · Power Series

A power-series solution substitutes $y=\sum a_nx^n$ into the equation and equates coefficients to obtain a recurrence.

Fix $x_0=0$ for notation. If $y=\sum_{n\ge0}a_nx^n$ has radius $R>0$, then on every compact subinterval of $(-R,R)$ the sum is smooth and may be differentiated term by term; shifted products must be reindexed before coefficients are compared. A recurrence first defines a formal series. One must then prove a positive radius—by a coefficient estimate, comparison, or identification with a known convergent series—and finally substitute the resulting sum on $|x|<R$. **Complete legitimacy model.** For $y'=2y$, $y(0)=c$, comparison gives $(n+1)a_{n+1}=2a_n$, hence $a_n=c2^n/n!$. The factorial ratio gives $R=+\infty$, so termwise differentiation is valid everywhere and the sum $ce^{2x}$ solves the Cauchy problem.

content.markdown:
Find the power-series solution at $0$ of $y'=xy$ with $y(0)=1$, derive its coefficient recurrence, and justify convergence.

### Target

Derive every coefficient of the power-series solution at zero, prove its convergence radius, identify the sum, and verify the prescribed initial value.

### Strategy

Differentiate the unknown series, shift the product by $x$, compare the constant coefficient separately, and then solve the even and odd recurrences before invoking the exponential radius.

### Hypotheses

The equation is posed over $\mathbb R$ near zero; the coefficient $x$ is analytic; coefficient comparison is initially formal; the identified exponential series has infinite radius, which later licenses termwise differentiation.

### Complete solution

Write $y=\sum_{n\ge0}a_nx^n$. Then $y'=\sum_{n\ge0}(n+1)a_{n+1}x^n$, while $xy=\sum_{n\ge1}a_{n-1}x^n$. Coefficient comparison gives $a_1=0$ and

$$(n+1)a_{n+1}=a_{n-1}\qquad(n\ge1).$$

With $a_0=y(0)=1$, all odd coefficients vanish and $a_{2k}=1/(2^k k!)$. Therefore

$$y(x)=\sum_{k\ge0}\frac{x^{2k}}{2^k k!}=e^{x^2/2}.$$

The exponential series has infinite radius, so the formal solution converges for every real $x$; differentiation verifies the equation.

### Boundary check

A coefficient recurrence alone produces only a formal series. Convergence must be established before the series is treated as a differentiable function solving the differential equation.

content.markdown:
# Root multiplicity determines the basis, not just the exponent

For $ay''+by'+cy=0$ with $a\ne0$ and constants in $\mathbb K$, the characteristic polynomial is $P(r)=ar^2+br+c$. Simple real roots give two exponentials, a real repeated root gives $e^{rx}$ and $xe^{rx}$, and conjugate roots $\alpha\pm i\beta$ with $\beta\ne0$ give the real pair $e^{\alpha x}\cos(\beta x)$ and $e^{\alpha x}\sin(\beta x)$.

## Why the field must be named

Over $\mathbb C$, conjugate roots support complex exponential basis functions. Over $\mathbb R$, those functions are replaced by their real and imaginary parts. The solution space still has dimension two over its chosen field, but the displayed basis and constants belong to that field.

## Reactivate the characteristic substitution

This prerequisite retrieves Week 12's exponential trial while retaining the field and multiplicity data needed for Week 58.

content.markdown:
Over $\mathbb K=\mathbb R$ on $\mathbb R$, solve $y''-y'-2y=0$ and certify the fundamental pair needed for later variation of constants.

### Target

Factor the characteristic polynomial with multiplicities and certify a fundamental pair whose nonzero Wronskian supports subsequent order-two variation of constants.

### Strategy

Derive the two simple real roots, verify their exponentials directly, compute the Wronskian on the entire interval, and combine independence with the dimension theorem.

### Hypotheses

The equation is homogeneous with real constant coefficients and nonzero leading coefficient on $I=\mathbb R$; its solutions are real-valued and twice continuously differentiable.

### Complete solution

The characteristic polynomial is $P(r)=r^2-r-2=(r-2)(r+1)$, with two simple real roots $2$ and $-1$. Therefore $y_1=e^{2x}$ and $y_2=e^{-x}$ solve the equation. Their Wronskian is $W=y_1y_2'-y_1'y_2=-3e^x$, which never vanishes. The real homogeneous solution space is consequently $\operatorname{span}\{e^{2x},e^{-x}\}$ and has dimension two.

### Boundary check

This basis construction belongs to two simple roots. A repeated root requires $xe^{rx}$, while a nonreal pair requires a field-aware complex or sine-cosine representation.

content.markdown:
# A forced solution is particular plus homogeneous freedom

On an interval $I$, normalize $y''+p(x)y'+q(x)y=g(x)$ with $p,q,g$ continuous. If $(y_1,y_2)$ is a homogeneous basis with $W=y_1y_2'-y_1'y_2\ne0$, impose $u_1'y_1+u_2'y_2=0$. Then $u_1'=-y_2g/W$ and $u_2'=y_1g/W$. The complete forced family is $u_1y_1+u_2y_2+C_1y_1+C_2y_2$.

## Why resonance creates a polynomial factor

For a constant-coefficient operator $P(D)$, the trial $e^{\lambda x}$ is annihilated when $P(\lambda)=0$. Multiplying by $x^m$, where $m$ is the root multiplicity, moves the trial outside the homogeneous space. This is a structural correction, not a memorized guess.

## Reactivate a Wronskian and forcing system

The prerequisite activation reconstructs the coefficient system that the complete nonresonant model will solve.

On $I=\mathbb R$, find a particular solution of $y''-3y'+2y=e^{4x}$ from the fundamental pair $(e^x,e^{2x})$.

### Target

Derive a complete nonresonant particular solution with order-two variation of constants and verify that it reconstructs the exact exponential forcing.

### Strategy

Use the proved fundamental pair, fix one Wronskian convention, solve the gauge system for the two coefficient derivatives, integrate, assemble, and substitute.

### Hypotheses

The real interval is $\mathbb R$; the equation is normalized; coefficients and forcing are continuous; the fundamental solutions are $C^2$; and their Wronskian $e^{3x}$ never vanishes.

### Complete solution

The coefficients and forcing are continuous and the leading coefficient is $1$. With $y_1=e^x$, $y_2=e^{2x}$, one has $W=e^{3x}$. The gauge equations $u_1'y_1+u_2'y_2=0$ and $u_1'y_1'+u_2'y_2'=e^{4x}$ give $u_1'=-y_2e^{4x}/W=-e^{3x}$ and $u_2'=y_1e^{4x}/W=e^{2x}$. Choose $u_1=-e^{3x}/3$ and $u_2=e^{2x}/2$. Then $y_p=u_1y_1+u_2y_2=e^{4x}/6$. Since $16-12+2=6$, substitution gives $y_p''-3y_p'+2y_p=e^{4x}$.

### Boundary check

Changing the Wronskian convention changes both numerator signs. A consistent convention gives the same particular solution, while a mixed convention fails direct substitution.

# A calm oral rehearsal starts with hypotheses

The first four questions deliberately retrieve Weeks 57, 55, 50, and 42 at intervals of 1, 3, 8, and 16 weeks. The last question is an untimed written board-script rehearsal, so you can concentrate on a complete mathematical explanation rather than examination pace.

## Refresh the mathematics for today's reviews

For Week 58, Day 5 · Deliberate review and oral synthesis, first revisit Differential equations · General scalar equations, Integration · Antiderivatives, Power series · Operations, Differential equations · Linear systems. Each of the four reviews then applies one earlier idea to a new case before the final synthesis.

## Why unrelated retrieval remains deliberate

A concours presentation must preserve methods that are not cued by the current chapter. The system isomorphism, absolute integrability, termwise power-series integration, and sequential closedness are therefore reconstructed before the mixed ODE argument.

content.markdown:
On $\mathbb R$, solve $y''-2y'+y=e^x$ with $y(0)=0$, $y'(0)=1$, and determine its first five Taylor coefficients.

### Target

Model a complete board exposition joining repeated-root resonance, Cauchy data, a coefficient list, convergence radius, and direct verification.

### Strategy

Factor the operator as $(D-1)^2$, use the double-resonant polynomial factor, add the full homogeneous family, impose the two data, and read coefficients from the entire closed form.

### Hypotheses

The field is $\mathbb R$, the interval is all of $\mathbb R$, all coefficients and the forcing are continuous, the leading coefficient is nonzero, and the exponential-polynomial answer is entire.

### Complete solution

$P(r)=(r-1)^2$, so the homogeneous family is $(A+Bx)e^x$. For the forcing $e^x$, double resonance gives $y_p=(x^2/2)e^x$, because $(D-1)^2[e^x(x^2/2)]=e^x$. The data give $A=0$ and $B=1$, hence $y=e^x(x+x^2/2)$. Expanding the entire expression yields $a_0=0$, $a_1=1$, $a_2=3/2$, $a_3=1$, and $a_4=5/12$. Its radius is $+\infty$; termwise differentiation is valid everywhere, and substitution verifies both the equation and data.

### Boundary check

The factor $x^2$ comes from a root of multiplicity two. One factor of $x$ would remain homogeneous. The radius conclusion comes from the entire closed form, not from five computed coefficients.

# One linear map must control every small increment

Throughout this week, $E$ and $F$ are finite-dimensional real normed spaces, $U\subset E$ is open, $a\in U$, and a derivative is a bounded linear map $E\to F$. Every little-$o$ statement names both the source increment norm and the target remainder norm.

## Why the remainder is the definition

Several one-dimensional limits can coexist without describing one linear approximation. Fréchet differentiability controls the complete increment $h$, regardless of the direction from which $h$ tends to zero.

## Activate openness and the operator bound

## Worked model before the checkpoint

If $B(a,\rho)\subset U$ and $h\ne0$ satisfies $\|h\|_E<\rho$, then the whole endpoint $a+h$ lies in the domain. For a bounded linear $L$, $\|Lh\|_F\le\|L\|\,\|h\|_E$.

## Differential calculus · Frechet

$f$ is Fréchet differentiable at $a$ when $f(a+h)=f(a)+Df(a)h+o(\|h\|)$ for one linear map $Df(a)$.

The function $f:U\to F$ is Fréchet differentiable at $a$ when there is a linear map $L:E\to F$ and a remainder $r$ such that $f(a+h)=f(a)+Lh+r(h)$ for every sufficiently small $h$, with $$\frac{\|r(h)\|_F}{\|h\|_E}\longrightarrow0.$$ Openness supplies a ball around $a$, so all small increments are admissible. In finite dimension, linear maps are continuous; the derivative is denoted $Df(a)=L$.

content.markdown:
Two linear maps $A,B:E\to F$ both satisfy $f(a+h)=f(a)+Ah+o(\|h\|_E)=f(a)+Bh+o(\|h\|_E)$.

### Target

Prove uniqueness by scaling one arbitrary vector

### Strategy

Prove $A=B$ without assuming a preferred basis. Make the substitution $h=tv$ and justify the division.

### Hypotheses

Two linear maps $A,B:E\to F$ both satisfy $f(a+h)=f(a)+Ah+o(\|h\|_E)=f(a)+Bh+o(\|h\|_E)$.

### Complete solution

Subtracting gives $(A-B)h=r_B(h)-r_A(h)=o(\|h\|_E)$. Fix $v\in E$. For $t\ne0$, divide the norm identity at $h=tv$ by $|t|$; since $\|tv\|_E=|t|\|v\|_E$, the right side tends to zero. Thus $\|(A-B)v\|_F=0$. This holds for every $v$, hence $A=B$.

### Boundary check

## Worked model before the checkpoint

Suppose $L_1,L_2:E\to F$ both satisfy the Fréchet expansion. Subtraction gives $(L_1-L_2)h=o(\|h\|_E)$. For fixed $v$ put $h=tv$: after division by $|t|$, homogeneity yields $\|(L_1-L_2)v\|_F\to0$. Hence $(L_1-L_2)v=0$ for every $v$, so $L_1=L_2$.

# A line test sees only one family of approaches

The directional derivative follows the one-variable path $t\mapsto a+tv$. Fréchet differentiability is stronger because it controls every small vector increment by the same linear map.

## Why all directions are still not enough

Directional limits can exist and even all equal zero while a curved approach retains a first-order remainder. The missing requirement is uniform control in the full increment.

## Compute a directional limit on an affine line

## Worked model before the checkpoint

For $q(x,y)=x^2-y^2$, $a=(1,1)$, and $v=(1,2)$, expansion along $a+tv$ gives a quotient $-2-3t$, hence derivative $-2$.

## Differential calculus · Directional

The directional derivative in direction $v$ is the one-variable limit $\lim_{t\to0}[f(a+tv)-f(a)]/t$.

For $v\in E$, the directional derivative is $$D_vf(a)=\lim_{t\to0}\frac{f(a+tv)-f(a)}{t}$$ when this two-sided real limit exists. If $f$ is Fréchet differentiable at $a$, substitute $h=tv$ into the expansion and divide by $t$: the remainder quotient tends to zero, so $D_vf(a)=Df(a)v$. This implication does not reverse without additional hypotheses.

content.markdown:
For $f(x,y)=xy$, compute the directional derivative at $a=(1,2)$ in the direction $v=(3,-1)$ directly from the one-variable limit.

### Target

Compute a directional derivative from its defining one-variable limit and verify it against a known total derivative.

### Strategy

Parameterize the affine line $a+tv$, expand the scalar expression exactly, divide the increment by $t$, and only then take the real limit.

### Hypotheses

$f$ is defined on all of $\mathbb R^2$, so the line is admissible near zero. The requested directional derivative uses a two-sided real limit.

### Complete solution

Along the line $a+tv=(1+3t,2-t)$,

$$f(a+tv)=(1+3t)(2-t)=2+5t-3t^2.$$

Since $f(a)=2$, the directional difference quotient is

$$\frac{f(a+tv)-f(a)}{t}=5-3t$$

for $t\ne0$. Its limit as $t\to0$ is $5$. Therefore $D_vf(a)=5$. As a check, the gradient is $\nabla f(1,2)=(2,1)$ and its dot product with $v$ is also $6-1=5$.

### Boundary check

The existence of directional derivatives in every direction does not by itself produce a Fréchet derivative. The directional values must assemble into one linear map with a remainder that is small relative to the full increment.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Since $2|x^3y|\le x^6+y^2$, $|c(x,y)|\le\tfrac12\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$, so $c\to0$. Along $(tu,tv)$, the quotient $c(tu,tv)/t$ tends to zero: if $v\ne0$ it is $O(t^2)$, while if $v=0$ it vanishes. Thus all directional derivatives are zero. If a Fréchet derivative existed it would be the zero map, but along $y=x^3$, $c(x,x^3)/\sqrt{x^2+x^6}=1/2$, so the required remainder ratio does not tend to zero.

First study the definition, hypotheses, coordinate representation, and a complete model. Later, you may use 20 minutes of preparation and 20 minutes of presentation as optional exam-condition practice; every task remains open and feedback follows its submitted answer.

## A derivative transports velocity

For a differentiable curve $\gamma:I\to U$, the vector $\gamma'(t)$ lives in the source space. The linear map $Df(\gamma(t))$ sends it to the velocity of the image curve.

## Read a Jacobian as a linear map

## Differential calculus · Curve

For a differentiable curve $\gamma$ and differentiable $f$, $(f\circ\gamma)'(t)=Df(\gamma(t))\gamma'(t)$.

Let $I\subset\mathbb R$ be an interval, $U\subset E$ open, $f:U\to F$ differentiable, and $\gamma:I\to U$ differentiable at $t$. Then $f\circ\gamma$ is differentiable at $t$ and $$(f\circ\gamma)'(t)=Df(\gamma(t))\,\gamma'(t).$$ In coordinates, the Jacobian matrix of $f$ multiplies the column of curve velocities. Every evaluation point and source-target type remains visible.

content.markdown:
Let $f:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R^2$ be $f(x,y)=(x^2-y,xy)$ and let $\gamma(t)=(\cos t,\sin t)$. Compute $(f\circ\gamma)'(0)$ by the differential-along-a-curve formula.

### Target

Compute the velocity of an image curve by evaluating a Jacobian at the curve point and applying it to the curve velocity.

### Strategy

Write the Jacobian with its source and target dimensions, compute the curve point and velocity separately, multiply in the type-correct order, and verify by direct differentiation.

### Hypotheses

The polynomial map is differentiable on the open set $\mathbb R^2$, and the trigonometric curve is differentiable with image in that domain.

### Complete solution

The Jacobian is $$J_f(x,y)=\begin{pmatrix}2x&-1\\y&x\end{pmatrix}.$$ The curve satisfies $\gamma(0)=(1,0)$ and $\gamma'(0)=(0,1)$. Hence $$D f(\gamma(0))\gamma'(0)=\begin{pmatrix}2&-1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\binom01=\binom{-1}{1}.$$ Direct differentiation gives $f(\gamma(t))=(\cos^2t-\sin t,\cos t\sin t)$ and the same derivative $(-1,1)$ at zero.

### Boundary check

The vector $\gamma'(0)$ belongs to the source of $Df(\gamma(0))$. Reversing the multiplication or evaluating $Df$ at $\gamma'(0)$ is not type-correct.

## The decisive estimate is hidden in the inner increment

If $f(a+h)-f(a)=Ah+r(h)$, then the input seen by $g$ is $k=Ah+r(h)$. Proving $k=O(\|h\|)$ is what turns the outer little-$o$ remainder into a little-$o$ remainder in $h$.

## Control the inner increment by the source norm

## Worked model before the checkpoint

From $k=Ah+r(h)$ and $r(h)=o(\|h\|)$, choose a neighborhood with $\|r(h)\|\le\|h\|$. Then $\|k\|\le(\|A\|+1)\|h\|$.

## Differential calculus · Chain rule

The finite-dimensional chain rule is $D(g\circ f)(x)=Dg(f(x))\circ Df(x)$.

Let $U\subset E$ and $V\subset F$ be open, let $f:U\to V$ be differentiable at $a$, and let $g:V\to G$ be differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is differentiable at $a$ and $$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$ Writing $f(a+h)=f(a)+Ah+r(h)$ makes the outer increment $k=Ah+r(h)=O(\|h\|_E)$; the outer remainder $s(k)=o(\|k\|_F)$ is therefore $o(\|h\|_E)$.

Let $f:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R^2$ be $f(x,y)=(x+y,x-y)$ and $g:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R$ be $g(u,v)=u^2+3v$. Compute $D(g\circ f)(1,2)$ as a composition of linear maps.

### Target

Compute a composite derivative as two typed linear maps and verify the result from the explicit composite expression.

### Strategy

Differentiate the inner map, evaluate the outer derivative at the inner value, compose in source-to-target order, and use direct coordinates only as a check.

### Hypotheses

Both maps are polynomial and hence Fréchet differentiable on their full Euclidean domains; the inner image is automatically in the outer domain.

### Complete solution

For $h=(h_1,h_2)$, $Df(1,2)h=(h_1+h_2,h_1-h_2)$. Since $f(1,2)=(3,-1)$, $$Dg(f(1,2))(k_1,k_2)=6k_1+3k_2.$$ Therefore $$D(g\circ f)(1,2)h=Dg(f(1,2))(Df(1,2)h)=9h_1+3h_2.$$ The coordinate check $g(f(x,y))=(x+y)^2+3(x-y)$ gives gradient $(2x+2y+3,2x+2y-3)=(9,3)$ at $(1,2)$.

### Boundary check

The outer derivative is evaluated at $f(1,2)$, not at $(1,2)$ unless those points happen to coincide. Composition order follows the types $E\to F\to G$.

Today releases the deferred Day 3 and Day 4 dossiers, then uses ordinary mathematical questions with immediate feedback. The final exposition rehearses theorem speech but is not labelled as a second oral examination.

For Week 59, Day 5 · Correct the sittings and synthesize the derivative theory, first revisit Differential calculus · Directional, Normed vector spaces · Definition, Topology · Path-connected sets, Vector-valued functions · Derivative, Jacobians. content.markdown:
Let $f(x,y)=(e^{x+y},x^2-y)$ and let $\gamma(t)=(t,t^2)$. Compute $(f\circ\gamma)'(0)$ and explain which hypotheses license the calculation.

### Target

Synthesize Fréchet differentiability, the Jacobian representation, and the curve form of the chain rule in one fully typed example.

### Strategy

State the open domains and differentiability facts, compute $Df(0,0)$ and $\gamma'(0)$, apply the linear map to the velocity, then check by direct differentiation.

### Hypotheses

The polynomial-exponential map is Fréchet differentiable on the open set $\mathbb R^2$, and the polynomial curve is differentiable with image in that domain.

### Complete solution

$f(0,0)=(1,0)$ and $$J_f(0,0)=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad \gamma'(0)=\binom10.$$ Therefore $(f\circ\gamma)'(0)=J_f(0,0)\gamma'(0)=(1,0)$. Directly, $f(\gamma(t))=(e^{t+t^2},t^2-t^2)=(e^{t+t^2},0)$, whose derivative at zero is $(1,0)$.

### Boundary check

This model uses differentiability of $f$, not merely directional derivatives. It also evaluates $Df$ at the curve point before applying it to the velocity.

lessons.summary: Define Differential calculus · Gradient. Represent a scalar derivative by a gradient only after fixing the Euclidean inner product, and distinguish intrinsic functionals from basis-dependent coordinate columns.

content.markdown:
# The derivative comes first; the gradient represents it

Let $U$ be an open subset of a finite-dimensional real normed space $E$, let $x\in U$, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ be differentiable at $x$. The derivative $Df(x)$ is intrinsically an element of the dual space $E^*$. When $E$ is equipped with a stated inner product, one and only one vector represents that functional.

## Why coordinates can mislead

In an orthonormal basis, the gradient column is the column of partial derivatives. In a non-orthonormal basis or under a weighted inner product, those two columns are generally different. The Riesz representation identity, not visual similarity, decides which vector is the gradient.

## Reactivate the derivative as a linear functional

**Complete analogous model before this checkpoint.** For $a(u,v)=u^2v$, expansion gives $a((u,v)+(s,t))-a(u,v)=(2uv)s+u^2t+o(\lVert(s,t)\rVert_2)$, so $Da(u,v)(s,t)=2uvs+u^2t$. The linear term is identified before any inner product is used.

content.markdown:
## Differential calculus · Gradient

In an inner-product space, the gradient is the vector satisfying $Df(x)h=\langle\nabla f(x),h\rangle$.

For a finite-dimensional Euclidean space $(E,\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle)$ and a differentiable $f:U\to\mathbb R$, the gradient at $x\in U$ is the unique vector $\nabla f(x)$ such that $Df(x)h=\langle\nabla f(x),h\rangle$ for every $h\in E$.

**Complete analogous model before this checkpoint.** In standard Euclidean $\mathbb R^2$, if $r(u,v)=u^2+3uv$, then $Dr(u,v)(a,b)=(2u+3v)a+3ub$. Therefore $\nabla r(u,v)=(2u+3v,3u)$. Cauchy–Schwarz yields $Dr(u,v)h\le\lVert\nabla r(u,v)\rVert_2$ for every unit $h$, with equality in the positive gradient direction when the gradient is nonzero.

On $E=\mathbb R^2$ with $\langle u,v\rangle_A=u_1v_1+4u_2v_2$, let $p(x,y)=x^2+xy$. Find the $A$-gradient of $p$ at $(1,2)$.

### Target

Use the Gram coefficients of the declared inner product to recover the representative of a known derivative functional.

### Strategy

Differentiate first, write an unknown representing vector, expand its inner product with an arbitrary increment, and equate coefficients.

### Hypotheses

The domain is the open set $\mathbb R^2$, the function is differentiable, and $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_A$ is a positive-definite inner product.

### Complete solution

$Dp(1,2)(h_1,h_2)=4h_1+h_2$. If $g=(g_1,g_2)$ represents this functional for $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_A$, then $g_1h_1+4g_2h_2=4h_1+h_2$ for every $h$. Hence $g_1=4$ and $g_2=1/4$, so $\nabla_Ap(1,2)=(4,1/4)$. The Euclidean coordinate vector $(4,1)$ represents the same derivative only for the standard inner product.

### Boundary check

The derivative is a linear functional before an inner product is chosen. Changing the inner product changes its representing gradient vector, although it does not change the functional itself.

## Separate derivative coefficients from gradient coordinates

**Complete analogous model before this checkpoint.** For the non-orthonormal basis $C=((1,1),(0,1))$ and $r(x,y)=2x-y$, the Euclidean gradient is $(2,-1)$, while its $C$-coordinates solve $(2,-1)=2(1,1)-3(0,1)$ and equal $(2,-3)$. The coefficients of $Dr$ on the basis vectors are $(1,-1)$, a different column.

content.markdown:
# Second order means a symmetric bilinear approximation

Let $U\subset\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ be of class $C^2$. The Hessian matrix $H_f(x)=(\partial_{ij}f(x))$ is symmetric by Schwarz's theorem. In the canonical Euclidean basis it represents the quadratic term $h\mapsto\langle H_f(x)h,h\rangle$.

## Why the remainder remains part of the formula

The linear and quadratic terms only classify local behavior when the omitted term is genuinely smaller than $\lVert h\rVert^2$. Writing $o(\lVert h\rVert^2)$ records the exact scale that licenses the later sign argument.

## Differentiate a gradient map before naming its Hessian

**Complete analogous model before this checkpoint.** For $r(u,v)=u^2v+v^2$, $\nabla r=(2uv,u^2+2v)$ and $D(\nabla r)(u,v)(a,b)=(2va+2ub,2ua+2b)$. Its canonical matrix is the symmetric Hessian $\begin{pmatrix}2v&2u\\2u&2\end{pmatrix}$.

## Differential calculus · Hessian

The Hessian represents the second derivative as a symmetric bilinear form when $f$ is twice continuously differentiable.

For $f\in C^2(U,\mathbb R)$, the Hessian at $x$ is the symmetric matrix $H_f(x)=(\partial_{ij}f(x))_{1\le i,j\le n}$. Taylor-Young states, as $h\to0$ with $x+h\in U$,

$$f(x+h)=f(x)+\langle\nabla f(x),h\rangle+\frac12\langle H_f(x)h,h\rangle+o(\lVert h\rVert_2^2).$$

**Complete analogous model before this checkpoint.** For $r(u,v)=u^3+uv^2$, $H_r(u,v)=\begin{pmatrix}6u&2v\\2v&2u\end{pmatrix}$, symmetric because $r$ is polynomial. At $(1,0)$, the quadratic Taylor term is $3a^2+b^2$ for increment $(a,b)$.

content.markdown:
For $f(x,y)=x^2+2xy+3y^2$, compute the Hessian and use it to classify the critical point at the origin.

### Target

Compute the complete symmetric Hessian and insert it into Taylor-Young at a fixed interior point.

### Strategy

Verify $C^2$ on the open domain, compute the gradient and all second partials, evaluate at the point, and retain the little-o remainder.

### Hypotheses

The domain is open, the function is $C^2$ on a neighborhood of the base point, and all vectors and matrices use the canonical Euclidean structure.

### Complete solution

The gradient is $\nabla f=(2x+2y,2x+6y)$, so the origin is a critical point. The constant Hessian is

$$H=\begin{pmatrix}2&2\\2&6\end{pmatrix}.$$

Its leading principal minors are $2>0$ and $\det H=12-4=8>0$. Sylvester's criterion therefore shows that $H$ is positive definite. The second-order test gives a strict local minimum at the origin. In fact, because the function is this positive-definite quadratic form, the minimum is global and has value $0$.

### Boundary check

A singular Hessian makes the second-order test inconclusive. For $g(x,y)=x^4+y^4$, the Hessian at the origin is zero, yet the origin is a strict minimum.

content.markdown:
# Interior, regularity, and sign are three separate checks

For an unconstrained local extremum of a differentiable function on an open set, every line through the point is available in both directions, forcing the derivative to vanish. At second order, positive semidefiniteness is necessary at a local minimum, while positive definiteness at a critical point is sufficient for a strict local minimum.

## Why a zero gradient is only the start

A critical point may be a minimum, a maximum, or neither. The Hessian resolves nondegenerate cases; when its quadratic form has a zero direction, higher-order terms decide and the second-order test must stop without guessing.

## Expose the domain-boundary exception

**Complete analogous model before this checkpoint.** The function $r(t)=-t$ on the constrained domain $(-\infty,0]$ has a local minimum at the boundary point $0$, but $r'(0)=-1$. The missing positive direction prevents the two-sided line argument.

content.markdown:
## Differential calculus · Optimization

At an interior differentiable local extremum, the derivative vanishes; second-order information then classifies nondegenerate critical points.

Let $U$ be open in a finite-dimensional normed space and let $a\in U$ be an interior local minimum of a function differentiable at $a$. For each $v$, openness gives $a+tv\in U$ for small positive and negative $t$. The one-variable function $\varphi_v(t)=f(a+tv)$ has a local minimum at zero, so $\varphi_v'(0)=Df(a)v=0$. Thus $Df(a)=0$ and, in Euclidean space, $\nabla f(a)=0$.

**Complete analogous model before this checkpoint.** If a differentiable $r:(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)\to\mathbb R$ has a local minimum at zero, then the right difference quotients are nonnegative and the left quotients are nonpositive. Their common limit is therefore zero, so $r'(0)=0$.

On $\mathbb R^2$, let $p(s,t)=s^2+2st+5t^2$. Prove from the second-order criterion that the origin is a strict local minimum.

### Target

Turn a positive-definite Hessian at an interior critical point into a strict quadratic lower bound through Taylor-Young.

### Strategy

Verify the critical-point equation, certify positive definiteness of the symmetric Hessian, and dominate the little-o remainder by part of the positive quadratic term.

### Hypotheses

The domain is open, the base point is interior, the function is $C^2$ nearby, the gradient vanishes, and the Euclidean Hessian is symmetric positive definite.

### Complete solution

$p$ is $C^2$ on the open set $\mathbb R^2$, $\nabla p(0,0)=0$, and $H_p=\begin{pmatrix}2&2\\2&10\end{pmatrix}$. The leading principal minors are $2>0$ and $20-4=16>0$, so the symmetric Hessian is positive definite. Taylor's formula is exact here: $p(h)=\tfrac12\langle H_ph,h\rangle$. Positive definiteness therefore gives $p(h)>p(0)$ for every sufficiently small nonzero $h$; the origin is a strict local minimum.

### Boundary check

The conclusion uses an interior critical point and a positive-definite Hessian. Positive semidefiniteness alone would not supply the required strict quadratic lower bound.

## Resolve two singular-Hessian cases beyond second order

**Complete analogous model before this checkpoint.** Both $u^6$ and $u^3$ have zero first and second derivative at zero. Continue with $F(x,y)=e^x+e^y+e^{-x-y}$ on the open set $\mathbb R^2$.

### Target

Part II · solve the stationary equations exactly

### Strategy

Compute $DF$ and $\nabla F$, solve $\nabla F=0$ without logarithmic ambiguity, and prove that the origin is the only critical point.

### Hypotheses

Continue with $F(x,y)=e^x+e^y+e^{-x-y}$ on the open set $\mathbb R^2$.

### Complete solution

$\nabla F=(e^x-e^{-x-y},e^y-e^{-x-y})$. At a critical point, $e^x=e^y=e^{-x-y}$. Injectivity of the real exponential gives $x=y$ and $x=-x-y$. Thus $x=y=0$. Conversely the gradient vanishes at the origin, so it is the unique critical point.

### Boundary check

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: $F(0,0)=3$, so $K$ is nonempty. It is closed because $F$ is continuous. If $(x,y)\in K$, then $e^x,e^y,e^{-x-y}\le3$, hence $x,y\le\log3$ and $x+y\ge-\log3$. activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Take the feasible point $(1,0)$ and set $M=F(1,0)$. The bounds from Part I, with $M$ in place of $3$, show that $\{F\le M\}$ is compact; its intersection with the closed nonempty set $C$ is compact, and outside it $F>M$, so a constrained minimum exists. For fixed $x\ge1$, the derivative in $y$ is $e^y-e^{-x-y}$ and the second derivative is positive, so the unique minimizing $y$ is $-x/2$. The reduced function is $\phi(x)=e^x+2e^{-x/2}$, with $\phi'(x)=e^x-e^{-x/2}>0$ for $x\ge1$. Hence the unique constrained minimizer is $(1,-1/2)$. There $\partial_yF=0$ but $\partial_xF=e-e^{-1/2}>0$; the active boundary prevents movement toward smaller $x$, so the unconstrained zero-gradient theorem does not apply.

Let $G(u,v)=u^4+v^2-2u^2$ on $\mathbb R^2$. Classify every critical point and determine the global minima.

### Target

Model a complete board exposition that separates existence, critical-point algebra, Hessian classification, and the global conclusion.

### Strategy

Use coercivity for existence, solve the decoupled gradient equations, calculate the Hessian at each candidate, and compare the exact values at the resulting local minima.

### Hypotheses

$G$ is $C^2$ on the open Euclidean space $\mathbb R^2$. Because $G(u,v)\to+\infty$ as $\lVert(u,v)\rVert_2\to\infty$, compact sublevels give a global minimizer.

### Complete solution

$\nabla G=(4u^3-4u,2v)$, so the critical points are $(0,0)$ and $(\pm1,0)$. The Hessian is $\operatorname{diag}(12u^2-4,2)$. At the origin it is indefinite, so the origin is a saddle. At $(\pm1,0)$ it is $\operatorname{diag}(8,2)$, positive definite, so both are strict local minima. Coercivity gives global existence, and $G(\pm1,0)=-1<G(0,0)=0$; since every global minimizer is critical, the two points $(\pm1,0)$ are exactly the global minimizers.

### Boundary check

The Hessian labels the isolated candidates locally. Coercivity is the separate existence argument that permits the final global comparison; a local classification alone would not prove attainment on $\mathbb R^2$.

activities.promptMarkdown:

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: $J$ is $C^2$ on open $\mathbb R^2$ and is coercive because $2|xy|\le x^2+y^2$ while the quartic terms dominate the quadratic terms; hence a compact sublevel argument gives a global minimizer. The critical equations are $4x^3-2y=0$ and $4y^3-2x=0$. They give $(0,0)$ or, for nonzero coordinates, $y=2x^3$ and $x=2y^3$, whence $x^8=1/16$ and the sign equations force $(x,y)=(1/\sqrt2,1/\sqrt2)$ or $(-1/\sqrt2,-1/\sqrt2)$. The symmetric Hessian is $H_J=\begin{pmatrix}12x^2&-2\\-2&12y^2\end{pmatrix}$. At the origin its determinant is $-4$, so the point is a saddle. At either nonzero critical point, $H_J=\begin{pmatrix}6&-2\\-2&6\end{pmatrix}$ has leading minors $6$ and $32$, so each is a strict local minimum. A global minimizer exists and must be critical; the saddle cannot be one, so the two strict minima are exactly the global minimizers. Their common value is $1/4+1/4-1=-1/2$.
